meta.note: RAW machine output. Verification pass aborted on an API session limit (207/240 agents failed); only 19 adversarial verdicts completed. Treat unverified findings as leads.

raw_findings.title: Client accepts the PBKDF2 iteration count from the /challenge response with no floor — a MITM or hostile server can force 1 iteration
raw_findings.description: `/challenge` echoes the account's pinned PBKDF2 count back to the client, and the client uses that number verbatim to derive the app key. The `?? 100_000` only supplies a default when the field is ABSENT; any present numeric value is used as-is. `1 ?? 100_000` evaluates to `1`. The server-side floor added for audit F3 (`validIterations`, src/server/routes.ts:96-100) is enforced ONLY on `/register` — it is never applied to the value the client reads back on `/challenge`, and the client performs no validation of its own (no comparison against `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[this.config.securityLevel]`, no minimum, no integer check). The same unchecked pattern appears on the re-auth path at src/client/authClient.ts:144 (`getPbkdf2Iterations() ?? 100_000`, reading a localStorage value written from the same untrusted response). Because the client then transmits `signAuthChallenge(appKey, challenge)` to the server, the downgraded derivation is converted into a transmitted, offline-verifiable oracle for the user's passkey.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An active network attacker (or the app operator / a compromised edge, all in scope per the threat model) intercepts the POST to `/challenge` for victim@example.com and rewrites the JSON body to `{"challenge":"<attacker-chosen 64 hex>","pbkdf2Iterations":1}`. The client computes appKey = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256(passkey, SHA-256(appId:email), c=1) and POSTs `signature = ed25519_sign(SHA-256("ttc-auth-v1:"+appKey), authLoginMessage(challenge))`. The attacker captures that signature. Offline, for each candidate passkey they run ONE HMAC-SHA256 (instead of 600,000), derive the auth keypair, and check the signature — a full dictionary/rules attack at essentially zero cost. Once the passkey is recovered they re-derive the real appKey at 600k and decrypt every `encryptedSecret` in the victim's record (obtainable from the same MITM position, or from any DB read). The victim sees only a failed login, indistinguishable from a network error, and the attack is repeatable on every login attempt.
raw_findings.recommendation: Apply the same `validIterations` band CLIENT-side to any iteration count that arrives over the wire or out of localStorage: reject (do not silently clamp) anything that is not an integer in [100_000, 1_000_000], and additionally refuse to derive below `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[config.securityLevel]` unless the account is explicitly flagged legacy. Export `PBKDF2_MIN`/`PBKDF2_MAX` from core/config.ts so the server and client share one definition, and add a test asserting `loginWithEmail` throws when `/challenge` returns `pbkdf2Iterations: 1`.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rn "pbkdf2Iterations|PBKDF2_ITERATIONS|securityLevel" src tests` and read tests/audit-zai-fixes.test.ts, tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts ("F3 — Server trusts client-supplied pbkdf2Iterations with no floor") and tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts in full. Every F3 test posts to `/register` and asserts a 400 from the SERVER. `grep -rn "PBKDF2_MIN|Math.max|floor" tests src/client` returns no client-side floor anywhere. No test drives `loginWithEmail`/`deriveAppKey` against a malicious `/challenge` response.

raw_findings.title: appKeyToBytes silently maps non-hex characters to 0x00 and accepts 16/24-byte keys — a non-hex 64-char appKey yields an all-zero AES key
raw_findings.description: `appKeyToBytes` does `parseInt(pair, 16)` with no charset or length validation. `parseInt("zz",16)` is NaN, and assigning NaN into a `Uint8Array` stores 0. A 64-character non-hex string therefore produces 32 zero bytes — a fully predictable AES-256 key — and `encryptSecret` succeeds without any error. Length is equally unvalidated: `new ArrayBuffer(appKey.length / 2)` plus WebCrypto's acceptance of 16/24/32-byte AES keys means a 32-hex-char appKey silently becomes AES-128 despite every doc comment claiming AES-256-GCM (crypto.ts:3, :69). I verified all three behaviours by executing the exact function body under Node's WebCrypto. The codebase already knows this pattern is dangerous and guards against it in the signature path — src/server/signature.ts:10-13 explicitly rejects non-hex with the comment "parseInt('GG',16) yields NaN and silently coerces to a 0 byte" — but the identical guard is missing on the KEY-derivation path, where the consequence is far worse than a failed verify. `encryptSecret`, `decryptSecret` and `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` are all public API (`src/core/index.ts` does `export * from "./crypto.js"`, reachable as `@tetrac/login-sdk/core`), and `armAppKey(appKey: string)` is exported from `/client` with no validation either.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator building a custom flow (or migrating from another SDK) calls the exported helper as `encryptSecret(privateKeyHex, userPassword)` or `armAppKey(userPassword)` — a natural reading of a function whose parameter is named `appKey` and typed `string`. With a 32-character passphrase such as "correct-horse-battery-staple-abc", appKeyToBytes yields 0c00ec0000000eba000e00000a00f6bc: a 16-byte AES-128 key of which 10 bytes are zero (~48 bits of real entropy), and the call succeeds silently with no exception, no warning, and correct-looking round-trip decryption. Every wallet in that deployment is then encrypted under a trivially brute-forceable key, and an attacker who reads the database (explicitly in scope) recovers every private key. In the degenerate case of a 64-character non-hex secret the key is all zeros and the attacker needs no brute force at all.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add the same explicit guard `if (!/^[0-9a-f]{64}$/i.test(appKey)) throw new Error("Invalid appKey: expected 64 hex characters")` at the top of `appKeyToBytes` (and mirror it in `armAppKey`), so a malformed or low-entropy key fails loudly at import instead of producing a working-but-worthless cipher. Reuse the existing HEX64_RE shape. Add a test asserting `encryptSecret("x", "z".repeat(64))` and `encryptSecret("x", "ab".repeat(16))` both reject.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "all-zero|non-hex|appKeyToBytes|AES-128|invalid appKey" tests/crypto.test.ts tests/ciphertext-tampering.test.ts tests/audit-crypto.test.ts` returns nothing. tests/audit-crypto.test.ts only exercises well-formed 64-hex keys (`"ab".repeat(32)`), and tests/crypto.test.ts:39 comments "AES-GCM keys are 32 raw bytes (64 hex), so use real derived keys here" — i.e. the tests deliberately avoid the malformed case rather than covering it.

raw_findings.title: encryptSecret uses no AES-GCM additionalData, so a wallet ciphertext is not bound to its chain/role/publicKey metadata
raw_findings.description: `encryptSecret` calls `crypto.subtle.encrypt({ name: "AES-GCM", iv }, ...)` with no `additionalData`. The `EncryptedWallet` metadata that travels alongside the ciphertext — `chain`, `role`, and crucially `publicKey` — is therefore completely unauthenticated: it is plain server-supplied JSON returned by `/user-data`. The GCM auth tag proves only "this ciphertext was produced under this appKey", not "this ciphertext belongs to THIS wallet entry". Nothing downstream re-derives the address from the decrypted secret and compares it: `useSolanaSigner` takes the advertised address straight from `wallet.publicKey` (line 43) and never checks it against `Keypair.fromSecretKey(hexToBytes(secret)).publicKey`. Since one user's whole bundle is encrypted under one appKey, entries within a record are freely interchangeable and the metadata is freely rewritable.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A hostile app operator (explicitly in the threat model) — or anyone with DB write access via a leaked replica credential — edits the stored user record and replaces the `publicKey` field of the solana/funds `EncryptedWallet` entry with an address they control, leaving `encryptedSecret` untouched. On the next `/user-data` fetch the client decrypts successfully (the tag still validates — the ciphertext is unmodified), and `useActiveWallet()`/`useSolanaSigner().publicKey` surface the ATTACKER's address as the user's Solana funds address. Any app rendering that as a deposit/receive address sends the user's incoming funds to the attacker, with no crypto error at any point. A second variant swaps the ciphertexts of the `funds` and `signing` roles, so the user signs a "session-wallet" transaction with their funds key.
raw_findings.recommendation: Bind the context into the AEAD: add an `aad` parameter to `encryptSecret`/`decryptSecret` and pass `additionalData = utf8(`${appId}|${userPublicKey}|${chain}|${role}|${walletPublicKey}`)`, so any metadata rewrite or cross-entry swap fails the tag check. Version the ciphertext prefix so existing `iv:ct` blobs still decrypt. As cheap defence-in-depth independent of the format change, have `useSolanaSigner`/`toSolanaKeypair` assert `Keypair.fromSecretKey(...).publicKey.toBase58() === wallet.publicKey` and throw on mismatch.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "additionalData|AAD|aad" src tests` returns zero hits — the concept appears nowhere in the codebase or the test suite. tests/ciphertext-tampering.test.ts and tests/audit-crypto.test.ts ("H1 RESOLVED") only cover bitflips WITHIN the ciphertext and wrong-key rejection; neither touches metadata rewriting or cross-entry swapping. src/react/useActiveWallet.ts:26-30 shows the team already reasoned about a "WRONG Solana address ... deposit address" hazard for a different cause, but no code authenticates the address field.

raw_findings.title: Web3 app key is SHA-256 of a signature over a publicly computable constant — one coerced signature is a permanent, unrotatable wallet compromise
raw_findings.description: For wallet accounts the encryption key is `SHA-256(hex(sign(walletAppKeyMessage(appId))))`. The preimage is a fixed string that anyone can compute: `WALLET_APP_KEY_MESSAGE + "\n\nApp: " + appId`, where `appId` is public (it ships in the client bundle and rides in the body of every request — src/client/authClient.ts:206). Solana ed25519 signing is deterministic, so the same wallet always produces the same signature and therefore the same app key. The consequences: (a) any site that persuades the user to sign that one exact string obtains the app key outright, with no server interaction; (b) the key can never be rotated — there is no counter, epoch, or salt in the message, so a user who ever signs it on a hostile page has no recovery path short of migrating to a new wallet; (c) the compromise is completely invisible server-side. The appId domain separation (CRYPTO-2/H4) blocks key reuse BETWEEN SDK deployments but provides no protection against a page that simply knows the target appId. The only mitigation is the advisory text "Only sign this on a site you trust" inside the message.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker reads the target app's public bundle to learn `appId = "myapp.example"`, then stands up a lookalike page. The page prompts the connected Phantom/Solflare wallet for two signatures: first over `walletLoginMessage(challenge)` (using a challenge it fetched from the real `/challenge` endpoint) and second over `walletAppKeyMessage("myapp.example")`. Signature 1 gives the attacker a valid `/login-wallet` credential — a real session, from which `/user-data` returns the victim's `EncryptedWallet[]`. Signature 2, SHA-256'd, IS the victim's app key, which decrypts every one of those ciphertexts. The attacker walks away with the plaintext private keys of all SDK-generated Solana and EVM wallets, permanently: the victim cannot rotate the app key without abandoning the wallet, and re-signing the same message on the legitimate app reproduces the same compromised key forever.
raw_findings.recommendation: This is an inherent property of signature-derived keys, so treat it as a documented, versioned risk rather than a silent one: (1) put an explicit, prominent warning in SECURITY.md/README (both are currently 0 bytes) that signing this string anywhere is equivalent to handing over the wallet; (2) add a rotation escape hatch by versioning the message (`App: ${appId} v${keyEpoch}`) and persisting `keyEpoch` on `UserData`, so a user who suspects a coerced signature can re-encrypt their bundle under a new epoch; (3) steer wallet users toward `enableBiometricUnlock`, which already wraps the app key rather than deriving it from a replayable signature.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/audit-crypto.test.ts "H4 RESOLVED — the wallet-app-key message is domain-bound by appId" in full: every assertion is about appId-based separation between two SDK apps (`walletAppKeyMessage("appA") !== walletAppKeyMessage("appB")`). No test, comment, or doc addresses a third-party page that knows the appId. `grep -rln "phish" docs PRD *.md src tests` returns nothing; audits/ is an empty directory; README.md and SECURITY.md are both 0 bytes.

raw_findings.title: No passkey entropy floor anywhere, and the strong-passkey generator is opt-in and hidden by default
raw_findings.description: `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` accepts any string, including "" and "1", with no minimum length or entropy check, and neither `AuthClient.registerWithEmail` nor the `/register` route imposes one (the server never sees the passkey, so only the client can). The bundled UI's only gate is `disabled={busy || !email || !passkey}` — non-empty. The CSPRNG generator in src/ui/passkey.ts is well built (128-bit floor, unbiased base58) but is rendered only when the integrator passes the `passkeyGenerator` prop: `LoginPanel` supplies no default for it, and `EmailMethod` returns `null` when it is falsy, so out of the box a user is presented with a bare text field. This is the multiplier on every offline-attack path: the server stores `authPublicKey = ed25519_pub(SHA-256("ttc-auth-v1:"+appKey))` alongside the wallet ciphertexts, and both are offline verifiers for the passkey given the (public) salt inputs `appId` and `email`.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A user signs up on an integration that did not opt into `passkeyGenerator` and types "hunter2". An attacker who reads the database (leaked backup, replica, world-readable Supabase `public` schema — all in scope) obtains `email`, `appId`, `pbkdf2Iterations`, `authPublicKey`, and `encryptedSecret`. They compute salt = SHA-256(`${appId}:${email}`) and run a wordlist through PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at the pinned 600k, checking each candidate against `authPublicKey` (one SHA-256 + one ed25519 keygen per guess). At ~600k iterations a commodity GPU still clears a 10^8-entry wordlist in days for a single high-value target; a 128-bit generated passkey is infeasible at any budget. On a hit, the attacker decrypts every wallet in the record. Chained with the iteration-downgrade finding above, the PBKDF2 work factor drops to 1 and even a large wordlist falls in seconds.
raw_findings.recommendation: Enforce a minimum in `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` (reject shorter than ~12 characters) so no code path can mint an app key from a trivial secret, default `passkeyGenerator` to `true` in `LoginPanel` so the CSPRNG path is the out-of-the-box experience, and surface a strength meter or a hard client-side minimum in `EmailMethod`. Also correct the comment at src/server/routes.ts:366 ("The server holds no passkey-derived secret") — `authPublicKey` is a passkey-derived value that functions as an offline verifier; the honest statement is that the server holds no value that is useful WITHOUT a successful PBKDF2 guess.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "passkey.length|minLength|too short|weak passkey" src tests` returns nothing. Read src/ui/passkey.ts and tests/ui-login-panel-ux.test.tsx:121 — the tests verify the generator produces >=16 bytes WHEN INVOKED, but nothing asserts it is on by default or that a weak hand-typed passkey is rejected. tests/audit-crypto.test.ts "C1 RESOLVED" asserts only `authPub !== appKey`, not that it is non-verifying.

raw_findings.title: deriveAppKeyFromPasskey defaults to 100k iterations and appId "ttc" on a public API surface
raw_findings.description: The exported `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` defaults `iterations = 100_000` (the level-1 count the config itself documents as "below OWASP 2023, legacy/compat only") and `appId = "ttc"` (which config.ts:66 states "provides NO cross-app isolation"). `src/core/index.ts` re-exports everything from crypto.js, so `@tetrac/login-sdk/core` and the package root both expose this two-argument form. The console.warn nudge for a default appId exists only in the `AuthClient` constructor (src/client/authClient.ts:123-129) and never fires for direct calls to the core helper. The result is that the least-effort call — `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(passkey, email)` — produces the weakest possible key, silently, while the safe call requires knowing to pass two extra arguments.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator writing a custom (non-AuthClient) registration flow, or a migration/recovery script, calls `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(passkey, email)`. Every wallet in that deployment is encrypted at 100k iterations under the shared "ttc" domain, with no warning emitted. A database-read attacker gets a 6x cheaper offline attack than the configured securityLevel 2 promised, and — because the salt is `SHA-256("ttc:" + email)` — a single precomputed table works against every deployment that made the same mistake, defeating CRYPTO-2 entirely.
raw_findings.recommendation: Make `iterations` and `appId` required parameters (no defaults) so the compiler forces an explicit, auditable choice; or default `iterations` to `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[2]` (600k) to match `DEFAULT_CONFIG.securityLevel` and emit the same appId console.warn from the helper itself.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:33 itself calls the two-argument form (`deriveAppKeyFromPasskey("letmein", "victim@example.com")`), demonstrating the default is the path of least resistance even inside the repo. `grep -rn "securityLevel" src` shows `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[this.config.securityLevel]` is plumbed only through AuthClient (authClient.ts:231), never into the core helper's default.

raw_findings.title: decryptSecret decodes base64url outside its try block, so malformed input escapes as a raw DOMException instead of the uniform error
raw_findings.description: `decryptSecret` deliberately normalizes crypto failures to one message ("Decryption failed: wrong key or corrupted ciphertext") to avoid distinguishing wrong-key from tampering, but the two `b64urlDecode` calls sit ABOVE the try block. `atob` throws a DOMException named `InvalidCharacterError` on any non-base64 character or on a length ≡ 1 (mod 4), so structurally-invalid input surfaces a different error name, message, and stack than cryptographically-invalid input. Callers that funnel this into a UI or log therefore get a distinguishable signal. (The `parts.length !== 2` check itself is sound — b64url output here contains only A-Za-z0-9-_ with padding stripped at crypto.ts:53, so ":" can never appear inside either component and any extra colon correctly rejects.)
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator writes `catch (e) { toast(e.message) }` around a reveal/unlock path fed by server-supplied `encryptedSecret`. A hostile server or a DB-write attacker can then distinguish, per stored blob, "this is not valid base64" from "this is valid base64 that did not authenticate" — confirming whether a targeted record was structurally modified versus key-mismatched. Low value on its own, but it breaks the uniform-error property the function is explicitly written to provide, and the same shape recurs in `unlock()`/`revealSecret()`, which wrap only `decryptWalletSecret` failures into "Re-authentication failed".
raw_findings.recommendation: Move the two `b64urlDecode` calls (and `importAesGcmKey`) inside the try, so every failure mode — malformed base64, bad IV length, rejected key import, tag mismatch — exits through the single "Decryption failed: wrong key or corrupted ciphertext" path. Optionally also validate `iv.length === 12` before calling decrypt.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/ciphertext-tampering.test.ts and tests/audit-crypto.test.ts "H1 RESOLVED": both use `rejects.toThrow()` with no message/type assertion, and both feed only well-formed base64url (a single character substituted at body[0], which stays in-alphabet). `grep -rn "b64url|malformed ciphertext" tests` finds no test for invalid-alphabet or bad-length input.

raw_findings.title: AES-256-GCM used for password-derived wallet encryption is not key-committing; unlock(creds, validateWith) is a potential partitioning oracle
raw_findings.description: AES-GCM offers no key commitment: a ciphertext can be crafted so that it decrypts successfully under many distinct keys (Len/Grubbs/Ristenpart, "Partitioning Oracle Attacks", USENIX 2021). That property matters specifically because the key here is password-derived, and because `AuthClient.unlock` deliberately uses "does this ciphertext decrypt" as its credential test on a ciphertext the caller supplies — in practice one fetched from the server via `/user-data`. There is no AAD, no explicit commitment tag, and no independent verifier bound to the appKey. This is a hardening gap rather than a demonstrated exploit: the failure branch of `unlock` throws locally and does not itself report back to the server, so a hostile operator would need an application-level side channel (a retry POST, an error report, an observable timing difference) to read the oracle bit.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A hostile app operator serves, as the user's `EncryptedWallet.encryptedSecret`, a multi-key GCM ciphertext constructed to authenticate under a chosen set of ~2^k candidate app keys (each corresponding to a candidate passkey at the account's pinned iteration count). Each `unlock(creds, validateWith)` the user performs then reveals, in one interaction, whether the true passkey lies in that set — replacing per-guess PBKDF2 work with a set-membership test and shrinking the search by k bits per unlock, provided the operator can observe success/failure (e.g. the app auto-retries against the server on the failure branch, or reports the exception to telemetry).
raw_findings.recommendation: Validate credentials against a value the client can bind independently rather than against arbitrary server-supplied ciphertext: `deriveAuthPublicKey(appKey)` is already computed and stored, so `unlock` can compare it (via the existing `timingSafeEqual`) to `user.authPublicKey` instead of trial-decrypting. If ciphertext-based validation is kept, add a key commitment — prepend `SHA-256("ttc-commit-v1:" + appKey)` to the blob, or adopt the AAD from the context-binding finding, both of which make multi-key ciphertexts infeasible.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "commit|partitioning" src tests` matches only SQL transaction `commit()` calls in src/storage/sql/*. No test or comment in tests/audit-crypto.test.ts, tests/ciphertext-tampering.test.ts, or tests/audit-client-vault.test.ts references key commitment, multi-key ciphertexts, or partitioning oracles.

raw_findings.title: SQLite driver: concurrent transaction() calls collapse into one shared transaction — a "successful" registration's writes get silently rolled back
raw_findings.description: `sqliteDriver` tracks transaction nesting with a single module-closure counter `depth` and treats *any* re-entrant call as an already-open nested transaction. But `fn` is `async`: `SqlAuthStore.putUser` awaits two statements inside `driver.transaction(...)`, and that `await` is a yield point. A second, unrelated `putUser` that arrives while the first is suspended observes `depth > 0` and returns `fn(driver)` with NO `BEGIN` of its own — its statements execute inside the *first* request's transaction. The two requests are now one atomic unit. If request A fails anywhere inside its transaction, the `ROLLBACK` discards request B's rows too, even though B's promise already resolved successfully and the route already returned 200 with a session token. I confirmed this by running the driver's exact code against better-sqlite3.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Two registrations overlap on a self-hosted SQLite deployment. Registration A hits any error inside its transaction (SQLITE_FULL, SQLITE_BUSY on a WAL file with a second handle such as a sweeper cron or a backup, a constraint failure). Registration B — a completely unrelated user — receives HTTP 200, a session token, and a client that now believes its client-side-generated wallet has been persisted. The `ttc_users` row holding that user's ONLY copy of the encrypted wallet blob was rolled back. Because the SDK is non-custodial and the server holds the sole copy of the ciphertext, the wallet is unrecoverable. Repro output from the verbatim driver code: `A failed: NOT NULL constraint failed` / `B ok` / `rows now: []`.
raw_findings.recommendation: Serialize `transaction()` on a promise chain (an async mutex) rather than counting depth — better-sqlite3 has one connection, so overlapping logical transactions must queue, not merge. Reserve the `depth > 0` passthrough for genuinely lexically-nested calls by threading a per-transaction driver object (as `pgDriver`/`mysqlDriver` do with their `tx` object) instead of handing back the shared `driver`.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for `depth`, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, `interleav`, `concurrent` — no test touches sqliteDriver's nesting. tests/sql-conformance-sqlite.test.ts runs the conformance suite, whose only concurrent case (`concurrent putUser for one email under two apps`, src/storage/conformance.ts:309 `await Promise.all([store.putUser(a), store.putUser(b)])`) *exercises* this path but asserts only that both writes land — it never makes one transaction fail, so the rollback-of-a-bystander failure mode is untested. tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts covers the KV path, not SQL.

raw_findings.title: SQLite driver: `depth` is incremented outside the try/finally, so one failed BEGIN permanently disables transactions for the process lifetime
raw_findings.description: `depth++` runs before `db.exec("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")`, and that `exec` sits OUTSIDE the `try { … } finally { depth--; }` block. If `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` throws — SQLITE_BUSY after the busy timeout when another connection/process holds the write lock, or "cannot start a transaction within a transaction" — the counter is never decremented. `depth` is then permanently `1`, so every subsequent `transaction()` call for the rest of the process's life takes the `if (depth > 0) return fn(driver)` branch and runs with NO BEGIN, NO COMMIT and NO ROLLBACK. The engine's central claim for `putUser` — "a crash between the two writes cannot leave an account whose email doesn't resolve" (engine.ts:83-86) — is silently false from that moment on, with no error, no log, and nothing pointing at the cause. Confirmed by running the verbatim driver code: after one failed BEGIN, `depth leaked to: 1`, and a subsequent transaction that throws leaves its row committed (`rows that should have been rolled back: [ { k: 'x' } ]`).
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A self-hosted SQLite deployment takes one transient SQLITE_BUSY (a `sqlite3` CLI session, a `.backup`, or a separate sweeper process holding the write lock past better-sqlite3's 5s busy timeout). From then on `putUser` is non-atomic forever. Any later failure between the `ttc_users` INSERT and the `ttc_email_index` INSERT — including a process kill/redeploy — leaves an account whose email never resolves. `getPublicKeyByEmail` returns null, `loginWithEmail` cannot find the account, and the client re-registers with a fresh `Keypair.generate()` publicKey, so the user is permanently locked out of the encrypted wallets stored under the old record.
raw_findings.recommendation: Move `db.exec("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")` inside the `try`, or increment `depth` only after BEGIN succeeds: `db.exec("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); depth++; try { … } finally { depth--; }`. Add a conformance case that forces BEGIN to fail once and then asserts a later failing transaction still rolls back.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for `depth`, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, `ROLLBACK`, `sqliteDriver` — tests/sql-conformance-sqlite.test.ts only ever constructs a fresh in-memory DB per case and never induces a BEGIN failure. No audit-*.test.ts references the driver's transaction bookkeeping.

raw_findings.title: Rate limiter fails OPEN when the RETURNING read yields no row (`Number(rows[0]?.count ?? 1)`)
raw_findings.description: On the `supportsReturning` path (Postgres and SQLite), `hitRateLimit` derives its whole decision from `Number(rows[0]?.count ?? 1)`. When the driver returns a row shape without a `count` field — or no rows at all — the engine does not error; it defaults to a count of **1**, which yields `{ allowed: true, remaining: maxAttempts - 1 }` no matter how many hits the row actually holds. This directly contradicts the store contract in src/storage/store.ts:87-90 ("ERRORS FAIL CLOSED … An implementation that catches a failure and returns `{allowed: true}` from `hitRateLimit` … has silently switched off a security control") and the engine's own header ("fail closed → no try/catch"). It is reachable two ways: (a) through the shipped SQLite driver, whose blanket `catch` re-runs the statement via `.run()` and returns `[{ affected: n }]` — I verified `.run()` succeeds on an `INSERT … ON CONFLICT … RETURNING count` statement in better-sqlite3 and that the engine then computes `1`; (b) through any third-party `SqlDriver`, since the port is documented as returning an "empty array for writes" (types.ts:28) — a driver author who classifies INSERT as a write returns `[]`, and the rate limiter is permanently disabled while every test that only checks `allowed === true` passes.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A custom `SqlDriver` (the SDK's advertised extension point) returns `[]` for INSERT statements. `createSqlAuthStore` boots clean — preflight never exercises `hitRateLimit`. Every call now returns `allowed: true, remaining: maxAttempts - 1`, so `/login`, `/register`, `/challenge` and `/search` have no throttle at all: an attacker enumerates registered accounts via `searchWallet` and floods `/challenge` unbounded. On the shipped SQLite driver, the same fail-open triggers on any transient `.all()` error (SQLITE_BUSY/LOCKED) — the counter is double-incremented and the request is nonetheless allowed.
raw_findings.recommendation: Throw instead of defaulting: `const raw = rows[0]?.count; if (raw == null) throw new Error("[tetrac] hitRateLimit: driver returned no count for INSERT…RETURNING — refusing to fail open"); count = Number(raw);`. Apply the same to the MySQL branch (`Number(rows[0]?.count ?? 1)`, engine.ts:278). Add a conformance case with a driver that returns `[]` and assert `hitRateLimit` rejects.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for `hitRateLimit`, `remaining`, `allowed` and read tests/rate-limit-self-extend.test.ts and tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts in full — both target the KV/`incr` path and the permanent-lockout bug (the opposite failure direction). src/storage/conformance.ts:415 asserts `r.allowed` is *true* for injection payloads, which this bug would satisfy rather than catch. tests/storage-conformance-negative.test.ts was checked for a fail-open driver case; it does not cover the SQL engine's RETURNING shape.

raw_findings.title: SQLite driver `query()` swallows every error from `.all()` and blindly re-executes the statement with `.run()`
raw_findings.description: The bare `catch { … }` is meant to handle only better-sqlite3's "this statement does not return data" TypeError, but it catches everything: SQLITE_BUSY, SQLITE_LOCKED, SQLITE_CONSTRAINT, SQLITE_FULL, interrupts. On any of those it re-executes the same statement via `.run()`. For a statement that *does* return data (every `RETURNING` statement the engine emits), `.all()` has already executed it, so the retry executes it a **second** time and discards the returned rows in favour of `[{ affected: n }]`. I verified against better-sqlite3 that `.run()` succeeds on an `INSERT … ON CONFLICT … RETURNING count` statement, that it increments the counter a second time, and that the resulting row shape carries no `count`.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Under write contention on a file-backed SQLite deployment, `hitRateLimit`'s `INSERT … RETURNING count` throws SQLITE_BUSY inside `.all()` (possibly after partially executing). The driver silently retries with `.run()`, which now succeeds: the counter is incremented twice and the driver hands the engine `[{ affected: 1 }]`, which engine.ts:267 turns into `count = 1` → request ALLOWED regardless of the real count. The same catch also masks SQLITE_FULL/SQLITE_CORRUPT on `takeChallenge`'s `DELETE … RETURNING challenge`: the challenge row is deleted by the retry but `challenge` is absent from the returned shape, so the engine returns null and a legitimate login is rejected while its single-use challenge is consumed.
raw_findings.recommendation: Decide up front instead of catching: better-sqlite3 exposes `stmt.reader` — use `return stmt.reader ? (stmt.all(...params) as T[]) : [{ affected: stmt.run(...params).changes }]`. Never retry a statement that may already have executed; let real engine errors propagate (the file header's own rule: "fail closed → no try/catch. Errors propagate.").
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for `stmt.all`, `sqliteDriver`, `affected`, `reader` — nothing tests the driver's error path. tests/sql-conformance-sqlite.test.ts drives only happy-path statements against `:memory:`, where neither BUSY nor FULL can occur.

raw_findings.title: Postgres `schema` option is interpolated raw into every statement and into the generated DDL — no identifier validation or quoting
raw_findings.description: `postgresDialect({ schema })` concatenates the caller's string directly into all five fully-qualified table names, into `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS ${schema}` in `ddl()`, and thereby into every SELECT/INSERT/DELETE the engine builds. There is no allowlist, no regex, no `"` quoting and no length bound anywhere in the file or in src/storage/sql/index.ts (`createPostgresAuthStore` passes `o` straight through, and the public `schemaFor("postgres", opts)` does the same). This is the one value in the SQL layer that is NOT bound as a parameter, which makes the engine header's claim — "injection safety → templates + bound params, always" (engine.ts:12) — materially untrue for the identifier path.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: The obvious multi-tenant deployment shape is schema-per-tenant: `createPostgresAuthStore({ client: pool, schema: `t_${tenantFromRequestOrEnv}` })`. Any tenant value reaching that option grants full statement injection on every auth query (`schema = 'tetrac; DROP SCHEMA tetrac CASCADE; --'` executes verbatim from `ddl()`, and `schema = 'other_tenant'` silently redirects the whole auth store — sessions, email index, encrypted wallet blobs — into another tenant's namespace, a cross-tenant read of every user's ciphertext). Even without hostile input, a schema string from an env var containing a hyphen or a leading digit yields opaque syntax errors at every query.
raw_findings.recommendation: Validate at dialect construction and refuse otherwise: `if (!/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,62}$/.test(schema)) throw new Error(...)`. Emitting `"${schema.replace(/"/g,'""')}"` additionally makes the identifier explicit and case-exact (see the next finding). Document that `schema` must be a static, deployment-time constant and never derived from a request.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for `schema:` — tests/sql-conformance-postgres.test.ts:33 builds `conf_${++n}_${process.pid}` and interpolates it into its own `DROP SCHEMA` (line 38), i.e. the tests assume a trusted identifier rather than asserting the SDK validates it. tests/sql-dialects.test.ts's injection assertion ("no parameter value is EVER interpolated into the SQL text") only iterates `params`, so a schema name is out of its scope by construction.

raw_findings.title: The Supabase `public`-schema guard is a case-sensitive exact-match, but Postgres folds unquoted identifiers — `schema: "Public"` bypasses it silently
raw_findings.description: Preflight's flagship protection — refusing to place auth tables in a schema that Supabase serves to the internet via PostgREST and the browser-shipped `anon` key — is gated on `schema === "public"`, a JavaScript string equality check. The schema name is then emitted unquoted (`${schema}.ttc_users`, `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS ${schema}`), and Postgres down-cases unquoted identifiers and ignores surrounding whitespace. So `"Public"`, `"PUBLIC"`, `"pUbLiC"` and `" public"` all resolve to the real `public` schema at the database while failing the `===` test. The tables are created in `public`, preflight reports no issue, `createSqlAuthStore` boots clean, and everything works — which is precisely the failure mode the code comment calls "the highest-severity misconfiguration available, and it is INVISIBLE from the app side".
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator sets `schema: process.env.DB_SCHEMA` and the value is `Public` (a capitalized env value, a copy from a Supabase dashboard label, or a Windows-ism). Preflight passes. Every `tetrac.ttc_*` table is really `public.ttc_*`, served over PostgREST to anyone holding the `anon` key that ships in the app's own JavaScript bundle. An unauthenticated attacker fetches `https://<project>.supabase.co/rest/v1/ttc_users?select=*` with that key and downloads every user's `data` blob — the complete encrypted wallet bundles — plus `ttc_sessions` (token digests, publicKeys, fingerprints) and `ttc_email_index`. The ciphertext is then offline-attackable against the user's chosen "passkey" secret.
raw_findings.recommendation: Normalize before comparing and before emitting: reject `schema.trim().toLowerCase() === "public"` (and, once the identifier is validated per the previous finding, emit it quoted so the value the guard checked is exactly the value Postgres resolves). Better still, resolve it at the database: `SELECT to_regclass($1)` / compare against `current_schemas(false)` so the check tests the schema Postgres actually used, not the string JavaScript was handed.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ and src/ for `allowPublicSchema`, `public_schema`, `PUBLIC`. tests/sql-conformance-postgres.test.ts:70-82 asserts only the exact lowercase literal (`schema: "public"` rejected twice); tests/sql-conformance-sqlite.test.ts:81 only asserts the *default* DDL never mentions `public`. No test uses a case- or whitespace-variant.

raw_findings.title: Generated Postgres DDL emits no RLS or REVOKE — the Supabase protection is schema placement only, and `allowPublicSchema` removes it entirely
raw_findings.description: The Postgres `ddl()` creates five tables holding session records, the email index and every user's encrypted wallet blob, and issues no `ALTER TABLE … ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and no `REVOKE ALL ON … FROM anon, authenticated` (I grepped all of src/ for `ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, `REVOKE`, `GRANT`, `rls` — zero hits). The entire Supabase defense rests on one thing: the tables not being in `public`. That is a single point of failure with no second layer, and it is defeated outright by the documented `allowPublicSchema: true` escape hatch, by the case-variant bypass above, or by an operator who later adds `tetrac` to Supabase's exposed-schemas list (a one-click dashboard setting). RLS-enabled-with-no-policies is deny-all for `anon`/`authenticated` while the table owner and `service_role` (which the SDK's own pool uses) bypass it — so it would cost nothing and neutralize the whole class.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator hits the preflight error, reads "pass allowPublicSchema: true", and does exactly that to unblock a deploy. The tables land in `public` with no RLS. Anyone with the `anon` key shipped in the app's JS bundle reads `ttc_users` over PostgREST and exfiltrates every encrypted wallet bundle. The same outcome follows if `tetrac` is ever added to the exposed schemas — the SDK provides no residual protection at the table level.
raw_findings.recommendation: Append to the Postgres DDL for every table: `ALTER TABLE <t> ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE <t> FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` plus `REVOKE ALL ON <t> FROM PUBLIC;` and, guarded on role existence, `REVOKE ALL ON <t> FROM anon, authenticated;`. Add a preflight check that queries `pg_class.relrowsecurity` and `has_table_privilege('anon', <t>, 'SELECT')`, erroring when `anon` can read. This makes the `allowPublicSchema` escape hatch survivable instead of total.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped src/, tests/ and all *.md for `ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, `REVOKE`, `GRANT`, `rls`, `Supabase` — the only hits are the prose in dialects/postgres.ts and src/storage/sql/types.ts:45. No test asserts any table-level permission, and README.md/SECURITY.md contain no Supabase guidance at all.

raw_findings.title: Rate-limit bucket identifiers are raw, un-normalized emails while every SQL key column is byte-exact — case variants get independent counters for one account
raw_findings.description: The routes pass `body.email` verbatim as the rate-limit `identifier`, but every account lookup on the same request routes through `normalizeEmail()` (engine.ts:122 `getPublicKeyByEmail` → `[normalizeEmail(email), appId]`). The SQL backends store `identifier` in byte-exact columns on purpose — MySQL `VARBINARY(320)`, Postgres `text` under a deterministic collation, SQLite `TEXT` with BINARY collation — so `victim@example.com`, `Victim@example.com` and `VICTIM@EXAMPLE.COM` are three distinct rows in `ttc_rate_limits` that all resolve to the same account. The deliberate (and correct) choice of byte-exact key columns is therefore not matched by normalization on the write side of the rate-limit path. The same holds for the Redis/KV path (store.ts:187 `${scope}:${b.identifier}`), so this is engine-independent, but it is the SQL dimension's collation choice that makes it exact rather than accidental.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker targeting `victim@example.com` gets `maxAttempts` requests per window against the `login` and `register` buckets for each case permutation of the local part and domain — 2^k distinct budgets for a k-letter address, all hitting the same account. This multiplies the budget for `/register` account-existence probing (the 409 "Account already exists" oracle at routes.ts:295) and for `/login` challenge-burning by orders of magnitude at zero cost. The primary auth gate is still an ed25519 signature, so this is amplification of enumeration/abuse rather than a credential-guessing win — hence low.
raw_findings.evidence: const limited = await rateLimited(req, { endpoint: "login", appId, identifier: body.email });
raw_findings.recommendation: Normalize identifiers at the bucket boundary, not per-backend: apply `normalizeEmail(body.email)` at routes.ts:280 and :377 (or normalize `bucket.identifier` once inside `checkRateLimit` when the endpoint's identifier is an email). Public keys and IPs must stay byte-exact.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/rate-limit-self-extend.test.ts and tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts in full and grepped tests/ for `identifier` and for case-variant email bucket assertions — every case uses a single fixed lowercase identifier. src/storage/conformance.ts:146-166 asserts bucket *isolation* by identifier/endpoint/app but never that two case-variants of one email share a bucket.

raw_findings.title: Preflight never verifies the driver can run a real transaction — a passthrough `transaction` boots clean and removes MySQL's challenge-replay defense
raw_findings.description: `createSqlAuthStore` runs `dialect.preflight(driver)`, and every dialect's preflight calls only `driver.query(...)` — never `driver.transaction(...)`. Yet types.ts:30-36 states that "the atomicity of challenge-consume and rate-limiting depends on this being a REAL transaction — not a no-op passthrough", and the SDK's own test helper models exactly the wrong shape (`transaction: (fn) => fn(driver)`, tests/sql-dialects.test.ts:35). The result is that the SDK's boot-time "refuse to start on silent catastrophe" mechanism — which does check strict mode, key-column types, table existence, DB collation and SQLite file permissions — has a hole precisely where the anti-replay guarantee lives. The same gap covers `pgDriver`: a client without `.connect()` (e.g. `@neondatabase/serverless` in HTTP mode) passes preflight and then throws on every single `putUser`, so registration is 100% broken in production with a clean boot.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A third-party author writes a `SqlDriver` for their engine, copies the passthrough `transaction` shape, and declares `supportsReturning: false`. `takeChallenge` (engine.ts:162-176) then issues a bare `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` and a `DELETE` on two different pooled connections with no surrounding transaction — the row lock protects nothing. Two concurrent `loginWallet` requests replaying one captured (challenge, signature) pair both read the same challenge before either delete lands, and both mint a session. Preflight reports no issue at any point.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add a dialect-independent capability probe to `createSqlAuthStore`: run `driver.transaction(async (tx) => { await tx.query(<trivial select>, []); throw SENTINEL; })`, catch the sentinel, and error if the callback never ran or if the driver did not surface the throw — that alone catches the passthrough and the missing-`connect` cases at boot instead of at the first registration or the first replay.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for `transaction`, `passthrough`, `PreflightError` and read tests/sql-conformance-sqlite.test.ts's preflight block (lines 119-152) plus tests/sql-conformance-postgres.test.ts:70-90 and tests/sql-conformance-mysql.test.ts:79-140 — every preflight test covers missing tables, `public` schema, web-served path, strict mode and column types; none probes transactional capability.

raw_findings.title: MySQL preflight validates only the key-column types and only once at boot — the `data` column and later sql_mode changes are unchecked
raw_findings.description: Two gaps in the MySQL preflight. (1) The column-type check filters `COLUMN_NAME IN ('app_id','public_key','email','token_hash','identifier','endpoint','challenge')` — the `data` column is absent, so a hand-rolled or migrated `ttc_users.data TEXT` (65,535-byte cap) instead of the shipped `MEDIUMTEXT` passes preflight silently, even though this dialect's own header calls a truncated UserData blob "permanently locked out of every wallet in it". Strict mode converts the truncation into a hard error rather than silence, which is fail-closed, but the user still cannot persist wallets past ~65 KB and nothing at boot said so. (2) The strict-mode check reads `@@SESSION.sql_mode` from one arbitrary pooled connection at construction time. Nothing re-checks it, so a later `SET GLOBAL sql_mode` (or a pool configured to set sql_mode per connection) reinstates silent truncation with the SDK still believing it verified the invariant.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An operator migrates an existing MySQL database and creates `ttc_users.data` as `TEXT`. Preflight passes (only key columns are inspected). A user accumulates wallets; once the JSON crosses 65,535 bytes `putUser` starts erroring in strict mode — or, if a DBA relaxes `sql_mode` globally after boot to unblock an unrelated job, the blob is truncated instead. A truncated blob is invalid JSON, so `getUser`'s `catch { return null; }` (engine.ts:75-79) reports the account as non-existent, `register` no longer 409s, and the next registration upserts over the row — destroying the sole copy of that user's wallet ciphertext.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add `data` to the inspected columns and error when `DATA_TYPE` is not `mediumtext`/`longtext`. Additionally check `@@GLOBAL.sql_mode` alongside the session value so a boot-time pass is not invalidated by the next connection, and consider re-asserting strict mode lazily on first write.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/sql-conformance-mysql.test.ts in full — lines 79-140 assert VARBINARY on key columns (`SELECT ... information_schema.COLUMNS`, line 87), MEDIUMTEXT on `data` in the *generated DDL text* (line 107), and a clean boot against a strict server (line 135). No test creates a schema with a `TEXT` data column and asserts preflight rejects it, and none re-checks sql_mode after boot.

raw_findings.title: MySQL `upsert()` discards the conflict target and preflight never inspects the index set
raw_findings.description: `upsert(_conflictCols, setClauses)` drops the conflict columns the engine declared and emits a bare `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, which MySQL fires on *whichever* unique index the row collides with. That is safe against the shipped schema — every table has exactly one unique index (its PRIMARY KEY), and the only secondary indexes (`KEY ttc_*_expires_idx`) are non-unique. But nothing enforces that: the MySQL preflight checks table existence and key-column data types and never queries `information_schema.STATISTICS`, so an operator who adds a plausible-looking unique index gets silently different upsert semantics from Postgres and SQLite, where the target is explicit.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An operator adds `UNIQUE KEY uq_pk (app_id, public_key)` to `ttc_email_index` to enforce one email per account. `putUser` for a second email under the same publicKey now issues `INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE public_key = ?`, which collides on that new index rather than on `(email, app_id)` and rewrites the *existing* row instead of inserting — the account's old email silently stops resolving while a different row is mutated. Preflight passes; Postgres and SQLite behave correctly, so the divergence is invisible until a MySQL-only support ticket. Requires operator action, hence low.
raw_findings.evidence:
// MySQL ignores the conflict columns — it keys off whichever unique index is hit.
    upsert: (_conflictCols, setClauses) => `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE ${setClauses.join(", ")}`,
raw_findings.recommendation: Extend the MySQL preflight to query `information_schema.STATISTICS` for the five tables and error on any `NON_UNIQUE = 0` index that is not the expected PRIMARY KEY — the upsert's correctness depends on that being the only unique index, so it should be asserted rather than assumed.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for `STATISTICS`, `UNIQUE`, `ON DUPLICATE` — tests/sql-dialects.test.ts:152-172 asserts only `supportsReturning`/`forUpdate`; tests/sql-conformance-mysql.test.ts inspects `information_schema.COLUMNS` but never `STATISTICS`. No test adds a secondary unique index.

raw_findings.title: Rate-limit rows embed emails and IPs and nothing sweeps them by default
raw_findings.description: `sweepExpired` exists and is correct, but it is opt-in: `createSqlAuthStore` returns the store without scheduling anything, and no export in src/storage/sql/index.ts starts a timer or documents a required cron beyond the code comment "Wire it to a cron." `ttc_rate_limits.identifier` holds the raw email or client IP of every request that was rate-limited (Postgres `text`, MySQL `VARBINARY(320)`, SQLite `TEXT`), and `ttc_sessions`/`ttc_challenges` retain expired rows indefinitely. Where the Redis backend evicted these within the window, the SQL backends keep them — and keep them in every backup and every read replica. Under the stated threat model (attacker can read a leaked backup or a replica), that turns a transient counter into a durable log of who tried to log into which tenant, from which IP, and when.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A leaked nightly dump of a long-running deployment yields the full `ttc_rate_limits` table: every email address that ever attempted `/register` or `/login` against every `app_id`, correlated with client IPs from the global `endpoint = 'ip'` bucket, going back to first deploy. Correctness is unaffected — every read already filters `expires_at > ?` — but the disclosure is a GDPR-relevant retention issue the integrator was never told to handle in prose that survives outside the source file.
raw_findings.evidence:
* This is not merely housekeeping: rate-limit rows embed **emails and IPs**. Redis
   * evicted them in 60s; a SQL table keeps them — and keeps them in every backup — until
   * something deletes them. That is a data-retention obligation.
   */
  async sweepExpired(limit = 1000): Promise<number> {
raw_findings.recommendation: Either start an interval sweeper inside `createSqlAuthStore` by default (opt-out via an option, guarded for serverless) or emit a `warn`-level preflight issue when no sweep has been configured, so the retention obligation is surfaced at boot rather than only in a source comment. Consider hashing the rate-limit `identifier` (HMAC with a server key) so the durable row carries no plaintext email or IP at all — the bucket only needs equality.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped src/storage/sql/ and tests/ for `sweepExpired`, `cron`, `setInterval`, `retention` — `sweepExpired` is called only from src/storage/conformance.ts:440/453 (correctness of the sweep itself) and never scheduled anywhere in src/. README.md and SECURITY.md contain no retention guidance (grepped for `Supabase`, `retention`).

raw_findings.title: Rate-limit buckets key on the RAW email while account lookup normalizes it — per-account throttling on /login and /challenge is fully bypassable by case variation
raw_findings.description:
`AuthStore.getPublicKeyByEmail` and the email index are both routed through `normalizeEmail()` (lowercase + trim), by explicit contract. The `RateLimitBucket.identifier`, however, is the caller-supplied string verbatim: `KvAuthStore.rateLimitKey` concatenates `b.identifier` unchanged (`src/storage/store.ts:187`), and `SqlAuthStore.hitRateLimit` binds `bucket.identifier` unchanged (`src/storage/sql/engine.ts:258`). `src/server/routes.ts` hands it `body.email` raw on /login (line 377), /challenge (line 222) and /register (line 280).

Consequence: `victim@example.com`, `Victim@example.com`, `VICTIM@EXAMPLE.COM` … all resolve to the SAME account (normalized index) but occupy DISTINCT rate-limit buckets. `EMAIL_RE` (`/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/`, routes.ts:50) accepts every casing, so the multiplier is 2^(number of letters) — ~65,000 fresh budgets for a typical address.

This is the ONLY per-account throttle by default: `trustProxyHeaders` defaults to `false` (config.ts:163), and `rateLimited()` skips the IP bucket entirely when it is off (`if (config.trustProxyHeaders) {` routes.ts:128). So on a default deployment the login/challenge budget for a named account is effectively unbounded.

The credential being guessed at /login is the user's "passkey" — a user-supplied secret string, i.e. a password — whose PBKDF2 output IS the app key that decrypts the stored wallet ciphertext. Unlimited online guessing against it is a wallet-compromise path, not just a nuisance.
raw_findings.recommendation: Normalize the identifier at the point the bucket is built, not in the backend: in `src/server/routes.ts`, pass `identifier: normalizeEmail(body.email)` on /login, /challenge and /register (import from `../storage/store.js`). Belt-and-braces: document on `RateLimitBucket.identifier` that email identifiers MUST already be normalized, and add a conformance case asserting `hitRateLimit({...,identifier:"A@B.com"})` and `hitRateLimit({...,identifier:"a@b.com"})` are the SAME bucket when the caller normalizes (and that the store itself never case-folds public keys or IPs).
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "normalizeEmail|toLowerCase|MixedCase|case-insensitiv|identifier:" tests/ — only hits are SQL-column-type assertions, the negative-control store, and fixed-case identifiers. grep -rln "MiXeD|uppercase|toUpperCase|@EXAMPLE" tests/ returns only tests/auth-client.test.ts (HTTP method casing) and tests/sql-dialects.test.ts (email-index normalization at the driver). tests/audit-server.test.ts:148-163 exercises attacker throttling but with a single fixed-case email. No test anywhere varies email case against a rate-limit bucket.

raw_findings.title: The conformance suite never exercises the one optional-field bucket shape (`appId` omitted = the global IP limiter), plus four other security-critical store invariants are untested
raw_findings.description:
`RateLimitBucket.appId` is optional and is omitted exactly once in the SDK — the global client-IP bucket (`src/server/routes.ts:131`). Every single bucket literal in `authStoreConformanceCases` supplies `appId` (lines 110, 131, 147, 163, 415). A third-party `AuthStore` can therefore pass the entire suite while mishandling the only shape whose key component is `undefined`.

That this is a live hazard is proven by the SDK's own SQL engine, which must special-case it: `const appId = bucket.appId ?? "";` (`src/storage/sql/engine.ts:249`). Without that line, `undefined` binds as SQL NULL, and because NULL ≠ NULL in a unique index, the `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (endpoint, app_id, identifier)` upsert inserts a brand-new row on every hit: `count` is always 1, `allowed` is always true, and per-IP rate limiting silently FAILS OPEN forever. (The mirror failure — `WHERE app_id = NULL` never matching — is equally silent.) Nothing in `conformance.ts` or in `store.ts`'s `RateLimitBucket` doc states that an omitted `appId` must yield a distinct, stable bucket key.

Other invariants the suite asserts in prose but never tests:
(a) CHALLENGE TENANT ISOLATION — there is a case for sessions ("sessions are isolated per tenant", line 238) and for users/email index, but none for challenges. No case does `putChallenge("app1", pk)` then `takeChallenge("app2", pk)`. A backend that omits appId from the challenge key lets a hostile co-tenant app burn/steal every challenge issued by another tenant.
(b) `deleteSession` TENANT SCOPING — `deleteSession("app2", h)` must not revoke app1's session. Untested.
(c) CHALLENGE RE-ISSUE — `putChallenge` twice must leave only the newest consumable. Untested; a backend using plain INSERT + `SELECT … LIMIT 1` keeps both, making a superseded challenge replayable.
(d) EMAIL-INDEX REPOINT — `putUser` for the same (appId, email) with a different publicKey must overwrite. Untested; an INSERT-IF-NOT-EXISTS backend silently keeps the stale mapping.
(e) `putUser` ATOMICITY — `AuthStore.putUser`'s doc says "Both, or neither — one transaction where the backend supports it" (store.ts:96-98). No case tests it.
(f) "ERRORS FAIL CLOSED" (invariant 3, store.ts:88-90) — no case and no fault-injection hook.
(g) DELIMITER SAFETY — there is a case for a DOTTED appId (line 362) but none for a colon-bearing appId or identifier, which is the delimiter `KvAuthStore` actually concatenates on.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator writes a Mongo/DynamoDB/Convex `AuthStore`, runs `authStoreConformanceCases` (all 20+ cases green, including the negative control's bar), and ships. Their `hitRateLimit` does `{ endpoint, appId: bucket.appId, identifier }` as the document filter. For the IP bucket `appId` is `undefined`, which Mongo's driver either strips (matching any appId) or stores as null in a way that never round-trips through their unique index. Result: the deployment turns on `trustProxyHeaders` believing it now has a global per-IP limiter, and that limiter counts to 1 forever. A single attacker IP gets unmetered access to /challenge, /login and /register — unbounded account enumeration and unbounded online passkey guessing — with a green conformance run as the evidence that the backend is correct.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add to `authStoreConformanceCases`: (1) an IP-bucket case — `hitRateLimit({endpoint:"ip", identifier:"1.2.3.4"}, 60, 3)` four times must deny the fourth, and must NOT share a counter with `{endpoint:"ip", appId:"app1", identifier:"1.2.3.4"}`; (2) `putChallenge("app1",PK_A,…)` → `takeChallenge("app2",PK_A)` must be null; (3) `deleteSession("app2",h)` must leave app1's session live; (4) re-issued challenge supersedes the previous; (5) `putUser` repointing an (appId,email) to a new publicKey; (6) an appId and an identifier containing `:` must not collide with a neighbouring namespace. Also state the appId charset restriction in `store.ts` rather than only in `src/server/routes.ts`.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "appId: undefined|endpoint: \"ip\"" src/ tests/ — the appId-less bucket appears in exactly two places: src/server/routes.ts:131 and tests/sql-dialects.test.ts:74. The latter is a RECORDING-DRIVER test (`recordingDriver`, no database) that only asserts placeholder/parameter counts and non-interpolation; it asserts nothing about bucket-key behavior. grep for `takeChallenge("app2"` / `deleteSession("app2"` across src/ and tests/ returns nothing. grep of tests/ for putUser+atomic/transaction returns nothing.

raw_findings.title: MemoryAdapter is production-usable with no runtime guard, no published warning, and no sweeper — unauthenticated unbounded heap growth and per-instance rate limits
raw_findings.description:
Three things compound:

1. NO PUBLISHED WARNING. The only "Not for production" text is a `//` line comment on line 1 of memory.ts. It is a line comment, not JSDoc, so tsup strips it: the shipped `dist/storage/index.d.ts:80` is bare `declare class MemoryAdapter implements StorageAdapter {` with no preceding doc block, so an integrator's editor shows nothing. `README.md` and `SECURITY.md` are both 0 bytes in this tree. `MemoryAdapter` is a first-class named export of `@tetrac/login-sdk/storage` sitting next to `RedisAdapter`/`UpstashAdapter`.

2. NO GUARD. `createAuthHandlers({ storage })` accepts any `StorageAdapter` and never checks (routes.ts:105-113). The production safety-guard in `selectStorageBackend()` (resolve.ts:47-53) can never fire on this path, because nothing routes `MemoryAdapter` through `resolve.ts` — `resolveStorageAdapter()` cannot return it at all.

3. NOTHING EVER SWEEPS. `MemoryAdapter` expires LAZILY — `alive()` only evicts on a read (memory.ts:17-25) — and its own comment concedes "rate-limit counters, abandoned challenges, and expired sessions are typically NEVER read again … That is a real leak, and this is its fix" (memory.ts:91-100). But grepping the whole of `src/` shows `sweepExpired` has NO caller outside `storage/` itself: the SDK never schedules it. It is a fix the integrator must discover from a source comment they will never read.

Security impact beyond "it doesn't scale": (a) rate-limit counters become per-process, so on any serverless/multi-instance deployment the effective login/challenge budget is multiplied by instance count; (b) unbounded, attacker-driven heap growth (below).
raw_findings.attack_scenario:
DoS: an unauthenticated attacker POSTs /challenge with a freshly generated, valid canonical base58 publicKey on every request. Each request creates TWO entries that are never read again and never swept: `ratelimit:challenge:{appId}:{newPk}` (60s TTL) and `challenge:{appId}:{newPk}` (300s TTL, ~64 bytes of value). Because each request uses a distinct publicKey, each gets its own fresh rate-limit bucket and is always `allowed`, and with `trustProxyHeaders` false (the default) there is no IP backstop. On Redis/Upstash the native TTL reclaims both; on `MemoryAdapter` the Map grows monotonically until the process OOMs — a persistent DoS from unauthenticated traffic at ordinary request rates.

Multi-instance: an integrator deploys `createAuthHandlers({ storage: new MemoryAdapter() })` to Vercel/Lambda. With N warm instances the per-email login limit is effectively N × maxAttempts because each instance holds its own counter; the attacker simply keeps issuing requests and lands on different instances.
raw_findings.recommendation: (1) Convert the warning to a JSDoc block on `class MemoryAdapter` with `@deprecated`-style emphasis so it reaches `dist/*.d.ts` and IDE hovers. (2) Add a boot-time guard in `createAuthHandlers`: if `NODE_ENV === 'production'` and the adapter is a `MemoryAdapter` (brand it with a `readonly ephemeral = true` field so third-party in-memory stores can opt in too), throw with the same message shape as `selectStorageBackend()`'s production refusal. (3) Either have `MemoryAdapter` self-sweep on a timer/`setInterval().unref()` or make the constructor require an explicit `{ sweepIntervalMs }` / `{ iUnderstandThisLeaks: true }`. (4) Restore README/SECURITY storage guidance — right now the package ships zero prose about backend selection.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "MemoryAdapter" README.md SECURITY.md CHANGELOG.md audits/ — no matches (README.md and SECURITY.md are 0 bytes; audits/ is empty). grep -rn "sweepExpired" src/ tests/ excluding src/storage/ — no scheduler, no caller; only tests/v050-storage-seam.test.ts:110-132 which calls it manually. tests/storage.test.ts:31-90 tests only `selectStorageBackend`'s env guard, which MemoryAdapter never passes through. No test asserts any production guard on the adapter handed to createAuthHandlers.

raw_findings.title: KvAuthStore.putUser writes the record and the email index as two independent, non-transactional operations — violating the atomicity its own AuthStore doc mandates, and untested
raw_findings.description:
`AuthStore.putUser`'s contract says: "Upsert the record AND maintain the email index. Both, or neither — one transaction where the backend supports it" (store.ts:96-98). `KvAuthStore` — the reference implementation every KV backend (Redis, Upstash, Vercel KV, Memory) runs through — issues two sequential awaits with no MULTI/pipeline, despite Redis supporting exactly that. If the second call fails or the process dies between them, the user record exists with no email-index entry.

The conformance suite does not test this: its email-index cases (lines 278-325) cover resolution, normalization and the concurrent no-lost-write property, but nothing asserts the pair is all-or-nothing. So a native backend can also ship this split and pass.

Blast radius on the shipped routes is limited because `issueSession` → `persistUser` re-runs `putUser` on every login, which self-heals the index; and in the SDK's own client flow a failed /register just yields a fresh keypair on retry. But a stranded record is invisible: /register's collision checks (`getUserByPublicKey` on a freshly minted key → miss; `resolvePublicKeyByEmail` → miss) both pass, so the deployment quietly accumulates orphaned `pubKey:{appId}:{pk}` blobs holding encrypted wallet material that no login path can ever reach again.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Redis failover / connection timeout during a registration burst: the `set` of `pubKey:{appId}:{pk}` (which carries the user's encrypted wallet bundle) commits, the `hset` of `email:{addr}` does not, and the route 500s. The account now exists but is unreachable by email. If the user had already been shown or funded any address from that bundle before retrying, that key material is orphaned server-side with nothing pointing at it. More generally: the SDK holds every other backend to "both or neither" while its own reference implementation does not, so the invariant is unenforceable in practice.
raw_findings.recommendation: Either (a) add an optional `multi?(ops)` / `pipeline?()` to `StorageAdapter` and have `KvAuthStore.putUser` use it when present (Redis MULTI, Upstash pipeline — both exist), falling back to the current sequence; or (b) reverse the order and document the weaker guarantee honestly on `AuthStore.putUser` ("KV backends provide index-after-record ordering, not atomicity"), and add a conformance case that pins whatever guarantee is actually promised. Also add a conformance case for `putUser` repointing an existing (appId, email) to a new publicKey.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "putUser" tests/ filtered for atomic|partial|both|transaction — no matches. src/storage/conformance.ts lines 278-325 contain the only email-index cases (resolution, case-normalization, concurrent-two-app no-lost-write); none covers the record+index pair. tests/storage-conformance-negative.test.ts's BUG 4 is read-modify-write on the index, a different defect.

raw_findings.title: Namespace-escape safety of the KV keyspace is enforced only in the HTTP route layer; the store boundary and its published contract never mention the ':' restriction
raw_findings.description:
`appScoped()` builds `${prefix}${appId}:${id}` with no validation. The ONLY thing preventing `appId = "a:b"` from colliding with `appId = "a"` + `id = "b:…"` is `APP_ID_RE` in `src/server/routes.ts:56`. I verified that every shipped entry point does call `validateAppId` before any store call — /challenge (205), /register (255), /login (347), /login-wallet (393), /connect-wallet (438), /search-wallet (511), and `headerAppId()` (160) for /logout, /user-data, /import-wallet — including the `config.appId` fallback. So this is NOT exploitable through the SDK's own routes today.

The weakness is structural: `KvAuthStore` is a public export of `@tetrac/login-sdk/storage`, `AuthStore` is advertised as the extension point third parties implement, and `src/storage/store.ts` — the file such an author reads — never states that `appId` is guaranteed colon-free or bounded in length. The conformance suite tests a DOTTED appId (line 362, because Mongo treats '.' as nesting) but never a colon-bearing one, even though ':' is the delimiter `KvAuthStore` actually concatenates on. Anyone composing `KvAuthStore` outside `createAuthHandlers` (an admin tool, a migration script, a custom route) inherits an unguarded string-concatenation keyspace.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator writes their own login route on top of `new KvAuthStore(redis)` (a documented, exported, supported composition) and passes the tenant id straight from a request header without re-implementing `APP_ID_RE` — which lives in a different module they never imported. Attacker sends `appId: "tenantA:AaBbCc…"` with `publicKey` chosen so that `pubKey:` + `tenantA:AaBbCc…` + `:` + pk equals the key of a record under `appId: "tenantA"`, and reads or overwrites another tenant's UserData blob (which contains that tenant's users' encrypted wallet bundles). Same construction collides `session:` keys, yielding cross-tenant session forgery.
raw_findings.recommendation: Move the charset check to the boundary that owns the keyspace: have `appScoped()` (or the `KvAuthStore` constructor/methods) assert `/^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$/` and throw otherwise — a cheap fail-closed check on a path already doing string work. Document the precondition on the `AuthStore` interface itself so native-backend authors see it, and add the colon-collision case to the conformance suite alongside the dotted-appId one.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "appScoped" src/ — defined once (server/keys.ts:12), used only inside KvAuthStore (store.ts:191,201,212,220,224,235); no validation at either site. tests/multi-app.test.ts covers per-app scoping and appId validation at the ROUTE layer only. grep of src/storage/conformance.ts for a colon-bearing appId or identifier returns nothing; the injection case (line 388-428) uses SQL/NoSQL payloads as VALUES, never as an appId.

raw_findings.title: keyPrefixes are integrator-overridable with no check that the resulting namespaces are unambiguous
raw_findings.description:
`resolveConfig` shallow-merges `override.keyPrefixes` over the defaults with zero validation — no uniqueness check, no requirement that a prefix ends with the ':' delimiter, no check that no prefix is a prefix of another. Yet `src/core/config.ts:8-10` asserts a security property that depends on exactly that: the session prefix is "disjoint from pubKey so an attacker-chosen publicKey can never collide with the session-token keyspace".

Because the delimiter is only ever appended AFTER the appId, a prefix that does not end in ':' merges with the appId segment. Concretely: `keyPrefixes: { challenge: "c", pubKey: "cp" }` makes `challenge` + appId `"pApp"` produce `cpApp:{pk}` — byte-identical to `pubKey` + appId `"App"` + the same pk. A challenge write would then overwrite a UserData blob (and `getUser` would return null on the JSON.parse failure at store.ts:194-197, i.e. the account silently disappears).

I am labelling this low because it requires an integrator misconfiguration, and with the SHIPPED defaults plus `validatePublicKey`/`hashSessionToken` no cross-keyspace collision is reachable (a 64-char lowercase-hex token digest is never valid canonical base58 for 32 bytes). But nothing enforces or tests that.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator renames prefixes for a shared Redis ("c" for challenges, "cp" for user records, to save memory) and also runs multi-tenant with `allowedAppIds` containing both `pApp` and `App`. An attacker who can request `appId: "pApp"` calls /challenge and the resulting `putChallenge` writes a 64-hex challenge string over `cpApp:{publicKey}` — the UserData record of the `App` tenant's user with that public key, containing their encrypted wallet bundle. `getUser` then parses the challenge as JSON, fails, and returns null (store.ts:196) — the victim's account, and every wallet ciphertext in it, is destroyed with no error surfaced anywhere.
raw_findings.recommendation: Validate in `resolveConfig`: assert the five prefix values are pairwise distinct, that none is a proper prefix of another, and that each ends with ':' (or whatever delimiter `appScoped` uses) — throw at construction otherwise. This is a startup-time check with no runtime cost.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep of tests/ for keyPrefixes overrides: only tests that pass `DEFAULT_CONFIG.keyPrefixes` verbatim (storage-conformance.test.ts:27, rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts:35, rate-limit-self-extend.test.ts). No test overrides prefixes or asserts any disjointness property. No validation exists anywhere in src/core/config.ts.

raw_findings.title: Next.js action dispatch resolves through Object.prototype — POST /api/auth/constructor invokes Object as a route handler
raw_findings.description:
`postRoutes` / `getRoutes` are object literals (prototype = `Object.prototype`) and the action name is taken straight from the URL path segment and used as a bare index. `postRoutes["constructor"]` resolves to the `Object` constructor — truthy, and a function — so the `handler ? handler(req) : error("Not found", 404)` guard passes and the route returns `Object(req)`, i.e. the Request object, where Next.js expects a Response. `postRoutes["__proto__"]` resolves to `Object.prototype` — truthy but not callable — so `handler(req)` throws a TypeError. Verified in node: `typeof ({challenge:1})["constructor"] === "function"`.

Strictly this is a robustness/error-handling defect, not a data-exposure one — no auth handler is reachable this way, and no `AuthStore` call is made. I include it because the same bare-index pattern is what turns into prototype pollution when the object is a data map rather than a dispatch table, and because it is an unauthenticated crash path on a public route.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Unauthenticated `POST /api/auth/constructor` (or `GET /api/auth/__proto__`) returns a non-Response object / throws inside the framework rather than the intended 404. Depending on the Next.js runtime this surfaces as an unhandled 500 with a framework stack trace instead of the SDK's `{"error":"Not found"}`, giving cheap version fingerprinting and a trivially scriptable error-log/alert flood.
raw_findings.recommendation: Build the tables with `Object.create(null)` (or use a `Map`), or guard the lookup with `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(postRoutes, action)` before indexing. One line, and it makes the 404 path total.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -n "constructor|__proto__|toString|Not found|404" tests/next-routes.test.ts — the file tests unknown-action 404s for POST (lines 59-63) and GET (76-80) using ordinary names only; no prototype-chain key is exercised. No hasOwnProperty / Object.create(null) anywhere in src/next/.

raw_findings.title: Wallet-login message has no origin or appId binding — any site can relay a login signature and (with the client-chosen appId in the app-key message) decrypt the victim's private keys
raw_findings.description:
`walletLoginMessage()` is the ONLY thing a Web3 wallet signs to prove ownership, and it contains nothing but a random hex challenge — no appId, no origin, no domain, no nonce-purpose string. The identical byte string is produced by every deployment of the SDK. `verifySolanaSignature` reconstructs exactly that string server-side, so a signature harvested by ANY site over `"Sign this message to verify wallet ownership: <hex>"` authenticates the signer at ANY other SDK deployment, provided the hex came from that deployment's `/challenge`.

`/challenge` is unauthenticated, accepts an arbitrary `publicKey`, and has no Origin/CSRF check (src/next/routes.ts:25-33 registers it as a bare POST; src/server/http.ts emits no CORS/Origin logic), so an attacker's BACKEND can pull a live challenge for a victim's address server-to-server, where CORS is irrelevant.

The damage is not limited to a session. `walletHandshake` prompts the wallet for TWO signatures in the same click — the login challenge AND `walletAppKeyMessage(this.config.appId)` — and `config.appId` is a client-side string the attacker sets freely (the victim app's appId is public in its JS bundle). `deriveAppKeyFromSignature(keySig)` is a bare SHA-256, so the second harvested signature IS the victim's wallet-decryption key for that app. The default `appId` is `"ttc"` (src/core/config.ts:155) and only the CLIENT warns about it (src/client/authClient.ts:123-129) — there is no server-side warning — so two default-configured deployments produce byte-identical prompts for both messages.

Contrast with `walletAppKeyMessage`, which WAS domain-bound by appId as audit fix H4/CRYPTO-2 (tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:89). That fix was never applied to the login message. This is the SIWE/EIP-4361 `domain`+`uri` binding that is missing.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Verified end-to-end against the shipped dist/ build. 1) Attacker runs evil.app using the same SDK with `config.appId = "victim.app"`. 2) Victim clicks "Connect wallet" on evil.app. 3) evil.app's backend POSTs `{appId:"victim.app", publicKey:<victim addr>}` to victim.app/api/auth/challenge and gets challenge C. 4) evil.app's frontend asks the wallet to sign `"Sign this message to verify wallet ownership: C"` (prompt 1 — names no site at all) and `walletAppKeyMessage("victim.app")` (prompt 2). Both look like a normal login. 5) Attacker relays (publicKey, sig1, C) to victim.app `/login-wallet` -> 200 + authToken. 6) GET /user-data with that token -> the victim's full `wallets[]` including `encryptedSecret`. 7) `deriveAppKeyFromSignature(sig2)` reproduces the victim's app key exactly; AES-GCM decrypt yields the plaintext private keys. PoC output: `session on victim.app: true / app key matches victim's: true / DECRYPTED VICTIM PRIVATE KEY => VICTIM_SOLANA_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_HEX`. Neither `allowedAppIds` nor `bindSessionToUserAgent` helps: the attacker uses the victim's own appId, and the attacker's backend is the client whose UA is fingerprinted.
raw_findings.recommendation:
