raw_findings.recommendation: Validate the resolved config at handler-construction time and refuse to boot on a non-positive/non-finite `sessionTtlSeconds` (and `challengeTtlSeconds`), the same fail-closed posture `selectStorageBackend()` already takes for a missing production backend. Also strip `undefined` values before the spread (`Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(override).filter(([,v]) => v !== undefined))`) so an unset env var falls back to the default instead of erasing it. Finally, make `SetOptions.exSeconds` handling explicit (`opts?.exSeconds != null`) so 0 is a hard error rather than silently "no TTL".
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -n "ttl|Ttl|TTL" src/storage/conformance.ts — the conformance suite has no zero/undefined-TTL case; its expiry cases use 1s TTLs. tests/server.test.ts:189-204 tests a positive TTL (100s) only. tests/storage.test.ts:19 ("honors TTL via an injected clock") likewise. No test in tests/ passes 0 or undefined for sessionTtlSeconds, and src/storage/resolve.ts's production preflight validates the storage backend only, never the AuthConfig.

raw_findings.title: logout silently no-ops (still returns 200 {ok:true}) whenever session verification fails — wrong appId header, UA drift, or publicKey mismatch
raw_findings.description: `logout` revokes only when `verifySession` returns a user, and returns `{ ok: true }` unconditionally. `verifySession` fails — and therefore revocation is skipped — for several conditions that are NOT "the token is already dead": (1) the client omitted or mis-set the `ttc-app-id` header on a deployment whose `config.appId` differs (`headerAppId` returns config.appId as fallback, so a multi-tenant client that forgets the header targets the wrong namespace); (2) `bindSessionToUserAgent` is on and the browser's UA changed since issuance (auto-update), which the SDK itself documents as an expected event at config.ts:113-115; (3) the presented `ttc-public-key` header does not match the session's owner. In every one of those cases the raw token remains LIVE server-side while the client tears down local state and the caller is told the logout succeeded. There is no server-side signal an integrator could log or alert on. Combined with finding 5 (a TTL that can be erased to "never"), "log out" can become a pure client-side illusion.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not a direct attacker primitive, but it removes the victim's remediation. A user on a shared/public machine clicks Log out; the SDK clears localStorage and reports success, but because the integration omits the appId header (or the browser auto-updated its UA under an enabled UA binding), the token was never revoked server-side. Anyone who captured that token beforehand — from the machine's localStorage before the clear, a browser-extension, a proxy log — keeps full account access (`/user-data` returns every encrypted wallet; `/import-wallet` accepts attacker ciphertext) for the remaining TTL.
raw_findings.recommendation: Revocation does not need full session verification — the raw token IS the capability, and `deleteSession(appId, hashSessionToken(token))` on an unknown hash is a harmless no-op. Delete unconditionally on any well-formed token (subject to rate limiting), and drop the publicKey/fingerprint preconditions on the logout path only. Keep the constant 200 response so nothing is leaked. If the appId header is absent on a multi-tenant deployment, that is a hard misconfiguration — surface it via a server-side warning rather than a silent success.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/server.test.ts:219-228 covers only the happy path ("logout revokes the presented session token and always returns 200 { ok }") with a matching token+publicKey and no appId header on a default-appId deployment. tests/client-logout.test.ts covers the client half (headers captured before clear, keepalive, skip when no token). grep -rn "logout" tests/ shows no case for a mismatched appId header, a UA-bound session with a changed UA, or a mismatched publicKey.

raw_findings.title: Client never clears a locally stored session on a 401, so a server-revoked or expired token leaves the app reporting an authenticated account indefinitely
raw_findings.description: `fetchUserData()` maps HTTP 401 to `null` and swallows it; `AuthProvider.refetchUser` stores that `null` in `user` and does nothing else. `getAuthStatus()` derives status purely from localStorage (`!!getAuthToken() && !!getPublicKey()`), so after the server has revoked or expired the session the client still reports `authenticated` (or `session_expired` if the vault happens to be locked) with `user === null` forever. This is exactly the state produced by the SDK's own single-active-session design: logging in on device B revokes device A's token, and device A has no way to notice — it just silently stops loading data. There is no re-login prompt, no `clearSession()`, and no distinction between "the vault auto-locked" (recoverable with a local re-auth ceremony) and "the server killed your session" (requires a full network login).
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not an attacker primitive; it is a security-relevant failure mode of the revocation design. It weakens incident response: a user who logs in elsewhere to evict a suspected intruder gets no confirmation on the compromised device, and an integrator building on `status` cannot detect server-side revocation at all, so UIs will show a logged-in shell around empty data instead of forcing re-authentication. It also makes finding 1's orphan sessions harder to notice.
raw_findings.recommendation: Distinguish 401 from "no data": have `fetchUserData` signal server-side rejection (throw a typed `SessionRevokedError` or return a discriminated result), and have `AuthProvider` call `clearSession()` and `refresh()` on it so `status` drops to `unauthenticated` and the app renders its login UI. Since revoked-elsewhere is the NORMAL outcome of the SDK's single-active-session rule, this needs to be a first-class state, not an inference.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "401|fetchUserData|clearSession|logout" src/react/*.ts* returns only useAuth.ts:79 (logout passthrough), AuthProvider.tsx:62 (the refetch above), and useBiometricUnlock.ts (F9 purge). tests/react-hooks.test.tsx and tests/auth-client.test.ts contain no case where /user-data returns 401 and the local session is expected to clear.

raw_findings.title: The in-memory app-key vault hangs off a well-known Symbol.for() global with mutable fields, so injected script can both read the hot key and permanently defeat the auto-lock
raw_findings.category: XSS blast radius / client-side control bypass
raw_findings.description: The vault state object is registered at `Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")` on `globalThis`. The property descriptor is `enumerable: false, writable: false` with the comment that this keeps it "out of for-in / JSON of globalThis" and that a stray assignment "can't silently swap out the live vault" — but `Symbol.for` is a cross-realm registry lookup, so `globalThis[Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")]` is a one-liner for any script on the page, and the OBJECT's fields are ordinary mutable properties. An XSS payload therefore gets (a) `.memoryAppKey` — the plaintext AES-256 key that decrypts every wallet, and (b) write access to `.autoLockMs` and `.lockDeadline`, which are the entire implementation of the idle auto-lock: setting them keeps the key armed indefinitely, and clearing `.lockOnHide` disables the hide/freeze/bfcache locks that `bindHideHandler` re-checks at fire time by design. The SDK's own framing ("It auto-locks after autoLockMs of inactivity (default 15s)... While locked, getAppKey() returns null, so every signer/decrypt path refuses to operate") reads as a bound on XSS exposure; against script running in the same realm it is not one. The honest residual — that a memory-only key is safe from *storage-scraping* XSS but not from *executing* XSS — is stated only for the storage half.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker lands XSS on the integrating app. Rather than racing the 15s auto-lock window, the payload does `const v = globalThis[Symbol.for('tetrac.vault')]; v.autoLockMs = 1e12; v.lockOnHide = false; setInterval(() => { v.lockDeadline = Date.now() + 1e12; }, 1000);` — the key now stays hot across tab hides, freezes, and bfcache restores. It then reads `v.memoryAppKey` and, with the session bearer token already sitting in localStorage under `ttc-auth-token`, calls `/user-data` to pull every `encryptedSecret` and decrypts them all offline. That is full, permanent wallet compromise from a single injection, with the SDK's stated time-bounding control neutralized rather than raced.
raw_findings.recommendation: Two things. (1) Documentation: state plainly, next to the auto-lock description, that auto-lock bounds exposure to a *lost/idle device*, not to script execution in the page — any XSS reads the key directly. That is the honest scope and it is currently implied to be broader. (2) Hardening: keep the policy fields (`autoLockMs`, `lockOnHide`, `lockDeadline`) in a module-private closure rather than on the shared object, exposing only the cross-copy identity through the symbol; and hold `memoryAppKey` as a non-extractable `CryptoKey` (Web Crypto `importKey(..., extractable: false)`) so `getAppKey()` hands out a signing/decrypting handle instead of raw hex — that alone downgrades XSS from "exfiltrate the master key" to "use it while the tab is open".
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "Symbol.for|tetrac.vault" tests/ — the only hit is tests/audit-client-vault.test.ts:35-39, which uses `delete (globalThis as any)[Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")]` purely as a test harness to simulate a page reload; there is no test or comment treating the global's reachability or field mutability as a security concern. tests/cross-tab-lock.test.ts covers CLIENTVAULT-7 (cross-tab lock propagation) only.

raw_findings.title: verifySession compares the session owner's publicKey with a non-constant-time `!==` while the fingerprint immediately below uses timingSafeEqual
raw_findings.description: Answering the question directly: this is NOT a real leak, and it should be recorded as such so it is not re-raised. `session.publicKey !== publicKey` is a plain JS string comparison, which in V8 short-circuits on length and then on the first differing byte, so it does carry a theoretical timing signal. But it is not reachable as an oracle: the comparison is only executed AFTER `store.getSession(appId, hashSessionToken(token))` returned non-null, i.e. the caller already holds a live 256-bit bearer token. The value being compared is the account's Solana public key — public by construction, echoed back in every `AuthResult`/`/user-data` response to that same token holder, and derivable from any on-chain activity. So the attacker would be mounting a remote nanosecond-scale timing attack, over a network, to recover a 44-character base58 value that the very next successful request would hand them in plaintext. The asymmetry with the fingerprint check three lines below (which correctly uses `timingSafeEqual` on a secret-ish value) is worth normalizing purely for reviewability.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No viable scenario. The only construction that even gets off the ground is an attacker who obtained a bare `ttc-auth-token` with no accompanying `ttc-public-key` (e.g. from a log that captures one header but not the other) and tries to brute-force the owner's public key one character at a time from response-time deltas. A single string compare of ~44 chars produces sub-microsecond differences, far below network jitter, and the SDK's per-target rate limiting is not even engaged on /user-data — but neither is any amplification. Treat as non-exploitable.
raw_findings.recommendation: Optional, for consistency only: switch to `timingSafeEqual(session.publicKey, publicKey)` so every credential-adjacent comparison in this function uses one primitive, and add a one-line comment recording WHY it does not matter here (the value is public and the caller already holds a valid token) so the next auditor does not re-file it as a finding.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "timingSafeEqual" src/ tests/ — used in src/server/challenge.ts:35 (challenge compare) and src/server/session.ts:94 (fingerprint compare) only. tests/timing-safe-edge-cases.test.ts and tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts:182-209 (F8) exhaustively cover the primitive's correctness but never assert anything about verifySession's publicKey comparison; grep for that line in tests/ returns nothing, so it is genuinely unreviewed — hence recording it as info rather than omitting it.

raw_findings.title: README.md, SECURITY.md and CHANGELOG.md are all empty (0 bytes) in the published package — the session model is documented only in source comments
raw_findings.description: `wc -l README.md CHANGELOG.md SECURITY.md` returns 0 for all three, and `audits/` is an empty directory. Every security-relevant property of the session lifecycle that an integrator must know exists only as a comment inside `src/`: that the raw bearer token is persisted to **localStorage** (not an httpOnly cookie) and is therefore readable by any XSS on the host app; that transport is header-based with no cookie/CSRF story; that the default TTL is 4h and is the only backstop when logout fails; that only ONE session per user is live, so logging in elsewhere silently kills this device with no client-side signal (finding 7); that there is no revoke-all endpoint; that `appId` defaults to `"ttc"` and provides no cross-app isolation until overridden; and that `allowedAppIds` is unset by default so any well-formed appId can mint a namespace in a shared database. Several of these are choices the integrator must actively compensate for (a strict CSP is effectively mandatory given localStorage token storage), and none are discoverable without reading the source.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not directly exploitable; it is the multiplier on the other findings. An integrator who assumes cookie-based sessions with httpOnly (the default assumption for an auth SDK) ships without a CSP; XSS then yields the bearer token from `localStorage['ttc-auth-token']` plus, if the vault is hot, the app key itself (finding 8) — full wallet compromise. An integrator who assumes `logout()` is authoritative does not notice finding 6. An integrator on a shared database who never sets `allowedAppIds` lets anyone mint namespaces.
raw_findings.evidence:
$ wc -l README.md CHANGELOG.md SECURITY.md
       0 README.md
       0 CHANGELOG.md
       0 SECURITY.md
$ ls -la audits/
  (empty)

src/client/session.ts:205-207 (the only record of where the bearer token lives) —
    localStorage.setItem(TOKEN_KEY, params.authToken);
    localStorage.setItem(PUBKEY_KEY, params.publicKey);

src/core/config.ts:64-67 —
   * existing encrypted wallets would no longer decrypt. The default "ttc" works out
   * of the box but provides NO cross-app isolation — override it in production.

src/core/config.ts:77-82 —
   * Optional allowlist of accepted `appId` values (v0.4.0). ... STRONGLY
   * recommended in production for a shared DB, so an attacker cannot mint arbitrary
   * namespaces (storage-bloat) or probe tenants by guessing ids.
raw_findings.recommendation: Ship a SECURITY.md that states, at minimum: (1) the session token is a bearer credential in localStorage — a strict CSP on the host app is a deployment REQUIREMENT, not a nicety, and XSS is game over for both the token and (while unlocked) the app key; (2) the 4h TTL and the single-active-session rule, including that there is no revoke-all and that logout is best-effort and fire-and-forget; (3) the production checklist that currently lives in comments — set a unique `appId`, set `allowedAppIds`, set `trustProxyHeaders` only behind a real edge, wire `sweepExpired` on durable backends for the email/IP retention obligation flagged at src/storage/sql/engine.ts:290-294.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Verified the files are genuinely empty rather than that I failed to read them: `wc -l` reports 0 lines for all three and `grep -n -i "localstorage|cookie|httponly|xss|bearer|session" README.md` produces no output. `ls -la audits/` shows an empty directory even though tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts:1 references "audits/zai-glm-52.md" and tests/server.test.ts:172 references "docs/5-PRD-FABLE-AUDIT.md" — neither path exists in the repo, so the prior audit trail survives only in the test suite.

raw_findings.title: /register binds an arbitrary identity publicKey with NO proof of possession unless authMethod==="wallet" — attacker squats a victim's on-chain wallet address and authenticates as it
raw_findings.description:
`register` only requires a signature when the client *chooses* to say `authMethod: "wallet"`. The attacker picks that field. By sending `authMethod: "email"` (or omitting it — it defaults to "email") together with `publicKey = <victim's public, on-chain Solana address>`, their own `email`, and their own `authPublicKey`, an attacker creates the canonical account record keyed to a wallet address they do not control. The only guard is `getUserByPublicKey(...)` returning 409, i.e. first-come-first-served on a *public* identifier.

After squatting, the account is fully attacker-owned: they log in via `/login` with their own email + auth keypair and receive a session whose `publicKey` is the victim's wallet address, giving read (`/user-data`) and write (`/import-wallet`) access to the record the victim's wallet maps to.

Two escalations make this fund-loss, not just squatting:
1. `connectWallet`'s self-heal (routes.ts:475-481) backfills the victim's client-encrypted `wallets[]` bundle into the attacker's record the first time the victim connects — the attacker then exfiltrates the ciphertext at leisure.
2. Because the squatted record carries `authMethod: "email"`, `useActiveWallet` (src/react/useActiveWallet.ts:30) computes `web3Identity = null`, so with the wallet adapter not connected it falls through to `user.wallets.find(w => w.chain === chain && w.role === "funds")` and returns `funds.publicKey` as the address the app displays/uses. If the attacker squats with a NON-empty `wallets` array, self-heal never fires (`!user.wallets?.length` is false) and the victim's real entry is never stored — the app renders the ATTACKER's address as the user's wallet/deposit address.

Because `appId` is taken from the request body (routes.ts:254) and `allowedAppIds` is undefined by default, this also works against any tenant on a shared DB.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker scrapes Solana addresses of a target app's user base (or of any chain-visible cohort), and for each one POSTs /register {publicKey: <victim address>, authMethod:"email", email:"attacker+N@evil.com", authPublicKey:<attacker's derived key>, wallets:[{chain:"solana",role:"funds",publicKey:"<ATTACKER ADDRESS>",encryptedSecret:"x"}]}. /search-wallet tells them which addresses are still unclaimed, and /register is not throttled for fresh identifiers. When a victim later logs in with their real wallet via /connect-wallet, the signature verifies, no new record is created, self-heal is suppressed by the pre-seeded wallets[], and the app's useActiveWallet renders the attacker's address as the user's funds wallet — deposits go to the attacker. Independently, the attacker logs in with attacker+N@evil.com and reads/writes the victim's record. PROVEN end-to-end against dist/: squat register 201 -> victim connectWallet 200 -> attacker /login 200 with session publicKey == victim wallet address -> attacker /user-data 200 returning the victim's stored ciphertext -> attacker /import-wallet 200 appending their own entry.
raw_findings.recommendation: Never let the client choose whether ownership is proven. Require a challenge+signature over `publicKey` for EVERY /register, regardless of authMethod: for email/biometric accounts the client already holds the identity keypair it just generated (Keypair.generate()), so it can sign the challenge with it at zero UX cost. Additionally: (a) make `connectWallet` refuse to issue a session when the existing record's `authMethod !== "wallet"` (an identity that was never proven by signature must not be reachable via a wallet signature, and vice-versa); (b) in `useActiveWallet`, never treat a `wallets[]` entry whose provenance is a server record as authoritative for a Web3 identity.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "authMethod" tests/*.ts — every hit is either a positive-path fixture or evm-verification.test.ts:37 ("authMethod='wallet' with EVM address is rejected at validation"). grep -rn "squat|pre-register|preregister|takeover|overwrite" tests/*.ts returns only concurrent-safety.test.ts:172 (email-index race) and storage-hash.test.ts:150. tests/audit-server.test.ts:117-141 documents "SERVERSIDE-5 residual: a well-formed identity still registers without proving control of the EMAIL" — that is the email-ownership gap, NOT the publicKey-ownership gap reported here; no test asserts anything about registering someone else's wallet publicKey with a non-wallet authMethod. Verified exploitable end-to-end against the shipped dist/ build.

raw_findings.title: Unauthenticated unbounded storage growth: /register neither throttles account creation nor bounds wallet-entry size (role and unknown keys are uncapped)
raw_findings.description:
Two independent gaps compose into an unbounded, unauthenticated write primitive against the datastore.

1. `validateWallets` bounds `encryptedSecret` (8192) and `publicKey` (128) but places NO length bound on `role` — and the validated objects are stored *wholesale*, so any extra attacker-invented JSON keys survive into the persisted record (`wallets: body.wallets ?? []` at routes.ts:323, `[...user.wallets, ...body.wallets]` at routes.ts:537). The 16-entry cap and the `maxWalletsPerUser` cap therefore bound the entry COUNT while the entry SIZE stays unbounded.

2. `/register`'s rate-limit bucket is keyed on `body.email ?? body.publicKey` — both attacker-chosen and fresh on every request, so the per-target counter is never incremented twice. The IP leg is skipped entirely because `trustProxyHeaders` defaults to `false` (routes.ts:128). Result: zero throttling of account creation.

User records are written with `store.putUser` and carry NO TTL (storage/store.ts:200-205), so the growth is permanent — there is no eviction and no admin cleanup path in the SDK.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker loops POST /api/auth/register with a freshly generated Solana keypair, a fresh email, authPublicKey='a'.repeat(64), and wallets:[{chain:"solana",role:"<10 MB string>",publicKey:"p",encryptedSecret:"c",junk:"<10 MB string>"} x16]. Each request is 201 and permanently writes a multi-hundred-KB-to-multi-MB row. MEASURED against dist/: 200 consecutive registrations => 200x 201, 0x 429 (default config, maxAttempts 10/60s); a single request with a 200 KB `role` plus a 200 KB extra key persisted a 400,398-byte record. On Upstash/Vercel KV (metered per byte and per command) this is a direct billing attack; on Postgres/Supabase it fills the disk and takes the app down for every tenant sharing the instance.
raw_findings.recommendation: (a) Bound `role` (e.g. <= 32 chars, or an allowlist of the roles the SDK actually uses) and REBUILD each entry from its four known fields rather than storing the client object verbatim: `{chain: e.chain, role: e.role, publicKey: e.publicKey, encryptedSecret: e.encryptedSecret}`. That also kills any `__proto__`/unknown-key passthrough into the record. (b) Add a total serialized-record byte cap enforced in persistUser. (c) Give /register a rate-limit leg that an attacker cannot re-key at will — the client IP when trustProxyHeaders is on, plus a global per-app account-creation counter (e.g. `{endpoint:"register", appId, identifier: appId}`) so unbounded signup is throttled even with a fresh identifier every time.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "8192|too many wallets|encryptedSecret too large|maxWalletsPerUser" tests/ src/ — the only test is tests/audit-server.test.ts:204-220 ("SERVERSIDE-4 RESOLVED — import-wallet enforces a per-user total cap"), which asserts the COUNT cap only. tests/server.test.ts:306-351 ("wallet payload validation (M3)") covers >16 entries, bad chain, and a missing field — never a field's length. grep -rn 'role' tests/*.ts | grep -i 'long|length|too|size|8192|bound' returns nothing. No test anywhere registers more than a handful of accounts, so the absent account-creation throttle is uncharacterized. Both halves measured against dist/.

raw_findings.title: Type confusion on `email`: a JSON array passes validateEmail and reaches normalizeEmail, throwing an unhandled TypeError on three unauthenticated routes
raw_findings.description:
`validateEmail` never checks `typeof email === "string"`. For a one-element array, `email.length` is `1` (passes the `> 320` bound) and `EMAIL_RE.test(email)` string-coerces `["a@b.com"]` to `"a@b.com"` (passes the regex). The value then flows into `resolvePublicKeyByEmail -> store.getPublicKeyByEmail -> emailKey -> normalizeEmail`, which calls `email.toLowerCase()` on an array and throws. The throw is not caught anywhere in the handler chain, so the returned Promise rejects. Reachable unauthenticated on `/challenge` (routes.ts:231), `/login` (routes.ts:367) and `/register` (routes.ts:299).

The same missing `typeof` check exists in `validateAppId` (an array or a number coerces and is accepted; `allowedAppIds.includes()` uses strict `===` so the allowlist at least fails closed) and in `validateAuthPublicKey` — I confirmed `authPublicKey: ["cc…64"]` is accepted and persisted as a JSON array, permanently bricking that account's login because `hexToBytes` has no `.startsWith` on an array. The bounded fields `publicKey` and `pbkdf2Iterations` DO type-check their input, so this is an inconsistency in the validator set, not a deliberate design choice.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Unauthenticated POST /api/auth/challenge with body {"email":["a@b.com"]}. Under Next.js the rejection is caught by the framework and returned as a 500 (error-log flood, and a cheap way to poison error budgets/alerting). `createAuthHandlers` is however explicitly documented as "framework-agnostic Web Request/Response" (routes.ts:1-2) and is wired directly into Express/Hono/Bun/plain-node servers; a host that awaits the handler without a try/catch hits Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` and the process exits — an unauthenticated one-request remote kill, repeatable into a crash loop. PROVEN against dist/: `challenge{email:[..]} => THREW TypeError: email.toLowerCase is not a function`, identically for login and register.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add an explicit `typeof x !== "string"` guard as the first line of validateEmail, validateAppId and validateAuthPublicKey (and to the `signature`/`challenge` reads, which are also unchecked). Regex `.test()` and `String()` coercion must never serve as the type check. Separately, wrap each exported handler body in a try/catch returning a generic 500 Response so no handler can ever reject — the SDK cannot assume its host catches for it.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "type confusion|typeof|non-string" over tests/audit-zai-fixes.test.ts, tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts and tests/server.test.ts — the ONLY type-check test in the suite is audit-zai-fixes.test.ts "rejects a non-number ('600000' string)" for pbkdf2Iterations (F3). tests/audit-server.test.ts:222-264 ("SERVERSIDE-11 RESOLVED — input validation rejects malformed publicKey / email") passes only STRING inputs ("   ", "x".repeat(100_000), "not-an-email"). tests/v050-storage-seam.test.ts:210 covers the oversized-string email on /login, again a string. grep -rln "__proto__" tests/ returns nothing. No test sends a non-string for email, appId or authPublicKey. Confirmed by executing all three routes against dist/.

raw_findings.title: Unauthenticated challenge overwrite lets anyone invalidate a named user's in-flight login
raw_findings.description:
`issueChallenge` performs an unconditional `putChallenge` for `(appId, publicKey)`. There is exactly one challenge slot per identity, and `/challenge` is unauthenticated and accepts any `publicKey`, or any `email` which it resolves to a publicKey (routes.ts:229-234). A third party can therefore overwrite the challenge a victim is in the middle of signing; the victim's subsequent /login or /login-wallet presents the stale value, `takeChallenge` returns the attacker-issued one, and `timingSafeEqual` fails.

This is a DIFFERENT mechanism from the rate-limiter lockout already characterized in tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts: it needs no counter exhaustion at all — one or two requests, well under `maxAttempts`, deny a login round trip, and the victim can never win the race because the attacker always gets to write last.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: For a deployment with derivable emails (the sustained-lockout test file cites Tetrac's own `{telegramId}@telegram.tetrac.xyz` scheme) or any wallet address visible on chain, an attacker sends POST /challenge {email: victim} once every couple of seconds. Every one of the victim's login attempts fails with 401 "Invalid credentials" — indistinguishable from a wrong passkey, so the victim believes they have lost their credentials and their non-custodial wallet. Traffic stays under the published limit, so the counter defense never triggers. PROVEN against dist/: the victim's challenge != the attacker-issued challenge, and the victim's login with a correctly signed, non-expired, never-used challenge returns 401 Invalid credentials.
raw_findings.recommendation: Stop keying the challenge slot solely on the identity. Either (a) make the challenge self-identifying — store under `(appId, publicKey, challengeId)` and have the client echo the id, so a fresh issue cannot clobber a pending one; or (b) keep a small bounded ring of live challenges per identity and have consumeChallenge atomically remove whichever member matches. Either way, issuing a challenge for an identity must not destroy that identity's outstanding challenges.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn "overwrit|re-issue|reissue|second challenge|invalidat" tests/*.ts — hits are server.test.ts:125 (connect-wallet not overwriting KEYS), storage-hash.test.ts:150 (hset semantics), concurrent-safety.test.ts:172 (email index). tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts:47-119 covers atomic get-and-delete and per-publicKey isolation, i.e. replay, not clobbering. tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts covers the counter-based lockout and its self-heal fix — a different mechanism this attack does not need. No test issues two challenges for one identity and then tries the first.

raw_findings.title: Account enumeration across distinct emails is unlimited under the default config (WI-4's mitigation only covers same-email repeats and trusted-proxy deployments)
raw_findings.description:
`/challenge` answers 200 (plus the account's `pbkdf2Iterations`) for a registered email and 400 "publicKey or email required" for an unknown one. The mitigation is a rate-limit bucket keyed on `identifier: body?.email` — i.e. on the very value being enumerated, so each probed email gets its OWN fresh counter and probing N distinct emails costs nothing. The only leg that would catch cross-email probing is the IP bucket, and `rateLimited` runs it exclusively `if (config.trustProxyHeaders)`, which defaults to `false` (config.ts:163).

`/register` is a second, equivalent oracle: 409 "Account already exists" for a taken email vs 201 for a free one, also bucketed by `body.email`.

The defense is real but incomplete in exactly the default configuration — the existing test names admit the boundary: "repeated /challenge for the SAME unknown email is throttled" and "trusted proxy: … across DIFFERENT emails".
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker with a list of a target company's employee emails (or a breach corpus) POSTs /api/auth/challenge {"email":"x"} once per candidate against any default-configured deployment. 200 => the person holds a non-custodial wallet with this app; 400 => they do not. There is no throttle, so the full list is checked at line rate, and the response additionally discloses each account's pinned PBKDF2 iteration count — revealing which accounts sit at the weak legacy 100k tier and are therefore worth attacking offline if the DB is later obtained. MEASURED against dist/ with DEFAULT config: 50 probes across 50 distinct unknown emails => all 400, zero 429; a registered email => 200, unknown => 400.
raw_findings.recommendation: Make /challenge indistinguishable for known and unknown emails: derive a deterministic decoy publicKey (e.g. HMAC(serverSecret, appId:email)) for misses, issue a real-looking challenge and return a plausible pbkdf2Iterations — the login step already fails closed. Add a per-(appId, coarse-source) enumeration counter that does not depend on trustProxyHeaders, and give /register a uniform response for taken vs free emails.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/audit-server.test.ts:68-92, describe "challenge UNKNOWN-email rate limiting (WI-4 enumeration hardening)": the first case probes the SAME email 3x and expects 429; the second case explicitly sets `trustProxyHeaders: true` to get cross-email throttling. Neither covers distinct emails under the shipped default (trustProxyHeaders:false). grep -rni 'enumerat' README.md SECURITY.md returns nothing (both files are 0 bytes). Measured the default-config behaviour directly against dist/.

raw_findings.title: signature and challenge are unbounded strings that are parsed and verified BEFORE the rate limiter runs, so the throttle cannot shed the load
raw_findings.description: login, loginWallet and connectWallet deliberately verify first and rate-limit only on failure (a correct fix for AUTHSESSION-3), but neither `signature` nor `challenge` is type- or length-checked, while every other request field is bounded (email 320, publicKey base58-32-bytes, authPublicKey 64 hex, wallets 16x8192). `hexToBytes` (signature.ts:6-18) runs a `clean.slice(i*2, i*2+2)` + `parseInt` loop over the whole string and allocates `clean.length/2` bytes; `walletLoginMessage(challenge)` plus `nacl.sign.detached.verify` then hash the whole message. All of that happens before `rateLimited(...)` is reached, so a rate-limited attacker still makes the server pay the full cost on every request.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker POSTs /api/auth/login-wallet with a valid publicKey and a 32 MB hex `signature`. MEASURED against dist/ with maxAttempts=1: the request returns 429 — and still consumed 514 ms of blocked, single-threaded event-loop time inside the handler (1 MB => 39 ms, 8 MB => 133 ms, a 20 MB `challenge` => 394 ms). A handful of concurrent uploads stalls the Node event loop for every other user; on serverless (Vercel) it converts attacker bandwidth into billed GB-seconds that the rate limiter is powerless to stop.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add cheap shape guards ahead of every verify call — `typeof signature === "string" && /^(0x)?[0-9a-fA-F]{128}$/.test(signature)` (ed25519 detached signatures are exactly 64 bytes) and `typeof challenge === "string" && HEX64_RE.test(challenge)` (generateChallenge is randomHex(32)). Both are near-O(1) rejects that preserve the verify-first property while making the pre-rate-limit work constant.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rn '8192|too many wallets|encryptedSecret too large' src/ shows length bounds only for wallet fields; routes.ts contains no bound on signature or challenge anywhere. tests/signature-edge-cases.test.ts and tests/timing-safe-edge-cases.test.ts cover malformed/odd-length hex and OOB reads in timingSafeEqual (audit F8) — correctness, not size. tests/ledger-login.test.ts covers the off-chain envelope candidates. No test measures handler cost or asserts a length bound on signature/challenge. Timings measured against dist/.

raw_findings.title: Next.js action dispatcher resolves inherited Object.prototype properties, returning a non-Response or throwing instead of 404
raw_findings.description: `postRoutes` and `getRoutes` are plain object literals, and the dispatcher indexes them with the raw, attacker-controlled catch-all segment. `Object.prototype` members are inherited, so `postRoutes["constructor"]` is the `Object` function (truthy and callable) and `postRoutes["toString"]` is `Object.prototype.toString`. The `handler ? … : error("Not found", 404)` guard never fires for those names, and the declared `Promise<Response>` return type does not hold.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Unauthenticated POST to /api/auth/constructor or /api/auth/toString returns a raw Request/String object to Next.js instead of a Response (Next then throws its own internal error); POST /api/auth/__proto__ and /api/auth/hasOwnProperty throw a TypeError out of the handler. PROVEN against dist/: `POST /__proto__ => THREW TypeError: handler is not a function`; `POST /constructor => (NOT a Response: [object Request])`; `POST /toString => (NOT a Response: [object String])`; `POST /hasOwnProperty => THREW TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object`. Impact is a 500 plus error-log flood on four well-known unauthenticated paths rather than the intended 404 — cheap alert fatigue and a fingerprint that the deployment runs this SDK.
raw_findings.recommendation: Build the tables with `Object.create(null)` or a `Map`, and/or gate the lookup on `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(postRoutes, action)`. A `Map<string, Handler>` with `.get()` is the smallest change and makes the class of bug unrepresentable.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep -rln "constructor|__proto__|prototype" tests/ returns only tests/ui-login-panel-ux.test.tsx (unrelated UI test). tests/next-routes.test.ts:59-64 and :76-81 assert 404 for the arbitrary unknown actions "nope" and "whatever" — never for an inherited property name. Verified against dist/next.

raw_findings.title: Insecure defaults plus zero shipped documentation: allowedAppIds off, appId "ttc", trustProxyHeaders off, and README.md / SECURITY.md are empty files
raw_findings.description:
Every integrator obligation this SDK's security properties depend on lives ONLY in source comments, and `package.json` sets `"files": ["dist"]` — so an npm consumer receives neither the source nor any prose. `README.md` and `SECURITY.md` in the repo are both 0 bytes, and `audits/` is empty; `grep -rn "allowedAppIds|trustProxyHeaders|enumerat" README.md SECURITY.md` returns nothing.

The defaults that need documenting are exactly the ones that fail open:
- `allowedAppIds` is undefined, so `validateAppId` accepts ANY well-formed appId from the request body or the `ttc-app-id` header. On a shared DB an attacker mints arbitrary namespaces (compounding the /register storage finding), writes records into another tenant's namespace, and probes tenants via /search-wallet?appId=… (exists:true vs 404). config.ts:78-82 calls an allowlist "STRONGLY recommended in production" — but nothing enforces or surfaces it.
- `appId: "ttc"` is the default and is mixed into the PBKDF2 salt, so a deployment that never overrides it gets NO cross-app key isolation and shares a precomputation domain with every other default deployment (config.ts:66: "provides NO cross-app isolation — override it in production").
- `trustProxyHeaders: false` disables the IP rate-limit leg entirely (routes.ts:128), which is what makes the enumeration and account-creation findings above reachable.
- Email ownership is never verified — tests/audit-server.test.ts:132-141 calls it "an integrator obligation", which an integrator who never reads the test file will not know.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator installs @tetrac/login-sdk from npm, follows the doc-free public surface, and deploys on Vercel against a shared Upstash instance with no config beyond `storage`. They get: default appId "ttc" (no key-domain separation), no appId allowlist (any client can write into any namespace of their shared DB), no IP rate limiting (unbounded email enumeration and unbounded account creation), and no email verification (anyone can claim any email). Nothing in the shipped package tells them otherwise and there is no boot-time warning.
raw_findings.evidence:
export const DEFAULT_CONFIG: AuthConfig = {
  appId: "ttc", // override per-deployment for cross-app key isolation (see AuthConfig.appId)
  securityLevel: 2,
  challengeTtlSeconds: 300,
  sessionHeader: "ttc-auth-token",
  publicKeyHeader: "ttc-public-key",
  appIdHeader: "ttc-app-id",
  sessionTtlSeconds: 14_400,
  bindSessionToUserAgent: false,
  trustProxyHeaders: false,
  trustedProxyHops: 0,
raw_findings.recommendation: Emit a one-time boot-time console warning from `createAuthHandlers` when `config.appId === "ttc"` or `config.allowedAppIds` is undefined (the SDK already has a storage preflight concept to hang this on). Ship a real README/SECURITY.md documenting the four obligations above, and consider making `appId` a REQUIRED option with no default so cross-app key separation cannot be silently forgotten.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `wc -l README.md SECURITY.md` => 0 for both; `ls audits` => empty. grep -rn 'allowedAppIds|trustProxyHeaders' across all .md files in the repo returns nothing. tests/multi-app.test.ts exercises appId isolation only with explicitly configured appIds, and tests/clientip-proxy.test.ts covers XFF parsing rather than the default's consequences. No test or doc asserts any boot-time guidance.

raw_findings.title: Registration's email-collision check is TOCTOU and the email index write is unconditional last-write-wins
raw_findings.description: The 409 collision check and the subsequent `persistUser` are two separate round trips with no compare-and-set between them, and `KvAuthStore.putUser` writes the index with a plain `hset` (storage/store.ts:200-205). Two concurrent /register calls for the same email can both pass the check; the second `hset` then silently replaces the first account's `email -> publicKey` mapping, orphaning the first user's record and their encrypted wallets (they can no longer resolve their publicKey from their email). Reported as low because the maintainers have already characterized it — but the characterization test asserts nothing that would fail if it regressed or worsened; it only logs the observed statuses.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who can observe or trigger a victim's signup (an invite flow, or simply flooding /register for a predictable corporate email while onboarding is running) fires concurrent registrations for the same email. If both land, the attacker's publicKey wins the index and the victim's record is orphaned — the victim's /login now resolves to the attacker's account. A narrow timing window, not a reliable takeover, but the consequence when it lands is loss of access to a non-custodial wallet.
raw_findings.recommendation: Make the email claim atomic in the AuthStore port: add `claimEmail(appId, email, publicKey): Promise<boolean>` implemented as HSETNX / INSERT-ON-CONFLICT-DO-NOTHING, make it a required conformance case alongside the existing atomic-takeChallenge invariant, and have /register return 409 when it returns false.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts:155-187 — "two concurrent registrations with same email — only one succeeds" — the comment at :169-176 states plainly "in a race, both may see no existing email and both create… the SECOND registration overwrites the first's email->publicKey index", the test is explicitly labelled "informational — it documents the race condition", the computed `twoHundreds` count is never asserted on, and the only expectation is `expect(storedPk).not.toBeNull()`. So this is KNOWN and UNFIXED with no guarding assertion. src/storage/store.ts:200-205 confirms the write is still an unconditional hset in v0.6.0.

raw_findings.title: Gate-mode passkey secret is a UI gate only — any same-origin script decrypts it with zero WebAuthn assertion
raw_findings.description: When the authenticator does not support the PRF extension, `registerPasskey` falls back to "gate" mode and stores a random 32-byte secret in IndexedDB as `{ cryptoKey, iv, ciphertext }` — the AES-GCM key handle is stored IN THE SAME RECORD as the ciphertext it protects (`gateStore`, lines 202-219). `crypto.subtle.generateKey(..., false, ["encrypt","decrypt"])` marks the key non-extractable, which prevents exporting the RAW KEY BYTES, but it does not prevent USING the key: any script on the origin can open the same DB, read the same record, and call `crypto.subtle.decrypt` with the stored handle. The WebAuthn assertion in `derivePasskeySecret` is therefore purely advisory — the code shape is literally `if (assertion) { gateLoad() }` with the assertion result never bound to the decryption, never verified (no rawId / clientDataJSON / authenticatorData / UV-flag check), and discarded entirely. For an account created with `registerWithBiometric`, this gate secret IS the app key (`authClient.ts:392 const appKey = await derivePasskeySecret(registration)`), which `core/crypto.ts:66 importAesGcmKey` imports directly as the AES-256-GCM key for every wallet ciphertext. The module header at webauthn.ts:155-159 asserts the opposite: "Reading the record back yields nothing usable without crypto.subtle.decrypt, which can only run via the in-memory non-extractable key handle" — the handle is persisted in the record, so that sentence describes no barrier at all.
raw_findings.recommendation: A browser-local "gate" cannot be a cryptographic gate — there is no origin-scoped secret that a same-origin script cannot also use. Either (a) remove gate mode and fail closed when `ext.prf?.enabled` is false (`throw new Error('This device cannot protect a passkey-derived key: PRF unsupported')`), or (b) keep it but rename it honestly, require it to be explicitly opted into (`webauthn.allowNonPrfFallback: false` by default), surface `registration.mode` in the returned `AuthResult`/hook state, and delete the webauthn.ts:153-159 comment block claiming at-rest safety it does not provide. Do not present gate mode to integrators or users as biometric protection of key material.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep'd tests/webauthn-gate.test.ts, tests/biometric-gate-resistance.test.ts, tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts, tests/webauthn-migration.test.ts and all tests/audit-*.test.ts. Every gate-mode test exercises raw WebCrypto primitives only (`round-trips a hex secret through a non-extractable AES-GCM key`, `the wrapping key is non-extractable (exportKey rejects)`, `decrypt fails when the ciphertext is tampered`, IV reuse). NOT ONE test asserts that a fresh assertion is required to obtain the gate secret, and none simulates a same-origin reader. The only fail-closed assertion test, tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:263 `a declined/absent assertion fails closed`, is run against a **prf** registration (`freshEnable(appKey, "prf")`) and only covers the honest caller going through the SDK API. tests/webauthn-migration.test.ts:8 even states the property outright as a test convenience: "the assertion result is unused on the gate path".

raw_findings.title: enableBiometricUnlock silently degrades to gate mode, persisting ANY account's app key at rest and breaking the memory-only vault invariant
raw_findings.description: `deriveWrapKey` HKDFs the wrapping key from `secretHex` — the value returned by `derivePasskeySecret`. In PRF mode that is a value re-derived from the authenticator on every call and never stored, so the wrapped blob really is inert at rest. In gate mode it is the IndexedDB-resident secret from finding #1, recoverable by any same-origin script. The HKDF salt is `b64urlDecode(credentialId)` and the info string is the constant "ttc-biometric-unlock-v1" — both public and sitting in the same localStorage the attacker already reads (`MARKER_KEY = "ttc_biometric_unlock"`, line 39; `REG_KEY = "ttc_biometric_reg"` in useBiometricUnlock.ts:19). So for a gate-mode credential the entire wrap is transparent: gate secret -> HKDF -> AES key -> app key. This is a strict regression against the SDK's headline client-vault guarantee (`session.ts:4-7`: "The app (encryption) key lives in MEMORY ONLY ... storage-scraping XSS finds no key at rest") and it applies to EVERY account type — an email or Web3 account that merely turns on 'unlock with Touch ID' has its app key durably at rest. Nothing surfaces the degradation: `enableBiometricUnlock` returns the registration but never inspects `mode`, `UseBiometricUnlockResult` (useBiometricUnlock.ts:48-63) exposes no `mode` field, and the hook JSON.stringifies the registration straight into localStorage without looking at it.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An email-account user on a non-PRF platform authenticator clicks 'Enable biometric unlock' (the SDK prompts Touch ID twice, so the user is convinced the key is now hardware-protected). `registerPasskey` returns mode 'gate'; `wrapAppKey` writes the PBKDF2-derived app key into `unlock_blobs` under a key derived from a secret that lives in `gate_secrets` on the same origin. Later, XSS on the app (or a malicious extension) runs: read `gate_secrets[credId]`, `crypto.subtle.decrypt` it to get `secretHex`, read `localStorage['ttc_biometric_unlock']` for the credentialId, redo `HKDF-SHA256(ikm=secretHex, salt=b64urlDecode(credId), info='ttc-biometric-unlock-v1')`, decrypt `unlock_blobs[credId]` -> the account's real app key. This works when the vault is LOCKED and the user is absent — precisely the window the memory-only design was built to protect, and precisely the window XSS would otherwise have found empty. The attacker never triggers a biometric prompt.
raw_findings.recommendation: Refuse to enable biometric unlock on a non-PRF credential: after `registerPasskey`, `if (registration.mode !== "prf") throw new Error("Biometric unlock requires an authenticator with PRF support")`. If the fallback must stay, expose `mode` on `UseBiometricUnlockResult` and in the `enable()` return so an integrator can warn the user, and correct the AT-REST SAFETY comment to state that gate-mode blobs are recoverable by same-origin script.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts is the feature's audit test. Its gate-mode case (line 229 `gate mode: round-trips a web3-style app key`) only checks the happy-path round-trip; the fail-closed cases test a tampered blob and a declined assertion in PRF mode. No test asserts that gate-mode enablement is refused, that `mode` is surfaced, or that an attacker without an assertion cannot reach the wrapped key. grep of tests/audit-client-vault.test.ts confirms the memory-only invariant is tested (`expect(sessionStorage.getItem("ttc_ek")).toBeNull(); // storage-scraping XSS finds nothing`) but never re-checked after enableBiometricUnlock.

raw_findings.title: Silent PRF->gate downgrade makes a biometric-primary account's wallets device-bound and permanently unrecoverable
raw_findings.description: `registerPasskey` decides the mode from `config.preferPrf && ext.prf?.enabled`; when the authenticator has no PRF the mode silently becomes 'gate' and `gateStore` mints a fresh `randomBytes(32)`. `AuthClient.registerWithBiometric` then makes that value the account's app key and encrypts the whole wallet bundle under it. The consequence is that a biometric-primary account's ONLY copy of the key that decrypts its wallets is a random value in one browser profile's IndexedDB, with no server-side escrow (by design), no derivation from anything the user knows or holds, and no export prompt. It is not backed by the authenticator at all — a synced passkey (iCloud Keychain, 1Password) will happily assert on a second device, `allowCredentials` will match, the assertion will succeed, and then `gateLoad` returns null. The mode is never surfaced to the integrator or user: `registerWithBiometric` returns `{ result, registration }` and `PasskeyRegistration.mode` is the only signal, which `BiometricMethod.tsx:64` passes to `onRegistered` without inspection.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not attacker-driven — a guaranteed-loss footgun, and one a hostile operator can also weaponize. Concrete path: user signs up with 'Continue with biometric' on a device whose platform authenticator lacks PRF. Wallets are generated, encrypted under the gate secret, and the ciphertext is stored server-side. The user funds the wallet. Then any of: they clear site data; Safari ITP evicts IndexedDB after 7 days without a first-party interaction; the browser evicts under storage pressure; they get a new phone/laptop and use their synced passkey; they use a second browser. `derivePasskeySecret` throws `Gate secret not found for this credential` and `loginWithBiometric` fails permanently. The wallet ciphertext on the server is undecryptable by anyone, forever. A hostile app operator can also engineer this deliberately (ship `preferPrf: false`) so every user's key is a value the operator's own JS can read from IndexedDB while the user believes it is Touch-ID-protected.
raw_findings.recommendation: Abort `registerWithBiometric` when `registration.mode !== 'prf'` rather than creating an account whose key cannot survive the browser profile. If gate mode is retained, (a) return `mode` in the AuthResult so the app can force an immediate key export/backup, (b) document in the type that a gate-mode biometric account is single-browser-profile and non-recoverable, and (c) have `BiometricMethod` render a warning instead of an identical 'Continue with biometric' button.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep'd tests/ for 'gate' and 'preferPrf': tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:191 sets `preferPrf: true` and flips `credMode` manually to exercise both branches; nothing tests the recoverability/portability consequence, and no test asserts that gate-mode primary registration is refused or flagged. No mention in CHANGELOG.md/README.md/SECURITY.md (all three files are empty, 0 lines).

raw_findings.title: Wrapped app-key blobs and gate secrets are orphaned in IndexedDB by re-enrollment and by a fire-and-forget logout purge
raw_findings.description: Every purge path is keyed off the SINGLE credentialId held in `localStorage[MARKER_KEY]`. `enableBiometricUnlock` overwrites that marker (line 183) without first purging whatever the previous marker pointed at, and `useBiometricUnlock.enable` (useBiometricUnlock.ts:100-109) likewise overwrites `REG_KEY` with `saveReg(reg)` and never calls `disable()` first. So a second enrollment strands enrollment #1's `unlock_blobs` entry AND (in gate mode) its `gate_secrets` entry in IndexedDB with nothing left pointing at them — `disableBiometricUnlock`, the logout hook, and `purge()` can all only reach the current marker. Second orphan source: the logout hook removes the marker synchronously and then fires `void blobDelete(credentialId).catch(() => {})` / `void gateDelete(...)` as unawaited promises; a logout immediately followed by a navigation or tab close (the common case — `AuthClient.logout()` is explicitly designed for that: 'logout is instant and never blocked by the network') drops those IndexedDB transactions on the floor, leaving both records behind with the marker already gone.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: User enables biometric unlock, later re-enrolls (new device passkey, 'Touch ID stopped working', or an app that calls enable() on each login). Orphan blob #1 — an AES-GCM ciphertext of the account's real app key — now lives in IndexedDB permanently, surviving `disable()`, `logout()`, and account switch; the UI reports `isEnabled: false` and the user believes the state is gone. In gate mode the matching orphaned `gate_secrets` record is right beside it, so an attacker with XSS/extension access at ANY later time recovers `unlock_blobs.getAllKeys()`, pairs each with `gate_secrets[k]`, decrypts, HKDFs, and unwraps the app key — with no assertion (finding #1/#2) and no live session. The same holds for the logout-race orphan: the user logs out on a shared machine, closes the tab, and their app key is still sitting decryptable on that machine.
raw_findings.recommendation: In `enableBiometricUnlock`, read the existing marker and `await purge(previousCredentialId)` before writing the new one. Make purge exhaustive rather than marker-driven: `IDBObjectStore.clear()` both `unlock_blobs` and `gate_secrets` on logout/disable (there is never a legitimate reason to keep a blob for a credential you are not currently using). Await the deletes in `disableBiometricUnlock`, and in the logout hook prefer clearing the stores over a per-key delete so a dropped transaction leaves nothing selectively behind.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:273 (`disable purges the blob`) and :289 (`clearSession (logout) purges the unlock blob + gate secret`) both test a SINGLE enrollment and both explicitly drain the microtask queue (`await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0))`) before asserting — i.e. the test harness papers over exactly the fire-and-forget window that a real navigation would truncate. No test enrolls twice, and no test asserts the store is empty (only `store.get(reg.credentialId)` is checked).

raw_findings.title: Unlock blob is not bound to an account, appId, or session — unlockViaBiometric arms whatever key it decrypts
raw_findings.description: The wrapped blob is keyed only by `credentialId` and its plaintext is a bare app-key string; `wrapAppKey` passes no `additionalData` to AES-GCM and stores no `publicKey`, `appId`, `email`, or `authMethod` alongside it. `unlockViaBiometric` then calls `armAppKey(appKey)` unconditionally, with no check that the recovered key belongs to the account currently in the session (`getPublicKey()` is never consulted). The vault it arms is the process-global one shared by every bundle copy (`session.ts:62 Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")`), so the wrong key becomes the ambient signing/decryption key for every downstream `useSigner`/`decryptWalletSecret`/import path. `deriveWrapKey` also omits `appId`, so on an origin hosting more than one SDK deployment the identical blob is unwrappable by each of them.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Shared/kiosk browser, or any app where logout does not run (tab closed, server-side session TTL expiry, an app that calls `clearSession` only on explicit logout). User A logs in, enables biometric unlock — blob wraps A's app key, marker + registration persist in localStorage. The tab is closed without logout, so the purge hook never fires. User B (same OS account / same enrolled biometric on that device) opens the app; `hasBiometricUnlock()` returns true, the UI offers 'Unlock', the assertion succeeds against the device's own biometric, and A's app key is armed into the vault while the session/publicKey headers belong to B. Every wallet decrypt for B then fails opaquely; worse, any flow that ENCRYPTS under the armed key (wallet import / re-encryption) writes ciphertext into B's server record that only A's key can ever open — silent, permanent loss of the imported key. The same primitive makes cross-app confusion possible on a shared origin since appId is absent from the derivation.
raw_findings.recommendation: Store `{ v, appId, publicKey, iv, ciphertext }` and pass `additionalData = utf8(`${appId}:${publicKey}`)` to both encrypt and decrypt, so a blob cryptographically refuses to open outside the account it was made for. In `unlockViaBiometric`, compare the blob's `publicKey` against `getPublicKey()` before `armAppKey` and throw otherwise. Mix `appId` into the HKDF info string (`ttc-biometric-unlock-v2:${appId}`) for cross-app separation on a shared origin. Note the SDK already treats appId as the domain separator everywhere else (`core/crypto.ts:30 sha256(`${appId}:${email...}`)`, config.ts:54-74) — this path is the exception.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep'd tests/multi-app.test.ts and tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts for appId/publicKey binding on the unlock path: multi-app.test.ts covers server-side appId namespacing of pubKey/session/challenge/rate-limit keys only; biometric-unlock.test.ts's DISTINCTION GUARD (line 321) checks that `{registration}` and `{biometricUnlock}` resolve to different keys for the same credential, but never that a blob refuses to open for a different account. No test arms an unlock blob against a mismatched session.

raw_findings.title: The WebAuthn ceremony is never validated and never reaches the server — challenge is client-generated, UV is requested but not verified
raw_findings.description: Both ceremonies use a locally generated `challenge: randomBytes(32)`, and `derivePasskeySecret` inspects nothing about the returned assertion beyond `if (!assertion)`: `rawId` is never compared to `reg.credentialId`, `clientDataJSON` (type/origin/challenge) is never parsed, `authenticatorData` is never parsed, so the UV and UP flags and the signature counter are never checked, and the assertion signature itself is never verified against anything. `userVerification: "required"` is requested on both create and get but is only ever a request. The server correspondingly never sees a WebAuthn artifact: `loginWithBiometric` proves control with an ed25519 signature over the SERVER's challenge using a key derived from the passkey secret (`authKey.ts:24 signAuthChallenge`), and `routes.ts:370 verifyAuthSignature` is the only check. In PRF mode this is sound — the PRF output cannot be produced without the authenticator, so the crypto carries the ceremony. It is worth stating precisely because (a) an integrator reading 'WebAuthn biometric login' will assume the server has evidence a user-verifying ceremony occurred, and it has none; (b) in gate mode a Chrome DevTools virtual authenticator or any patched client satisfies the gate; (c) if a browser/authenticator combination silently degrades `required` to presence-only, the SDK cannot detect it. `registerPasskey` also never checks that the created credential's `rp.id` matches, and `rpIdOf` (line 61-63) accepts any operator-supplied `config.rpId`, so an operator can widen the credential to the registrable parent domain and share it across every subdomain.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: (a) Integrator-facing: an app builds an authorization decision on 'the user logged in with biometric, so a user-verifying ceremony happened on this request' — it did not; the server saw only an ed25519 signature, which for a gate-mode account is backed by a same-origin-readable secret (finding #1). (b) A malicious client driving the page through CDP enables a virtual authenticator with `hasUserVerification:false, isUserVerified:true`, and every gate-mode ceremony (login, `revealSecret({registration})` behind ExportKeyPanel's 'Confirm with Face ID / Touch ID to reveal', `unlockViaBiometric`) passes with no human present. (c) An operator setting `webauthn.rpId` to the eTLD+1 makes the credential assertable from every subdomain, so a compromised marketing subdomain can drive assertions for the wallet app's credential.
raw_findings.recommendation: Document explicitly that the WebAuthn ceremony is a CLIENT-SIDE key-derivation step, not a server-verified authentication factor, and that all server-side assurance comes from the PRF-derived ed25519 key. In PRF mode, additionally parse `authenticatorData` and reject when the UV bit (0x04) is clear, and compare `assertion.rawId` to `reg.credentialId` — cheap defense against a downgrading platform. If server-verified WebAuthn is ever wanted, the challenge must be issued by `/challenge` and the assertion verified server-side against a stored credential public key.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep'd tests/ for clientDataJSON, authenticatorData, rawId, origin, and challenge freshness on the WebAuthn path — zero hits. tests/webauthn-migration.test.ts:80-88 confirms the property is relied upon rather than defended: the mock is `get: async () => ({ getClientExtensionResults: () => ({}) })` with the comment 'Gate-path assertion: only "non-null with extension results" matters', and gate unlock succeeds against an assertion object that has no rawId, no clientDataJSON and no authenticatorData.

raw_findings.title: WebAuthn credential ID is transmitted and persisted server-side as the account email, creating a credential-ID oracle and a squattable namespace
raw_findings.description: `biometricEmail()` builds the account identifier as `bio_${reg.credentialId}@passkey.local` and it is sent to `/challenge`, `/register`, and `/login` and stored in `UserData.email` plus the email index. Under the stated threat model (attacker reads the DB) this exposes every biometric user's raw WebAuthn credential ID, which is the stable, cross-session identifier of their authenticator credential and also the HKDF salt for the unlock wrap key (biometricUnlock.ts:66). Because `/challenge` returns 200 + challenge for a known identifier and 400 `publicKey or email required` for an unknown one (routes.ts:229-233), any credential ID becomes probeable for account existence. Separately, `/register` requires no proof of possession for non-wallet methods — `else if (!body.authPublicKey) return error(...)` is the entire check (routes.ts:313-315) — while a duplicate email returns 409 (routes.ts:298-301), so the `bio_*@passkey.local` namespace is squattable by any caller: `EMAIL_RE = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/` accepts these addresses, so they are indistinguishable from ordinary email accounts. Note also that base64url credential IDs are case-SENSITIVE while the email index case-folds them (`storage/store.ts:67 normalizeEmail -> email.toLowerCase().trim()`, applied at `store.ts:180`), shrinking the identifier space; the practical collision risk for authenticator-generated IDs is negligible, but the identifier is being normalized in a way its encoding does not permit.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker with DB read (leaked backup, world-readable Supabase `public` schema, replica) harvests every biometric user's credential ID and can (a) correlate the same authenticator across any other system that exposes credential IDs, and (b) confirm which app deployments a given credential is enrolled on by probing `/challenge`. Squatting: a caller who learns a credential ID before the victim registers on that app posts `/register` with `email: bio_<credId>@passkey.local`, `authMethod: "email"`, and an attacker-chosen `authPublicKey`; the victim's later `registerWithBiometric` gets 409 `Account already exists` with no fallback path in the client (authClient.ts:400), permanently blocking that authenticator credential from that deployment.
raw_findings.recommendation: Do not use the raw credential ID as the account identifier. Derive the internal id from the PRF/gate secret instead — e.g. `bio_${sha256('ttc-bio-id-v1:' + appKey).slice(0,32)}@passkey.local` — so the server-stored identifier is unlinkable to the authenticator credential, is not squattable by anyone who merely observed a credential ID, and is hex (case-fold-safe). Longer term, require a proof of possession of `authPublicKey` at registration (sign the server challenge with the auth key) so the email/biometric namespace cannot be claimed without the corresponding private key.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep'd tests/multi-app.test.ts, tests/audit-server.test.ts, tests/server.test.ts and tests/next-routes.test.ts for 'passkey.local' and 'bio_' — zero hits; no test covers the biometric identifier's construction or its exposure. tests/audit-server.test.ts:269 uses a PRF-shaped app key only as an appKey fixture. The unauthenticated-registration property is visible in routes.ts comments (the 409 fallback for email accounts) but the biometric namespace consequence is not addressed anywhere.

raw_findings.title: Default config leaves /register with no effective rate limit — unauthenticated, unbounded, permanent storage writes
raw_findings.description: Two defaults combine to remove every rate-limit ceiling from `/register`. (1) `trustProxyHeaders` defaults to **false** (src/core/config.ts:163), and `rateLimited()` only evaluates the IP bucket `if (config.trustProxyHeaders)` — so on a default deployment the IP leg is skipped entirely. (2) The remaining per-target bucket for `/register` is keyed on `identifier: body.email ?? body.publicKey`, and in the no-email path `publicKey` is a value the CALLER mints — a fresh Solana keypair per request. Every request therefore lands in a brand-new counter, `count === 1`, `allowed: true`, forever. The route then writes `pubKey:{appId}:{publicKey}` via `persistUser` with **no TTL** (src/storage/store.ts:201: `this.kv.set(appScoped(...), JSON.stringify(user))` — no `exSeconds`). `validateWallets` permits 16 entries × 8192-char `encryptedSecret`, so one request persists ~131 KB permanently. The code comment at routes.ts:118-123 asserts the opposite — "Every rate-limited endpoint passes a per-target bucket, so nothing is left unprotected when the IP leg is skipped" — which is false precisely where the target is attacker-minted. Note `maxWalletsPerUser: 64` guards only `/import-wallet` (routes.ts:534), never `/register`.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker generates a fresh ed25519 keypair offline and POSTs `/api/auth/register` with `{publicKey: <fresh base58>, authPublicKey: <64 random hex>, wallets: [16 × {chain:"solana", role:"r", publicKey:"p", encryptedSecret: "A".repeat(8192)}]}` — no email, no session, no signature. Trace: publicKey present → validateAppId ok → validatePublicKey ok (canonical base58) → no email → authPublicKey passes HEX64_RE → validateWallets passes → pbkdf2Iterations absent → rateLimited() skips the IP bucket (trustProxyHeaders false) and the register bucket is fresh → getUserByPublicKey null → authMethod undefined ≠ "wallet" and authPublicKey present → persistUser writes ~131 KB with no TTL → 201. Repeat at 100 req/s = ~13 MB/s = ~1.1 TB/day of permanent rows. On Upstash/Vercel KV that is a direct billing attack; on Redis it is OOM and eviction of live sessions and challenges; on Postgres/Supabase it fills the volume. Rotating `appId` too (allowed by default, see separate finding) multiplies the namespaces so no single-key cleanup helps.
raw_findings.recommendation: Do not rely on a caller-minted identifier as the sole rate-limit key on a CREATE endpoint. Either (a) always evaluate a global/IP bucket for /register with a separate, higher `registerRateLimit` (falling back to the constant "unknown" bucket is acceptable here because register is not an endpoint a victim needs unblocked), or (b) add a config-level global registration ceiling (`maxRegistrationsPerWindow`) enforced against an appId-scoped counter, and (c) cap `wallets` on /register the way /import-wallet is capped by `maxWalletsPerUser`. Also correct the comment at routes.ts:118-123, which currently tells maintainers the gap does not exist.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped tests/ for register + rate-limit coverage: `grep -rn 'register' tests/*.test.ts | grep -i 'rate|429|limit'` returns only tests/rate-limit-self-extend.test.ts:176-197, which registers twice with the SAME email (and even there the assertion is conditional because 409 fires first). `grep -rn '429' tests/*.test.ts` shows coverage for challenge, login, search and the IP bucket, never for register with a rotating publicKey. `grep -rn 'maxWalletsPerUser' tests/` hits only audit-server.test.ts:205 (import-wallet). `grep -rn 'bloat|flood|unbounded' tests/` returns nothing covering this path. Not previously found.

raw_findings.title: No passkey strength policy anywhere — the wallet-encrypting secret is an unconstrained user-typed string, and the strong generator is opt-in
raw_findings.description: For email accounts the app key that encrypts every wallet private key is `PBKDF2(passkey, SHA-256(appId:email), iterations)` (src/core/crypto.ts:23-33). There is no minimum length, no entropy floor, no strength meter, and no server-side rejection of a weak passkey anywhere in the SDK — not in `AuthConfig` (no such knob exists in src/core/config.ts), not in `AuthClient.registerWithEmail` (src/client/authClient.ts:230-254 passes `params.passkey` straight into the KDF), and not in the shipped UI. The `/ui` package DOES contain a correct CSPRNG generator with a 128-bit floor (src/ui/passkey.ts:33 `MIN_PASSKEY_BYTES = 16`), but it is **opt-in**: `passkeyGenerator?: boolean | PasskeyGeneratorConfig` (src/ui/types.ts:177) is undefined by default, and `pkGenConfig` short-circuits with `if (!passkeyGenerator) return null` (EmailMethod.tsx:47), rendering a bare `<input type="password" required>` with no `minLength` and no validation. `1` is an accepted passkey. This matters more here than in a normal password field because the SDK's own threat model states the ciphertext is server-side and the attacker can read the database.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Attacker obtains a database read (leaked backup, read replica, world-readable Supabase `public` schema, slow-query log — all explicitly in scope). Each `pubKey:{appId}:{publicKey}` row is a JSON `UserData` containing `email`, `pbkdf2Iterations`, and `wallets[].encryptedSecret`. The salt is fully derivable: `SHA-256(appId + ":" + normalizedEmail)`, and `appId` is either the published default "ttc" or trivially learned. The attacker now runs a pure offline dictionary attack at 600k PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 per guess against every user, testing candidates by attempting AES-256-GCM decrypt (an exact oracle — the auth tag verifies). Users who typed a common password lose their wallet private keys outright and irreversibly; the SDK's non-custodial claim rests entirely on a secret it never constrains. No online rate limit applies because the attack is offline.
raw_findings.recommendation: Make the generator the DEFAULT (`passkeyGenerator` defaulting to on) rather than opt-in, and add a hard minimum in `AuthClient.registerWithEmail` — reject below a configured `minPasskeyEntropyBits` (default ≥ 80 bits, or a documented length floor) with a typed error rather than silently deriving a weak key. Add the knob to `AuthConfig` so integrators who supply their own UI inherit the floor. Whatever the choice, it must be stated in the (currently empty) README: this is the single secret standing between a database leak and every user's funds.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rniE 'weak passkey|min.*passkey|passkey.*polic|entropy' tests/` — the only hits are tests/ui-login-panel-ux.test.tsx:110-130, which test `generateStrongPasskey`'s own 16-byte clamp (the opt-in generator), never the typed-input path. `grep -rn 'passkeyGenerator' tests/` returns nothing asserting a default-on behavior. `grep -rn 'minLength|length <|strength|zxcvbn' src/ui src/client` returns nothing. No prior finding covers input-side passkey policy.

raw_findings.title: `allowedAppIds` defaults to undefined — any well-formed appId is accepted, breaking the shared-database multi-tenant model by default
raw_findings.description: `allowedAppIds` is optional and absent from `DEFAULT_CONFIG` (src/core/config.ts:154-184). `validateAppId` therefore only enforces `APP_ID_RE` and skips the allowlist branch entirely: `if (config.allowedAppIds && !config.allowedAppIds.includes(appId))`. Every unauthenticated route reads `appId` from the request body (`const appId = body.appId ?? config.appId` — challenge:204, register:254, login:346, loginWallet:392, connectWallet:437, searchWallet:510) and every authenticated route reads it from a request header (`headerAppId`, routes.ts:158-161). Since `appId` is also the server-side storage namespace, a default-configured deployment lets any anonymous caller operate inside ANY namespace in the shared database — including namespaces belonging to other tenants. The doc comment calls the allowlist "STRONGLY recommended in production", but nothing defaults it on, warns about its absence, or refuses to boot without it, and the README that would say so is 0 bytes.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Two apps share one Redis/Upstash/Postgres, which the SDK advertises as supported (config.ts:70-72). App B is public; App A (appId "app.alpha") is internal or IP-restricted. Neither sets `allowedAppIds`. Against App B's public endpoint the attacker: (1) POSTs `/challenge {appId:"app.alpha", email:"victim@corp.com"}` → 200 with `{challenge, pbkdf2Iterations}` if the account exists on A, 400 if not — a cross-tenant account-enumeration oracle A can neither see nor block; (2) repeats it 11 times in a minute → `ratelimit:challenge:app.alpha:victim@corp.com` is exhausted, so the VICTIM's own /challenge on App A returns 429 — a targeted cross-tenant login lockout, sustainable indefinitely; (3) each call also overwrites `challenge:app.alpha:{victimPk}` (a single key per publicKey, store.ts:212), invalidating A's in-flight logins; (4) POSTs `/register {appId:"app.alpha", publicKey:<attacker pk>, authPublicKey:<hex>}` → App B mints a record AND a session under `pubKey:app.alpha:*` / `session:app.alpha:*`. Because App A's `headerAppId` falls back to its own `config.appId === "app.alpha"`, App A's `/user-data` and `/import-wallet` then accept that bearer token — the attacker is an authenticated App A user without ever reaching App A's registration flow or whatever gating (invite, waitlist, SSO) App A layers on top. (5) Rotating `appId` freely also mints unbounded namespaces, compounding the register-flood finding.
raw_findings.recommendation: Default `allowedAppIds` to `[config.appId]` (fail-closed: a single-app deployment then accepts only its own namespace, which is what single-app deployments actually want) and require an explicit opt-in — e.g. `allowedAppIds: "*"` — for the open-namespace behavior. At minimum, emit a server-side startup warning from `createAuthHandlers` when `allowedAppIds` is undefined AND the deployment is production, mirroring the fail-closed posture already used in `selectStorageBackend`.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rn 'allowedAppIds' tests/ src/` — only tests/multi-app.test.ts:188-197, which asserts that WHEN the allowlist is set an undeclared appId is rejected. No test exercises the DEFAULT (undefined) case, and tests/multi-app.test.ts:200-211 only checks the single-app fallback round-trips. The cross-tenant register/session-mint path via a spoofed appId is not covered anywhere.

raw_findings.title: Default `appId: "ttc"` silently voids the cross-app key domain separation the crypto layer is built on; the only warning is a browser console.warn
raw_findings.description: `appId` is the sole domain separator for app-key derivation: the PBKDF2 salt is `SHA-256(appId : email)` (src/core/crypto.ts:30) and the wallet app-key message is `"...\n\nApp: ${appId}"` (src/core/index.ts:30). Its default is the literal `"ttc"`, shared by every deployment that changes nothing, and the same literal is hardcoded as the default PARAMETER of the exported primitives — `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(..., appId = "ttc")` and `walletAppKeyMessage(appId = "ttc")` — so a caller using the core exports directly gets it even when their `AuthConfig` says otherwise. The only guardrail is a `console.warn` fired in the browser from `AuthClient`'s constructor (src/client/authClient.ts:123-129). There is no equivalent check in `createAuthHandlers`, no production refusal, and the README that would state the requirement is 0 bytes. A console warning is not a control: it is invisible in production builds, invisible to anyone integrating via the React `AuthProvider` on a server-rendered page, and invisible to a code reviewer reading the npm page.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Two independent deployments both ship with the default.
