Grepped tests/ — no test asserts documentation content. Nothing prior addresses this.

raw_findings.title: Ledger app key is firmware-dependent: the off-chain envelope cascade makes SHA-256(sig) non-deterministic per (wallet, appId), risking unrecoverable wallet loss
raw_findings.description: A hardware account's app (encryption) key is SHA-256(hex(sig)) over walletAppKeyMessageHw(appId) (src/client/authClient.ts:298-303). A Ledger cannot sign raw bytes, so it signs an OFF-CHAIN ENVELOPE, and signMessage cascades over TWO structurally different envelopes (legacy 20-byte header, then v0 85-byte header), falling back only on device status 0x6a81. The two envelopes are different preimages -> different ed25519 signatures -> TWO DIFFERENT APP KEYS for the same wallet and same appId. Nothing pins which envelope was used at registration: not client-side, not in UserData (src/core/types.ts:37-73 has no such field), not in anything sent to the server. The server hides the divergence entirely, accepting a signature over the raw message OR either envelope (src/server/signature.ts:47-52), so login SUCCEEDS under either envelope while the app key silently differs. This breaks the SDK's own recovery promise (src/core/crypto.ts:36-38, 'Recoverable on any device by re-signing the same challenge message'). The codebase already solved this exact class of problem for the passkey path by pinning the KDF parameter per user (src/server/routes.ts:244, 'pin the count per-user so future level changes don't orphan this account'); the pattern is not applied to the hardware envelope.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No attacker required; the trigger is routine, and the loss is unrecoverable because the server stores only ciphertext. (1) Alice registers with a Ledger whose Solana app accepts only the v0 header: the legacy attempt returns 0x6a81, v0 succeeds, appKey_v0 encrypts her generated wallet secrets, and the ciphertext is persisted. (2) She updates the Ledger Solana app (or restores the same seed onto a second Ledger with older/newer firmware) so the legacy header is now accepted. The cascade tries legacy FIRST, it succeeds, and she derives appKey_legacy != appKey_v0. (3) /connect-wallet returns 200 and setSession arms appKey_legacy, so she appears fully logged in -- but every decryptWalletSecret throws and revealSecret reports the misleading 'Re-authentication failed - wrong credentials'. connectWallet will not overwrite the stored bundle (src/server/routes.ts:475-481 only backfills when user.wallets is empty), so the ciphertext is intact and permanently undecryptable. A hostile app operator or an XSS payload can also force the v0 branch deliberately (it controls the injected signMessage) to lock a user out of their own wallet while their login still succeeds.
raw_findings.recommendation: Pin the envelope layout per account the way pbkdf2Iterations is pinned: record which candidate produced the app-key signature at registration (e.g. an offchainEnvelope: 'legacy' | 'v0' field on UserData, returned by /challenge like pbkdf2Iterations is) and derive from ONLY that layout on every subsequent login/unlock, failing closed rather than cascading. As an interim mitigation, have deriveAppKey try each candidate and keep the one that successfully decrypts a known wallet.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep of offchainMessageCandidates/encodeOffchainMessage across src+tests; read tests/ledger-login.test.ts in full. Its stability tests (lines 88-116) derive with ledgerSign() -- the LEGACY envelope -- on BOTH sides of every comparison, so they can never observe the legacy-vs-v0 app-key divergence. ledgerSignV0 (line 39) is used only for server signature acceptance (line 59-64), never for deriveAppKeyFromSignature. grep for deriveAppKeyFromSignature across tests confirms no test derives an app key from the v0 envelope. No pin/fallback exists anywhere: grep 'offchainEnvelope|envelope' in src/core/types.ts, src/server, src/storage returns nothing.

raw_findings.title: isPrintableAscii admits newline (0x0A) yet still emits format byte 0x00 (RestrictedAscii), producing an off-chain envelope that violates the Solana spec and that the cascade cannot recover from
raw_findings.description: Solana's off-chain message spec defines MessageFormat::RestrictedAscii as printable ASCII 0x20-0x7E only; a newline is NOT in that set (it belongs to LimitedUtf8). The SDK's isPrintableAscii explicitly whitelists 0x0A and prepareMessage then labels the message format 0x00, so encodeOffchainMessageLegacy/encodeOffchainMessage emit an envelope whose declared format contradicts its own body. The SDK's own comment elsewhere states the consequence: 'a newline (0x0a) makes the device reject the message (status 0x6a82) or demand Blind Signing' (src/core/index.ts:36-39). This is not academic -- the SDK's DEFAULT software app-key message contains two newlines (src/core/index.ts:19-20, 30). Worse, 0x6a82 is not the cascade trigger: signMessage only falls back on '0x6a81' (src/ledger/solanaSigner.ts:91), so a 0x6a82 header rejection aborts the whole flow. The layout comment at line 62 ('Printable ASCII (0x20-0x7e) plus newline (0x0a) - what the RestrictedAscii format allows') asserts something the spec does not say and that src/core/index.ts contradicts.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Not attacker-driven, but it is the mechanical cause of finding #3 (blind-signing coaching) and an interop break. Concretely: an integrator renders <ExportKeyPanel walletSignMessage={ledgerSigner.signMessage}> WITHOUT the optional hardwareWallet prop (the tested default -- tests/ui-hardware-wallet.test.tsx:121-126 asserts hardwareWallet:undefined). authClient.deriveAppKey then selects walletAppKeyMessage(appId), which contains '\n\n'. The SDK builds a legacy envelope with format=0 and a 0x0A body; the device either rejects it (0x6a82, no cascade -> hard failure) or demands blind signing. Separately, any spec-conformant verifier (solana verify-offchain-signature, another wallet) re-deriving the format byte computes format=1 for the same message, producing a DIFFERENT preimage, so a signature the SDK considers valid will not verify anywhere else -- the app key becomes non-portable off this SDK.
raw_findings.recommendation: Make isPrintableAscii spec-exact (0x20..0x7E, drop the 0x0A exemption) so a newline-bearing message is correctly classified LimitedUtf8 (format 1) or rejected with the existing actionable error, and widen the cascade's header-rejection predicate beyond the single literal '0x6a81' (at minimum add 0x6a82 / 0x6a80) so a format rejection falls through to the next candidate instead of aborting.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: Read tests/ledger-signer.test.ts and tests/ledger-login.test.ts in full. ledger-signer.test.ts:190 and :211 assert format byte 0x00 only for the newline-free string 'Hi'. ledger-signer.test.ts:118-129 pushes a message that DOES contain a newline ('Sign in to Tetrac\nnonce: 12345') straight through encodeOffchainMessageLegacy and asserts success -- so the mislabeling is currently baked in as expected behaviour against a mock device that signs anything. ledger-login.test.ts:118-132 only asserts that walletAppKeyMessageHw itself has no newline; it never tests the encoder's behaviour on a newline. grep '0x6a82' across src+tests: one comment in src/core/index.ts, zero code paths, zero tests.

raw_findings.title: The SDK instructs users to enable Blind Signing on their Ledger to recover from an error that enabling Blind Signing cannot fix, permanently weakening the device for every dApp thereafter
raw_findings.description: mapLedgerDeviceError translates any BLIND_SIGNATURE_REQUIRED condition into the imperative 'Enable Blind Signing in the Ledger Solana app and retry.' This string is surfaced by useSolanaLedger into deviceStatus/error for EVERY operation -- connect, deriveAddresses, confirmAddress, signTransaction, signOffchainMessage (src/ledger/useSolanaLedger.ts:166, 207, 225, 241, 256). Blind Signing is the Ledger's core protection: with it on, the device stops parsing and displaying transaction contents and asks the user to approve an opaque hash, for every Solana program, in every dApp, until manually turned off. Nothing in the SDK checks getAppConfig().blindSigningEnabled (src/ledger/useSolanaLedger.ts:264-268 exposes it and no caller in src/ consumes it), nothing warns about the blast radius, and nothing turns it back off. A LOGIN or KEY-EXPORT flow must never require it.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Chain, all inside the SDK's own documented usage: (1) A Ledger user opens an ExportKeyPanel that omits the optional hardwareWallet prop, so deriveAppKey picks walletAppKeyMessage(appId), which contains newlines (src/core/index.ts:19-20). (2) Per finding #2 the envelope is malformed and hw-app-solana throws the literal 'Missing a parameter. Try enabling blind signature in the app' (node_modules/@ledgerhq/hw-app-solana/lib-es/Solana.js:218). (3) mapLedgerDeviceError converts that into 'Enable Blind Signing in the Ledger Solana app and retry.' -- the SDK's own comment at src/ledger/transport.ts:73-76 confirms it matches exactly this string. (4) The user complies. The device now signs the unreadable blob, the SDK derives the SOFTWARE app key, decryption still fails, and they get 'Re-authentication failed - wrong credentials' (src/client/authClient.ts:196). Net result: zero benefit, and the user's hardware wallet now blind-signs everything. That directly amplifies the XSS threat in scope: useSolanaLedger exports raw signTransaction(path, bytes) and signOffchainMessage(path, envelope) with no path validation and no envelope well-formedness check, so XSS on the integrating app is an unconstrained Ledger signing oracle whose ONLY remaining control is the on-device display -- which this instruction has just disabled.
raw_findings.recommendation: Never instruct the user to enable Blind Signing from an authentication or key-export path. Replace the string with a non-actionable diagnostic (e.g. 'This message cannot be displayed on your Ledger. The app must send a device-displayable message -- contact the app developer.'), and fail closed. If a caller genuinely needs it for arbitrary transaction signing, gate that behind an explicit, separately-documented opt-in, check getAppConfig().blindSigningEnabled up front, and warn about the cross-dApp blast radius. Also validate in signOffchainMessage that the declared u16 length matches the buffer, and consider restricting signTransaction/signOffchainMessage to paths present in the derived set.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep 'blind|Blind|blindSigning' across src and tests. tests/ledger-signer.test.ts:247 asserts the mapping EXISTS (['Missing a parameter. Try enabling blind signature in the app', /Blind Signing/i]) -- i.e. this is codified intended behaviour, not a regression already fixed. grep 'getAppConfig|blindSigningEnabled' across src/: defined at useSolanaLedger.ts:264-268 and re-exported, with zero consumers in src/ and zero tests. No README/SECURITY/CHANGELOG/docs content mentions Ledger, hardware, or blind signing (grep -i 'ledger|hardware' over README.md, SECURITY.md, CHANGELOG.md returns nothing; docs/ and audits/ are empty).

raw_findings.title: The hardware-vs-software app-key domain is an unpersisted, caller-supplied, end-user-toggleable boolean, so the same wallet silently derives two different encryption keys
raw_findings.description: hardwareWallet selects between two entirely different app-key preimages (walletAppKeyMessageHw vs walletAppKeyMessage, src/core/index.ts:29-50), and therefore between two different AES keys for the same wallet and appId. That flag is never persisted anywhere: UserData (src/core/types.ts:37-73) records authMethod:'wallet' and nothing more, and grep shows zero occurrences of hardwareWallet under src/server or src/storage. It is re-supplied independently at three separate call sites -- LoginPanel/WalletMethod for login (src/ui/WalletMethod.tsx:43-47), ExportKeyPanel for reveal (src/ui/ExportKeyPanel.tsx:178), and AuthClient.deriveAppKey for unlock (src/client/authClient.ts:148-152) -- with different defaults at each. The reveal path defaults to undefined (i.e. software), which tests/ui-hardware-wallet.test.tsx:121-126 codifies. Worse, hardwareWalletToggle renders a user-facing 'I'm using a Ledger' switch whose UNCONTROLLED state is seeded per-mount from defaultOn ?? hardwareWallet ?? false (src/ui/LoginPanel.tsx:61-63), so an end user can flip the key domain between visits with no idea they are doing so. The SDK's own types acknowledge the hazard ('Whatever value ultimately drives login MUST match the value passed to <ExportKeyPanel hardwareWallet> for the same account', src/ui/types.ts:138-139) but nothing enforces it.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Bob registers via LoginPanel with hardwareWalletToggle ON: wallets are generated and encrypted under appKey_hw, ciphertext stored. On his next visit the uncontrolled toggle re-seeds to false (fresh mount, no persistence), he signs in, the server verifies his challenge signature and returns 200, and setSession arms appKey_sw. He is fully authenticated with the wrong key. Every wallet decrypt throws, and the only feedback the SDK gives is the generic 'Re-authentication failed - wrong credentials'. He then hits finding #3 and is coached into enabling Blind Signing while trying to recover. A hostile app operator can weaponize the same primitive: serve hardwareWallet:false on registration and true on a later 'account recovery' page (or vice versa), producing a support-driven flow in which the user is told to enter their seed elsewhere. Also note importWallet (src/server/routes.ts:523-540) appends to user.wallets with no key identifier, so a session armed with the wrong app key can permanently mix two key domains inside one account's bundle.
raw_findings.recommendation: Persist the key domain on the account the way pbkdf2Iterations is persisted (a keyDomain: 'wallet' | 'wallet-hw' field on UserData, returned by /challenge and used to select the message on every subsequent derive), so the flag is decided ONCE at registration and never re-supplied by UI state. Until then, make LoginPanel's toggle either controlled-only or persisted, and have unlock()/revealSecret() validate the derived key against a known wallet before reporting success (unlock already supports validateWith at src/client/authClient.ts:173-183 -- make it mandatory on the wallet path).
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep hardwareWallet across all of src and tests. tests/ledger-login.test.ts:107-115 documents the divergence as an expected 'mixing footgun' and asserts hw != sw, but nothing pins or persists the choice. tests/ui-hardware-wallet.test.tsx and tests/ui-login-panel-ux.test.tsx:146-250 test only that the flag is threaded and that the toggle is controlled/uncontrolled correctly -- neither tests cross-session persistence. grep hardwareWallet in src/server and src/storage: zero hits. grep for keyDomain/authMethod-hw in src/core/types.ts: nothing.

raw_findings.title: The vault auto-lock gate that the software signer enforces is completely absent from the Ledger signer path
raw_findings.description: The software signer is gated on the vault lock at two levels: useSolanaSigner returns null when locked (src/react/useSolanaSigner.ts:38, 'if (!wallet || !unlocked) return null;') and every signing call re-reads the app key at call time and throws VaultLockedError if the vault has auto-locked (src/react/useSigner.ts:36-41). getSolanaSigner returns a fully functional SolanaSigner with no session, authentication, or lock check whatsoever -- src/ledger/ imports nothing from client/session.js (verified: zero references to getAppKey, lockSnapshot, touchVault, or VaultLockedError anywhere under src/ledger/). An integrator who configures autoLockMs/lockOnHide (src/client/authClient.ts:117-120) and reasons 'an unattended tab cannot sign after N minutes' gets that guarantee for software wallets and not for hardware ones. Ledger signing also never calls touchVault(), so hardware activity does not extend the software window either -- the two subsystems are entirely disjoint.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An app configures lockOnHide + a short autoLockMs and exposes both software and Ledger accounts through the same signing UI. The user walks away with the tab open and the Ledger plugged in and unlocked. The software signer goes null on lock; the Ledger signer keeps working, and anything that can reach the page (a co-resident tab via a postMessage bridge, an XSS payload, a malicious browser extension with content-script access) can keep issuing sign requests. The residual control is the physical button press on the device -- real, but a different and weaker guarantee than the auto-lock the SDK advertises, and one that finding #3 actively degrades by coaching Blind Signing.
raw_findings.recommendation: Either subscribe the Ledger signer to the same lock store (return null / throw VaultLockedError when locked, and call touchVault() on each device signature so hardware use extends the window symmetrically), or document explicitly in the /ledger entry and in SECURITY.md that autoLockMs and lockOnHide do not apply to hardware accounts and that the on-device prompt is the only signing gate.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep 'getAppKey|lockSnapshot|touchVault|VaultLocked|session' over src/ledger/ returns 0 matches. grep 'getSolanaSigner|useSolanaLedger|createLedgerTransport|confirmAddress|deriveAddresses' over tests/ returns 0 matches -- the hook has no test coverage at all, so no prior audit encoded this. tests/cross-tab-lock.test.ts and the auto-lock tests cover only the software vault.

raw_findings.title: getSolanaSigner's target-mismatch guard silently no-ops in exactly the state it was written to catch (empty derived set)
raw_findings.description: Both integrity checks are conditioned on finding the target in addressesRef.current. When that array is empty -- deriveAddresses was never called, or disconnect() ran, which does setAddresses([]) at line 183 -- both find() calls return undefined and the guard passes unconditionally. The comment says the check exists to catch 'stale/hand-built targets before signing', which is precisely the post-reconnect / persisted-target case where addresses has been cleared. So the guard is absent whenever it would matter and present only when the caller already has fresh, self-consistent data.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An app persists the user's chosen Ledger account as {path, address} in localStorage and rebuilds the signer after a reconnect without re-deriving. XSS (in scope) rewrites that entry, so createLedgerSolanaSigner is constructed with an attacker-chosen address/path pair and no error is raised. Impact is bounded by the crypto and is genuinely limited: signOne attaches the device's signature under the wrong publicKey so verifySignatures() fails and the cluster rejects the transaction, and a login built on the mismatched pair fails verifySolanaSignature server-side (401). The realized damage is a confusing hard failure plus, if the path differs from the account's, a silently different app key -- not key theft. Reporting as low precisely because the signature binding is what saves it, not this guard.
raw_findings.recommendation: Fail closed: if addressesRef.current is non-empty require the target to be present in it, and if it is empty either refuse to build a signer or re-derive the single path on the device and compare the returned address to target.address before returning the signer.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep 'getSolanaSigner' over tests/ returns zero matches -- useSolanaLedger has no test file at all (tests/ cover only createLedgerSolanaSigner, the encoders, and mapLedgerDeviceError). No prior audit encoded this.

raw_findings.title: The blanket WebUSB catch turns a user's explicit denial of the device-permission prompt into a second, different permission prompt
raw_findings.description: createLedgerTransport catches EVERY throw from TransportWebUSB.create(), including TransportOpenUserCancelled, which @ledgerhq/hw-transport-webusb raises when the user dismisses navigator.usb.requestDevice (node_modules/@ledgerhq/hw-transport-webusb/lib-es/TransportWebUSB.js:59). The catch immediately calls TransportWebHID.create(), which fires navigator.hid.requestDevice -- a second native device-picker (node_modules/@ledgerhq/hw-transport-webhid/lib-es/TransportWebHID.js:20). On Chrome/Edge, where both APIs are supported, declining once therefore produces a second prompt for the same device rather than an abort. User cancellation is not the same failure class as 'this transport is unsupported' and should not be retried.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: A page embedding the SDK (or an iframe/overlay in a compromised integration) calls connect() on a user gesture. The user reconsiders and dismisses the WebUSB picker. Instead of stopping, the page is handed a second WebHID picker in the same gesture -- classic prompt fatigue that trains users to click through hardware-device consent, and that hands a hostile page a second chance at raw device access from one gesture. Once granted, the SDK's own signOffchainMessage/signTransaction (arbitrary path, arbitrary bytes, no validation) are reachable.
raw_findings.recommendation: Discriminate the error: re-throw TransportOpenUserCancelled / TransportWebUSBGestureRequired (both exported from @ledgerhq/errors) instead of falling through, and gate the WebHID attempt on TransportWebUSB.isSupported() being false or on a genuine interface-unavailable error. Consider preferring WebHID first, which is Ledger's own recommendation for browser integrations.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep 'createLedgerTransport' over tests/ returns zero matches; transport.ts is covered only by the mapLedgerDeviceError table in tests/ledger-signer.test.ts:242-257. No prior audit note or code comment addresses cancellation-vs-unsupported.

raw_findings.title: No on-device address verification is enforced, and the derivation path family is hardcoded to m/44'/501'/i'/0' with a probe at a different path
raw_findings.description: Three related gaps. (1) deriveAddresses calls getAddress(path) with display defaulting to false (node_modules/@ledgerhq/hw-app-solana/lib-es/Solana.js:64-73), so every address the UI shows and every address the account is registered under comes back over the wire without ever appearing on the device screen. (2) confirmAddress exists and returns the device-confirmed address, but the hook neither compares it to the derived-set entry nor records that confirmation happened -- there is no confirmed flag and getSolanaSigner does not require one, so an integrator who awaits confirmAddress and discards the result gets the status line 'Connected - Address confirmed' with zero verification. (3) The path family 44'/501'/i'/0' is hardcoded with no override, while the connect() probe uses the DIFFERENT 3-level path 44'/501'/0' -- the Ledger Live account layout. A user whose funds live at 44'/501'/0' will never see that account offered.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: Modest, because the login signature binds the address cryptographically: a page that lies about the derived address produces a signature under the real key presented under the fake key, which verifySolanaSignature rejects (401, fail-closed). The realized harm is (a) the user approves nothing on-device during account selection, so the SDK cannot claim device-verified account binding, and (b) a Ledger Live user who registers from a m/44'/501'/0'/0' address and later tries to recover from a tool that only exposes m/44'/501'/0' signs with a different key, derives a different app key, and cannot decrypt their bundle -- the recovery-path variant of finding #1.
raw_findings.recommendation: Track a per-address confirmed flag set only when confirmAddress's device-returned value matches the derived entry, and have getSolanaSigner (or at least the registration flow) require it. Make the derivation path family configurable, and enumerate both the 44'/501'/i' (Ledger Live) and 44'/501'/i'/0' (Phantom/Solflare) families so a user's existing account is reachable. Align the connect() probe with whatever family deriveAddresses uses.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep 'deriveAddresses|confirmAddress' over tests/ returns zero matches. grep for a confirmed/verified flag in src/ledger/useSolanaLedger.ts: LedgerDerivedAddress (lines 22-31) has only path/address/publicKey/index. grep "44'/501'" across src: only useSolanaLedger.ts:148 (probe, 3-level) and :199 (derivation, 4-level), no config surface.

raw_findings.title: mapLedgerDeviceError falls through to the raw device error string, contradicting its own documented security contract
raw_findings.description: The function's docblock states 'Returns only a static guidance string - never device data or a signature' (line 52). The final branch returns the unmodified thrown message. That string is written into React state and rendered by the host app via setError/setDeviceStatus (src/ledger/useSolanaLedger.ts:167-168, 208-209, 227, 242, 257). @ledgerhq transport errors and DOMExceptions can embed device/vendor/product detail. This behaviour is load-bearing -- the 0x6a81 cascade in solanaSigner.ts:91 only works because the hex status word survives this passthrough (the hook maps the error BEFORE the signer sees it) -- so it should not simply be removed, but the contract comment is wrong as written.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: No meaningful attack; the messages reachable in practice are TransportStatusError text of the form 'Ledger device: UNKNOWN_ERROR (0x6a81)' plus WebUSB/WebHID DOMException text, none of which carries key material. Reported as info because the comment materially overstates the guarantee and future maintainers may rely on it.
raw_findings.recommendation: Correct the docblock to state that unrecognized errors are passed through verbatim (and that the raw status word is deliberately preserved so callers such as signMessage can match on it), or return a structured { userMessage, statusWord } so the cascade can match on the code while the UI only ever renders sanitized text.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: tests/ledger-signer.test.ts:254-256 asserts the passthrough is intended ('passes through an unrecognized message unchanged'), confirming this is codified behaviour and not an already-fixed issue; no test or comment reconciles it with the line-52 contract.

raw_findings.title: verifySolanaSignature performs up to three ed25519 verifications over an unbounded, unvalidated challenge before any rate limiting
raw_findings.description: No route validates body.challenge for length or charset -- /login-wallet, /connect-wallet, /register and /login all pass it straight through (src/server/routes.ts:308, 370, 401, 450), and readJson imposes no body cap (src/server/http.ts:39-45). verifySolanaSignature builds walletLoginMessage(challenge) and runs nacl.sign.detached.verify over the whole thing at line 47. The routes deliberately verify BEFORE rate limiting (the verify-first design at routes.ts:398-404), so this work is fully unauthenticated and unthrottled. The hardware-wallet change added two further verification passes over the same input, tripling the cost for normal-sized challenges; the envelope candidates do bail early on oversized input (prepareMessage checks length at offchainMessage.ts:80-85 before the byte scan), so the amplification for huge inputs comes from the raw pass alone.
raw_findings.attack_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker POSTs /login-wallet with a valid-format publicKey, a well-formed 64-byte junk signature (so tweetnacl's size check at the top of verify passes and the message is actually hashed), and a multi-megabyte challenge string. The server performs SHA-512 over the full payload per request before the rate limiter is consulted, and the challenge is never even looked up because sigValid is false. Amplification is modest -- the attacker must upload the bytes -- which is why this is low rather than high, but it is unauthenticated CPU spend positioned ahead of every throttle.
raw_findings.recommendation: Validate the challenge shape at the route boundary before it reaches any crypto -- generateChallenge() is randomHex(32) (src/core/crypto.ts:143-145), so /^[0-9a-f]{64}$/ is an exact and free check. Likewise bound signatureHex to 128 hex chars. Both make the extra envelope passes trivially cheap.
raw_findings.prior_art_check: grep 'challenge.length|validateChallenge|CHALLENGE_RE' across src and tests: zero matches. src/server/routes.ts defines EMAIL_RE, HEX64_RE, APP_ID_RE and validators for email/appId/publicKey/authPublicKey/pbkdf2Iterations but none for challenge or signature. tests/audit-server.test.ts, tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts, tests/server.test.ts and tests/rate-limit-*.test.ts contain no oversized-challenge case.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Client applies no floor/ceiling to the `pbkdf2Iterations` value returned by `/challenge` — a response-tampering attacker can downgrade the login-time KDF to 1 iteration (server-side F3 floor is register-only)
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: Attacker must be able to alter the BODY of the `/challenge` HTTP response (plaintext/no-TLS network position, a hostile or compromised reverse-proxy/edge/WAF in front of the API, or write access to the user store) — read-only DB access is NOT sufficient, and there is no API path to persist a sub-100k value (see below). The downgrade is only an *escalation* when the attacker cannot equally tamper with the app's JS bundle (same-origin tampering already yields the plaintext passkey, making the downgrade redundant); it matters for split app/API origins, CDN+SRI-served bundles, or an API-side proxy compromise. Finally the victim's passkey must be low-entropy enough for a dictionary/rules attack — the gain is a cost reduction (~600,000x) of an oracle that already exists structurally, not a new one.
completed_verdicts.reason:
CODE TRUTH: every quoted line is verbatim and in context; no guard exists anywhere in the call chain, and no test covers it.

1. src/client/authClient.ts:265-267 reads exactly as quoted:
   `const iterations = pbkdf2Iterations ?? 100_000;`
   `const appKey = deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(params.passkey, params.email, iterations, this.config.appId);`
   `const signature = signAuthChallenge(appKey, challenge);`
   The value comes straight from `this.post<{ challenge: string; pbkdf2Iterations?: number }>("challenge", ...)` (line 259-262). `post` (line 200-211) does `const data = await res.json()...; return data as T;` — a bare cast, zero runtime validation. The `?: number` type is compile-time only. `1 ?? 100_000` is `1`.

2. It flows unchecked into the KDF. src/core/crypto.ts:32: `return bytesToHex(pbkdf2(sha256, utf8ToBytes(passkey), salt, { c: iterations, dkLen: 32 }));` — `c` is the raw wire value. No clamp, no integer check, no ceiling either (a hostile `1e10` hangs the main thread, since noble's pbkdf2 is synchronous — an extra consequence the finding did not claim).

3. The result IS transmitted: line 267-268 signs with `signAuthChallenge(appKey, challenge)` and line 268 POSTs it. src/client/authKey.ts confirms the oracle is deterministic and cheap to test offline: `authSeed = sha256("ttc-auth-v1:" + appKey)`, `nacl.sign.keyPair.fromSeed(...)`, `nacl.sign.detached(msg, kp.secretKey)` — ed25519 is deterministic, so a candidate passkey is verified with ~2 HMAC-SHA256 + one ed25519 sign instead of 600,000 HMACs.

4. The F3 floor is genuinely register-only. src/server/routes.ts:96-100 defines `PBKDF2_MIN`/`PBKDF2_MAX`/`validIterations`, and `grep -rn "validIterations" src/` returns exactly ONE call site: routes.ts:273 inside `register`. The `/challenge` handler ends at line 238 with `return json({ challenge, pbkdf2Iterations: user?.pbkdf2Iterations });` — echoed with no re-validation.

5. Same gap on the re-auth path, as claimed. authClient.ts:144 `const iterations = getPbkdf2Iterations() ?? 100_000;` and src/client/session.ts:291-297: `const n = parseInt(raw, 10); return Number.isFinite(n) ? n : null;` — finite-check only, no floor. The value is written by `setSession` (session.ts:208-209) from authClient.ts:274, i.e. the same untrusted `/challenge` number, so a downgrade persists into `ttc_pbkdf2_iter` for all later `unlock()`/`revealSecret()` calls — though only if the attacker also fakes a 200 on `/login`, since `post` throws before `setSession` runs on a non-OK response.

6. PRIOR-ART CHECK — the auditor is right. tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts ("F3 — register REJECTS an out-of-band pbkdf2Iterations (RESOLVED)") and tests/audit-zai-fixes.test.ts ("F3 — server PBKDF2 iteration floor") both drive `h.register(...)` exclusively and assert 400 from the SERVER. tests/server.test.ts:387 asserts `ch.pbkdf2Iterations === 600_000` from a *legitimate* handler. tests/auth-client.test.ts:52-66 (`wireFetch`) routes global fetch to the real in-process handlers, so it can never produce a malicious `/challenge` body. `grep -rn "PBKDF2_MIN|Math.max" src/client tests` → nothing. No client-side floor, no malicious-response test.

WHY SEVERITY IS MEDIUM, NOT HIGH — the finding's own claimed impact overreaches:
 (a) No API-reachable path. I enumerated every `persistUser` call (routes.ts:331 register, 474/480 connectWallet, 538 importWallet). Only register:327 ever sets `pbkdf2Iterations`, and it is gated by validIterations at :273; register 409s on an existing email (:298-301) and on an existing publicKey (:284-286), so an attacker cannot re-pin a victim's count. importWallet:530-538 only appends to `user.wallets`. So the F3 fix does hold against a purely-HTTP attacker; this requires an out-of-band tampering position.
 (b) Against the "hostile app operator" leg of the threat model it is not an escalation — that operator serves the client JS and can exfiltrate the passkey directly.
 (c) The `signAuthChallenge` value is sent on EVERY normal login anyway, so a response-tampering MITM already possesses a passkey-verification oracle at 600k cost without touching the iteration count. The bug reduces the cost; it does not create the oracle. It is not "wallet/key compromise" (critical) or "account takeover" (high) on its own — it is a meaningful weakening under preconditions.

CONCLUSION: real, unmitigated, one-line fix (`Math.max(PBKDF2_MIN, Math.min(PBKDF2_MAX, n))` client-side at authClient.ts:265 and :144, plus an `Number.isInteger` check) — and it is an incomplete completion of the already-shipped F3 fix, which is exactly the "defense exists but is incomplete" category. Report it at medium, not high.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: appKeyToBytes performs no hex/length validation on an exported crypto primitive — a real hardening gap, but unreachable through every shipped SDK flow (all five appKey producers emit 64 hex chars)
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: No actor in the stated threat model can supply `appKey`. Exploitation requires the INTEGRATOR to bypass `AuthClient`/`deriveAppKey*` entirely and call the exported `encryptSecret`/`decryptSecret`/`armAppKey` with a raw user-supplied string. Additionally, that string must be exactly 32, 33, 48, 49, 64 or 65 characters long — I verified `crypto.subtle.importKey` throws `DataError: Invalid key length` for every other length (e.g. the SDK's own `armAppKey("deadbeef")` → 4 bytes → DataError), so most naive misuse fails loudly on the first encrypt during development. - src/react/AuthProvider.tsx:58-67 refetches the whole record from `/user-data` on every mount; nothing is pinned client-side.

So the *observation* is code-true. The *finding* is not, for three independent reasons:

1. THE MISSING CONTROL DOES NOT PREVENT THE CLAIMED ATTACK. The flagship scenario is "the user is shown the attacker's deposit address." That path never decrypts anything: `useActiveWallet` (line 44-53) and `useWallets` (line 55-64) build `address` straight from the record and are the hooks an app renders while the vault may be LOCKED (`useSigner` throws `VaultLockedError` when locked; AuthProvider deliberately keeps `user` loaded across a lock, lines 78-80). AES-GCM `additionalData` is only checked inside `crypto.subtle.decrypt`. An attacker with DB write simply stores a fully self-consistent entry — `{chain:"solana", role:"funds", publicKey:<attacker>, encryptedSecret:<attacker's own blob under the attacker's own key>}` — whose AAD *he* computed. The display is poisoned identically with or without AAD. The real defect, if any, is "the display path trusts server metadata," not "encryptSecret lacks AAD," and the proposed binding does not close it.

2. THE REQUIRED CAPABILITY EXCEEDS OR SUBSUMES THE THREAT MODEL. The stated DB attacker has READ (backup, replica, world-readable schema, slow-query log) — read alone cannot mount this. The other named actor, the hostile app operator, serves the client bundle and can therefore just log `appKey`/passkey at login or ship a modified SDK; against him AAD buys exactly nothing. For the residual DB-WRITE insider, note the SDK already carries a partial, code-level cross-check the finding does not mention: for email/biometric accounts `UserData.publicKey` IS the Solana funds address (src/client/authClient.ts:234-239 `const identity = bundle.solana?.funds ?? …; publicKey: identity.publicKey`), and `useWallets.ts:61 isIdentity: w.publicKey === user?.publicKey` compares the entry against it, with the documented instruction at useWallets.ts:12-19 "Use this — not `role === "funds"` — to answer 'which wallet is the user?' … picking the wrong one means showing the wrong deposit address." A publicKey-only rewrite (exactly the attack described, "leaving `encryptedSecret` untouched") flips `isIdentity` to false, and `user.publicKey` is simultaneously the storage key (`pubKey:{appId}:{publicKey}`), the email-index target, and the value the client replays in `config.publicKeyHeader` on every authenticated call, so it cannot be moved without breaking the live session. That is an independent, already-shipped binding of the funds address, and the finding's "nothing downstream checks it" is therefore overstated.

3. THE SURVIVING SUB-CASE IS SPECULATIVE. Only the role/entry-swap variant is genuinely AAD-preventable. But swapping ciphertexts alone yields a signature from the wrong key against the advertised account — the transaction just fails on-chain (DoS, no gain). Swapping whole entries makes the app use the funds keypair where it meant the `signing` hot wallet, but the transaction contents are still built by the app, not the attacker; turning that into theft requires stacking a second, unstated capability. That is defense-in-depth, not a medium-severity exploit.

Net: accurate code reading, invalid causal chain and inflated severity. Binding `chain|role|publicKey` as AAD is a reasonable low-cost hardening item (it would make a DB-write role swap fail loudly at decrypt), but it must be reported as such, not as a wallet-address-theft vulnerability, and the report must not imply it defends the deposit-address rendering path — it does not.
completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Hardening: AES-GCM ciphertexts are not bound to their chain/role via additionalData, so a DB-write insider could swap two of one user's wallet entries and have the app sign with the funds key where it intended the `signing` key (does NOT affect the displayed-address path)

The publicKey-rewrite/deposit-address variant is out of scope for this control: it works equally well against an AAD-bound implementation (attacker writes a self-consistent entry encrypted under his own key) because useActiveWallet/useWallets never decrypt, and it is partially detectable today via `isIdentity` (useWallets.ts:61) for email/biometric accounts whose identity address is pinned to the storage key and session header.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: decryptSecret can throw a DOMException instead of an Error on non-base64 input (typed-API polish; no oracle — every shipped caller normalizes it)

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Low-level core helper `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` carries compat-floor defaults (100k / "ttc") that no shipped code path uses — documentation nit, not a defect
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: No attacker action exists. It requires an *integrator* to (a) bypass `AuthClient` entirely and hand-roll registration against an undocumented low-level primitive, (b) ignore the function's own docblock and the file header two lines above it that both state the count/appId are supposed to be passed in, and (c) still be running a deployment left on `DEFAULT_CONFIG.appId = "ttc"` (for which the SDK already emits a console.warn on the supported path). The payoff is a 6x reduction in offline PBKDF2 cost against an already per-email salt.
completed_verdicts.reason:
The quoted lines are verbatim real (src/core/crypto.ts:23-28 does default `iterations = 100_000, appId = "ttc"`, and src/core/index.ts:5 does `export * from "./crypto.js";`), but the finding's framing does not survive reading the surrounding code, the callers, or the prior-art tests.

1) NO SHIPPED CODE PATH USES THE DEFAULTS. `grep -rn "deriveAppKeyFromPasskey" src` returns exactly four hits, and all three call sites pass all four arguments: src/client/authClient.ts:145 `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(creds.passkey, email, iterations, this.config.appId)`, :232 and :266 identically, with :231 `const iterations = PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[this.config.securityLevel];`. Nothing in src/react, src/ui, src/next, or src/server reaches the 2-arg form. The only 2-arg callers in the entire repo are tests.

2) THE DEFAULTS ARE LOAD-BEARING INVARIANTS, NOT AN OVERSIGHT — and both are documented inline at the definition. `appId = "ttc"` is required to equal `DEFAULT_CONFIG.appId` or the helper would derive a *different* key than `AuthClient` on the same default config; crypto.ts:21 says so explicitly: `Default "ttc" must match DEFAULT_CONFIG.appId; override per deployment.` The identical pattern and identical justification appear at src/core/index.ts:29 `export function walletAppKeyMessage(appId = "ttc")`. Likewise `iterations = 100_000` is exactly the project's declared legacy floor, used deliberately as the pinned-count fallback at authClient.ts:144 `const iterations = getPbkdf2Iterations() ?? 100_000;` and :265 `const iterations = pbkdf2Iterations ?? 100_000;`, and enforced server-side as the minimum at src/server/routes.ts:96-99 `const PBKDF2_MIN = 100_000; ... n >= PBKDF2_MIN && n <= PBKDF2_MAX`. Raising the helper's default to 600k would orphan every legacy account that derives via that fallback.

3) THE CONTRACT IS STATED AT THE TOP OF THE VERY FILE CITED. src/core/crypto.ts:8-9: `//  (D2) The PBKDF2 iteration count comes from config.securityLevel (default 600k), // is pinned per-user, and is passed in to deriveAppKeyFromPasskey.` The finding presents the parameter default as the "least-effort path" while the file explicitly documents that the count is supplied by the caller.

4) PRIOR ART CLOSES THIS. tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:39-43 is literally titled `"H2 RESOLVED — 600k iterations + domain-separated salt (no longer the bare email)"` and pins `expect(DEFAULT_CONFIG.securityLevel).toBe(2); expect(PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[DEFAULT_CONFIG.securityLevel]).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(600_000);`. The weak-iteration issue was audited as H2 and resolved at the config layer that governs 100% of real registrations. tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:85-92 re-pins the same (`resolveConfig().securityLevel` is 2 = 600k, described in-test as "secure-by-default"). The finding re-raises a closed finding through a door no shipping code opens.

5) THE HEADLINE IMPACT CLAIM IS FALSE. "a single precomputed table works against every deployment ... defeating CRYPTO-2 entirely" is not what the code does: crypto.ts:30 is `const salt = sha256(utf8ToBytes(`${appId}:${email.toLowerCase().trim()}`));` — the salt is still per-email, so there is no cross-user table, only per-(email, "ttc") precomputation. And CRYPTO-2's guarantee is about deployments that *set* a unique appId; a deployment sitting on "ttc" is in the identical posture whether it calls the helper directly or goes through `AuthClient`, and the supported path already nudges it at authClient.ts:123-129. The incremental delta attributable to the helper's default is "no console.warn on a path the SDK never takes."

6) THE "SILENT" CLAIM FAILS FOR THE MIGRATION/RECOVERY HALF OF THE SCENARIO. A recovery script calling the 2-arg form against a 600k account gets a hard failure, not silence — tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:44-58 proves it: `await expect(decryptSecret(ct600k, key100k)).rejects.toThrow();` (AES-GCM auth-tag mismatch). Only a hand-rolled *registration* would be silent, and such a flow must also post its own `pbkdf2Iterations` (authClient.ts:244); omitting it yields a self-consistent legacy-100k account, not a mismatch.

Net: the code is exactly as described, but the described consequence requires integrator misuse of an undocumented primitive whose defaults are deliberate compat/consistency anchors documented three lines above them, with the real default (600k, level 2) pinned by existing tests. This is at most an `info`-level API-ergonomics note — "consider making `iterations`/`appId` required parameters on the core helper" — not a `low` security finding, and it should not be reported as one.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: deriveAppKeyFromPasskey's parameter defaults (100k iterations / appId "ttc") mirror the enforced server floor and DEFAULT_CONFIG — API-hygiene nit, not an exploitable weakness
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: Requires no attacker action at all. It requires an integrator to voluntarily bypass `AuthClient`, hand-roll a registration flow against the SDK's own server routes, and call the core helper with two arguments — a mistake the SDK itself never makes at any of its three call sites and that no documentation in the repo suggests (README.md and SECURITY.md are 0 bytes; `grep -rn deriveAppKey README.md docs/ PRD/` returns nothing). Only after that developer error does a database-read attacker gain anything, and the gain is a 6x (~2.6-bit) PBKDF2 work-factor reduction against one deployment's accounts.
completed_verdicts.reason:
The defaults are real, but every load-bearing claim built on top of them fails.

1) NO ATTACKER STEP; THE DEFAULTS ARE UNREACHABLE IN SHIPPED CODE. `grep -rn "deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(" src` returns exactly three call sites, and all three pass both arguments explicitly:
  src/client/authClient.ts:145 `return deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(creds.passkey, email, iterations, this.config.appId);`
  src/client/authClient.ts:232 `const appKey = deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(params.passkey, params.email, iterations, this.config.appId);`
  src/client/authClient.ts:266 `const appKey = deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(params.passkey, params.email, iterations, this.config.appId);`
with src/client/authClient.ts:231 `const iterations = PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[this.config.securityLevel];`. The parameter defaults never fire in any SDK flow. The "attack" is an integrator writing different code — no attacker in the stated threat model (DB read, malicious client, replay, XSS, cross-app, MITM, insider) can cause it.

2) 100k IS NOT "THE WEAKEST POSSIBLE KEY" — IT IS THE SERVER-ENFORCED FLOOR, DELIBERATELY. src/server/routes.ts:96-99:
  `const PBKDF2_MIN = 100_000;`
  `const PBKDF2_MAX = 1_000_000;`
  `function validIterations(n: unknown): boolean { return typeof n === "number" && Number.isInteger(n) && n >= PBKDF2_MIN && n <= PBKDF2_MAX; }`
with routes.ts:92-95 citing audit F3. The helper's default equals the minimum the server already refuses to go below. It is also load-bearing legacy compat, not an oversight: authClient.ts:144 `const iterations = getPbkdf2Iterations() ?? 100_000;` and authClient.ts:265 `const iterations = pbkdf2Iterations ?? 100_000;` — accounts predating per-user pinning derive at 100k, and tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:61-81 ("changing default from 100k to 600k does not break existing users") encodes exactly why raising this literal would orphan them.

3) THE appId HALF IS NOT INCREMENTAL. src/core/config.ts:155 `appId: "ttc",` is the SDK-wide default; an integrator using `AuthClient` with default config gets the identical "no cross-app isolation" property. The delta the finding identifies is a missing `console.warn`, not a missing control. And the function's own JSDoc already carries the guidance at the call site — src/core/crypto.ts:21: `Default "ttc" must match DEFAULT_CONFIG.appId; override per deployment.`

4) THE CRYPTO-2 CLAIM IS FACTUALLY WRONG. "a single precomputed table works against every deployment that made the same mistake, defeating CRYPTO-2 entirely" contradicts src/core/crypto.ts:30: `const salt = sha256(utf8ToBytes(`${appId}:${email.toLowerCase().trim()}`));` — the salt is per-EMAIL, so any table is per-(appId,email), i.e. per targeted user, exactly as with a non-default appId. Nothing is "defeated entirely"; cross-app separation is weakened precisely as much as the documented default config already documents at config.ts:65-66.

5) PRIOR ART CLOSED THIS. tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:39-42, under `describe("H2 RESOLVED — 600k iterations + domain-separated salt")`:
  `expect(DEFAULT_CONFIG.securityLevel).toBe(2);`
  `expect(PBKDF2_ITERATIONS[DEFAULT_CONFIG.securityLevel]).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(600_000);`
and tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:89 `expect(resolveConfig().securityLevel).toBe(2); // default level 2 = 600k (OWASP)`. A prior audit ruled on the iteration count at the config layer and deliberately left the low-level parameter at the legacy floor.

6) THE AUDITOR'S PRIOR-ART EVIDENCE IS BACKWARDS. tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:32 using the two-argument form is CI speed, not a production signal — the same repo raises Jest timeouts to 30s wherever it must derive at 600k (tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:59 `}, 30_000); // 600k PBKDF2 derivations are slow`). Test convenience is not an integrator-facing footgun.

What survives is an API-hygiene observation worth one line in a hardening section, not a "low": the low-level default (100k) disagrees with the package's own secure default (level 2 / 600k), so the signature would read better as `iterations: number` and `appId: string` required — which would also make the legacy `?? 100_000` fallbacks explicit at their two call sites. That is a refactor suggestion, severity info.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Default UI accepts any non-empty passkey as the wallet-encryption key: no client-side entropy floor anywhere, and the CSPRNG generator is opt-in (LoginPanel passes no default)
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: All of: (1) the account is an email/passkey account (wallet and WebAuthn-PRF accounts derive the appKey from a signature / PRF output and are unaffected); (2) the integrator did not pass `passkeyGenerator` to `LoginPanel` and did not build their own strength gate — the shipped default; (3) the user typed a guessable secret; (4) the attacker obtains a database read (leaked backup, replica, world-readable Supabase `public` schema, slow-query log) — explicitly in the stated threat model. No server bug is needed; the attack is entirely offline once the record is in hand. Cost per guess is one PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at the pinned count (600k at the default securityLevel 2), not the "one SHA-256 + one ed25519 keygen" implied by the finding's phrasing — the KDF dominates. That still leaves a large wordlist tractable on a single GPU for one high-value target.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Observation (not a vulnerability): AES-GCM wallet ciphertexts are not key-committing, but every actor who could mount a partitioning oracle already holds a free, unlimited OFFLINE passkey verifier (authPublicKey / encryptedSecret), so the oracle gains nothing
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: For the described attack to yield any advantage, the attacker would need a setting in which offline verification of a candidate app key is IMPOSSIBLE (as in Shadowsocks, the paper's motivating target), so that online interactions are the scarce resource. That precondition does not hold here for any actor in the stated threat model. The DB-reading attacker, the hostile operator, and the network MITM each independently possess an unlimited offline verifier at exactly 1 PBKDF2 per guess. On top of that, the attacker would still need (a) 2^k PBKDF2 evaluations to build the multi-key ciphertext, (b) the honest user to run unlock() against the crafted blob, and (c) an application-level side channel the SDK does not provide.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: encryptSecret binds no AAD (wallet chain/role/publicKey) — informational hardening note; the partitioning-oracle framing does not hold
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: To even reach the claimed oracle the attacker must be the app operator (or a full MITM / XSS on the page), i.e. must control the JavaScript that reads the passkey — which already yields the passkey directly. Separately, the attacker must run one PBKDF2(600k) per candidate to build the multi-key blob, and must ship ~1 ciphertext block per candidate through /user-data, and must have an app-level channel to observe the unlock() failure bit (which the SDK does not provide).
completed_verdicts.reason:
REFUTED on three independent grounds; each alone is fatal.

(1) The quantitative core of the finding is cryptographically wrong. A partitioning oracle saves ONLINE QUERIES, never KDF work. To build a GCM ciphertext that authenticates under a candidate set S, the attacker must KNOW every key in S — and each key here is `deriveAppKeyFromPasskey` = `pbkdf2(sha256, utf8ToBytes(passkey), salt, { c: iterations, dkLen: 32 })` (src/core/crypto.ts:32) at the account's pinned count (default 600k, src/core/config.ts:156 `securityLevel: 2`). So the attacker pays exactly the same per-candidate PBKDF2 he would pay offline, up front, and THEN has to wait on user interactions. The claim "replacing per-guess PBKDF2 work with a set-membership test" is false. Sizing is also wrong: targeted multi-key GCM ciphertexts grow ~linearly (≈1 block per key), so "~2^k candidates / k bits per unlock" means a 2^k-block blob — eliminating 2^30 candidates means ~16 GB shipped as `EncryptedWallet.encryptedSecret` in a JSON body, per unlock.

(2) The oracle is worthless because an OFFLINE verifier is already in the same table the attacker reads. `UserData` (src/core/types.ts:39-75) persists both `wallets: EncryptedWallet[]` — real ciphertexts under the true appKey (src/client/wallet.ts:44,56 `encryptedSecret: await encryptSecret(secretHex, appKey)`) — and `authPublicKey`, a deterministic function of the appKey: `deriveAuthPublicKey(appKey)` = `bytesToHex(nacl.sign.keyPair.fromSeed(sha256(utf8ToBytes("ttc-auth-v1:" + appKey))).publicKey)` (src/client/authKey.ts:14-21). Given `email`, `appId`, and the stored `pbkdf2Iterations`, any DB reader tests a passkey candidate fully offline with one PBKDF2 + one ed25519 base-point mult (or one GCM tag check). Partitioning oracles matter precisely when no offline verifier exists (the Shadowsocks case in Len/Grubbs/Ristenpart). Here one is stored server-side by design, so the "oracle" strictly dominated by an attack the same actor can already run for free, unobserved, and in parallel.

(3) The actor required makes it moot. `unlock(creds, validateWith)` runs entirely in the browser and the only caller is `await client.unlock(creds, user?.wallets?.[0])` (src/react/useAuth.ts:43) with `user` from `/user-data`. Substituting that blob requires being the app operator or a full MITM — the same party that serves the SDK bundle and the passkey input field. That party gets the plaintext passkey (or the armed appKey, or `revealSecret()`) in one shot; a one-bit-per-Touch-ID oracle is not an escalation. The finding itself concedes the leak channel doesn't exist in-SDK, and I confirmed it: `unlock` throws locally (src/client/authClient.ts:176-180), `reauthenticate` rethrows, and the only client fetches are register/login/challenge/user-data/logout (src/client/authClient.ts:201, 220, 468). No telemetry, no retry POST.

Prior art: the auditor's grep is correct that no test names "partitioning", but that is not evidence of a gap — tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:27-37 and tests/ciphertext-tampering.test.ts already pin the relevant properties (wrong key throws, any bitflip/IV/truncation throws, server stores only an ed25519 public key), and tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts:50-51 plus src/server/routes.ts:94 show the offline-brute-force model IS the modeled threat, with a server-enforced 100k–1M iteration band as the control.

What survives is much smaller and different from the claim: `encryptSecret` binds no AAD, so a wallet blob is not cryptographically tied to its `chain`/`role`/`publicKey` (src/core/types.ts:20-27). A hostile server could relabel or swap a user's own blobs (all under the same appKey) so a `signing` key surfaces as `funds`. That is defense-in-depth worth a line in the hardening section, is moot against the same hostile-operator actor, and note that adding AAD would not provide key commitment anyway — GCM-with-AAD is still not key-committing. Severity: info, not low, and the title/scenario as written overstate the attack.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: No minimum-entropy floor on the email passkey anywhere in the SDK, and the bundled UI ships the strong-passkey generator off by default — a user-typed weak secret is the only thing protecting the wallet vault against an offline attack on a read-only DB leak
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: All three must hold: (1) the integrator did not pass `passkeyGenerator` to `LoginPanel` and did not add their own validation — this is the shipped default, and `README.md`/`SECURITY.md` are both 0 bytes so nothing warns them; (2) the user picks a low-entropy secret (nothing stops "1"); (3) the attacker gets a read of the store — explicitly in scope (leaked backup, replica, world-readable Supabase `public` schema, slow-query log). No write access, no MITM, and no session token are needed. On success the attacker recovers the appKey and decrypts every `encryptedSecret` in the record — full, irreversible wallet theft. Not exploitable against a user who used the generator (128-bit floor) or against wallet/biometric accounts (no PBKDF2 path).
completed_verdicts.reason:
CONFIRMED — every load-bearing claim survives reading the source, and the prior-art check is clean.

1) No floor exists, at any layer. `src/core/crypto.ts:23-33` takes `passkey: string` straight into `pbkdf2(sha256, utf8ToBytes(passkey), salt, …)` with no length/entropy check. `src/client/authClient.ts:230-232` is the only caller on the register path and adds none: `const appKey = deriveAppKeyFromPasskey(params.passkey, params.email, iterations, this.config.appId);`. The re-auth path is the same (`authClient.ts:145`). `src/react/useAuth.ts:48` is a pass-through `wrap(...)`. The server cannot help — it never receives the passkey; `/register` (`src/server/routes.ts:241-334`) validates only `publicKey`, `email`, `authPublicKey` (hex64), `wallets`, and `pbkdf2Iterations`. So the claim "only the client can enforce this, and it does not" is exactly right. `grep -rn "passkey.length|minLength|too short|weak passkey|minPasskey|passkeyPolicy" src tests` returns nothing but `MIN_PASSKEY_BYTES` inside the generator itself — I re-ran it.

2) The generator is genuinely off by default. `src/ui/LoginPanel.tsx:27` destructures `passkeyGenerator,` with no default and forwards it raw at line 100; `src/ui/EmailMethod.tsx:47` is `if (!passkeyGenerator) return null;`, and the fallback branch at lines 166-178 renders a bare `<input type="password" … required />`. The submit gate at line 207 is `disabled={busy || !email || !passkey}` — non-emptiness only. This is not an oversight but a deliberate, test-pinned decision: `tests/ui-login-panel-ux.test.tsx` has `describe("regression — default render is unchanged")` → "EmailMethod without the generator: plain current-password input, no wrapper, no button", asserting `screen.queryByRole("button", { name: /generate a strong passkey/i })).toBeNull()`. That strengthens the finding's framing as an *insecure default* rather than a bug.

3) The offline verifier is real and everything it needs is in the same row. `UserData` (`src/core/types.ts:37-72`) persists `appId`, `email`, `authPublicKey`, `wallets: EncryptedWallet[]` (each with `encryptedSecret`), and `pbkdf2Iterations` — all written together at `routes.ts:317-331`. Salt is fully public: `sha256(utf8ToBytes(`${appId}:${email.toLowerCase().trim()}`))` (`crypto.ts:30`). Verifier chain confirmed at `src/client/authKey.ts:14-21`.

4) Prior art does not cover it. `tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:27-36` ("C1 RESOLVED") asserts only `expect(authPub).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f]{64}$/)` and `expect(authPub).not.toBe(appKey)` — exactly as the auditor said, nothing about non-verifiability. `tests/ui-login-panel-ux.test.tsx:120` ("clamps entropy to a 16-byte (128-bit) minimum") only tests `generateStrongPasskey` *when invoked*. H2 (`audit-crypto.test.ts:39-56`) pins 600k + domain-separated salt — real mitigations that cap this at medium, but orthogonal to passkey entropy.

TWO CORRECTIONS the report must make before publishing:

(a) The chaining sentence "Chained with the iteration-downgrade finding above, the PBKDF2 work factor drops to 1" is WRONG for the path a DB-reading attacker uses. `routes.ts:96-100` defines `const PBKDF2_MIN = 100_000; const PBKDF2_MAX = 1_000_000; function validIterations(n) { return typeof n === "number" && Number.isInteger(n) && n >= PBKDF2_MIN && n <= PBKDF2_MAX; }` and `routes.ts:273-275` rejects out-of-band values (audit F3). `/register` is the only writer of `pbkdf2Iterations` (grep confirms), and `/challenge` only echoes the already-validated stored value (`routes.ts:238`). A stored count of 1 is unreachable. Any downgrade claim must be argued on the client side — `authClient.ts:265` `const iterations = pbkdf2Iterations ?? 100_000;` accepts the server/MITM-supplied number with zero validation — which is a *different* finding with a *different* attacker (network/hostile operator, not DB reader). Delete the chain from this finding or it will be shot down.

(b) `authPublicKey` is not the "multiplier" — the wallet ciphertext already is, and it is cheaper to test. `encryptedSecret` is AES-256-GCM (`crypto.ts:72-93`), so its auth tag is itself an offline oracle: one AES-GCM decrypt per guess versus SHA-256 + an ed25519 scalar multiplication. The attack stands even if `authPublicKey` were deleted from the schema. Worth noting because the code comment at `audit-crypto.test.ts:31` claims "there is no fast hash to GPU-crack offline" — true of the *hash*, misleading about the record as a whole.

On the numbers, the finding is if anything conservative: hashcat mode 10900 on a single RTX 4090 benchmarks in the low MH/s at ~1k iterations, i.e. roughly 10^4 guesses/sec at 600k iterations, so a 10^8 wordlist is hours-to-a-day on one commodity GPU, not "days". The severity label is honest: mitigations present (600k PBKDF2 = OWASP 2023 min, per-user domain-separated salt so no rainbow table and no cross-appId reuse, AEAD) keep this below high, but the shipped default lets a user protect a private key with a one-character secret and the outcome on success is total wallet compromise — that is "meaningful weakening requiring preconditions", not mere hardening. Peer products enforce a floor (MetaMask 8 chars, Bitwarden 12); this one enforces none. Actionable fix: enforce a floor in `registerWithEmail` (the account-creation chokepoint, effective for honest users even though a malicious client bypasses it) and default `passkeyGenerator` on for `emailMode` signup/auto.

The mechanical claim is accurate — I confirmed every quoted line verbatim (src/core/crypto.ts:118-121 `if (!userAgent) return undefined;`, src/server/routes.ts:147-149, src/server/session.ts:57-59 and 92-97) — and the auditor's prior-art check is also correct: tests/session-fingerprint.test.ts covers no-UA at VERIFY time (line 80-86) but every case calls `register(h, UA_A)`, so issue-time-no-UA is untested. What does NOT hold up is the security consequence, on three independent grounds.

(1) No trust boundary is crossed — the "attacker" is the session's own owner. All four `issueSession` call sites mint a token for the party who just authenticated on that same request and hand it back in the response body: routes.ts:332 (register, after `authPublicKey required` / ed25519 challenge consume), :374 (login, gated on `sigValid && consumed`), :410 (loginWallet, `verifySolanaSignature`), :482 (connectWallet, same). There is no impersonation, admin, or third-party issuance path. So the only actor who can omit the UA is the credential holder minting their own session. They gain nothing: that same actor can already log in directly from curl, receive a session bound to curl's UA, and use it from curl. "Portable token" is not a privilege they lacked.

(2) The implicit fix is theater. The finding's premise is that an absent UA should pin the session to a sentinel/empty fingerprint. An absent User-Agent is a ZERO-ENTROPY fingerprint: any token thief reproduces it for free with `curl -H "User-Agent:"`. Pinning to it would block only an attacker who neglects to strip a header, while adding a real breakage class. The in-source comment shows this was a deliberate decision, not an oversight — crypto.ts:113-116: "Returns undefined for a missing/empty UA so the caller skips binding rather than pinning the session to the empty string."

(3) The finding calls this "a fail-open on a control the deployment explicitly turned on," but the SDK's own config doc disclaims control status for the mechanism entirely — config.ts:110-113: "Defense-in-depth only: it raises the bar for using a stolen bearer token from a different client, but the UA is attacker-spoofable and not a real device identity, so treat it as a speed bump, not a control." A UA is client-supplied on every request, so the binding was never server-enforced against a client that chooses its own headers; that is stated, not hidden. Note the default is off (config.ts:162).

What legitimately survives is much smaller than "security-control bypass": an integrator whose client sends no UA (Node undici, some server-to-server) silently runs with binding inert, and the stored value is indistinguishable from binding-off. That is an expectation/observability gap in the docs — worth one line in the `bindSessionToUserAgent` JSDoc ("clients that send no User-Agent are not bound") — not a reportable vulnerability. Reporting it at "low / security-control bypass / fail-open" overstates it to the point of being a false positive.
completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Doc gap: `bindSessionToUserAgent` is inert for clients that send no User-Agent (deliberate — an empty UA is a zero-entropy fingerprint), and this is not stated in the config JSDoc
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: None that yield an attacker gain. The only party able to omit the UA at issue time is the party who just completed authentication on that request (register/login/loginWallet/connectWallet all return the token to the caller), so the "attack" is a credential holder declining to bind their own session — a privilege they already have by logging in from curl. For the residual expectation gap: operator sets bindSessionToUserAgent: true AND the integrating client omits User-Agent AND a session token later leaks AND the thief happens not to strip their own UA — the last condition being free for the thief to satisfy, which is why the sentinel-pinning alternative provides no meaningful protection.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Full-blob, unversioned `putUser` makes every UserData write a read-modify-write race: a concurrent login (or a second import) can silently drop a just-imported wallet's encryptedSecret
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: (1) The integrator actually wires and calls the `/import-wallet` route — no code in `src/client` or `src/react` calls it; `grep -rn "import-wallet" src` returns only `src/next/routes.ts:31` (the route table) and two comments in `src/core/config.ts`, so the two-tab user scenario requires an integrator-built import flow. (2) Two writes to the SAME (appId, publicKey) record must overlap. On the login side the window between the snapshot read (`routes.ts:368 getUserByPublicKey`) and the write (`session.ts:70`) is only `verifyAuthSignature` + `consumeChallenge` + `deleteSession` + `putSession` — a few storage round trips, not attacker-controlled. On the import side the window IS attacker-widenable: `verifySession` reads the user at `routes.ts:527`, then `readJson` at :530 awaits the request body with no timeout or size guard (`http.ts:39-45` is a bare `await req.json()`), so a slow-drip body holds a stale snapshot open for seconds. (3) For the loss to be permanent the wallet's plaintext key must exist nowhere else — the client caches only token/publicKey/email/pbkdf2Iterations in localStorage (`src/client/session.ts:205-209`), never the wallets array, so a client-generated-then-imported key is unrecoverable; a genuinely "imported" key the user still holds a seed for is not. (4) The attacker-assisted variant presupposes an already-stolen session token, at which point the attacker can already read every ciphertext via `/user-data` and append arbitrary wallets (already-known F4, tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts:127-165); the incremental gain is destruction of a wallet imported during the window plus a stale `authTokenHash` pointer.
completed_verdicts.reason:
The code truth holds exactly as quoted; I could not find a guard anywhere.

1. `src/server/session.ts:64-71` is verbatim as claimed: `user.authTokenHash = tokenHash; delete (user as {authToken?: unknown}).authToken; await persistUser(store, user); return token;` — and `persistUser` is nothing but `await store.putUser(user)` (`session.ts:12-14`). The `user` object is the caller's snapshot: `login` reads it at `routes.ts:368` (`const user = publicKey ? await getUserByPublicKey(store, appId, publicKey) : null`) and hands the same object to `issueSession` at :374. `loginWallet` (:406/:410) and `connectWallet` (:464/:482) do the same.

2. `src/server/routes.ts:527-538` is verbatim as claimed: `importWallet` gets its snapshot from `verifySession` (which ends in `return store.getUser(appId, publicKey)`, `session.ts:98`), then `user.wallets = [...user.wallets, ...body.wallets]; await persistUser(store, user);`. No re-read, no version check.

3. Every backend's `putUser` is an unconditional whole-record overwrite. `KvAuthStore` (`store.ts:200-205`): `await this.kv.set(appScoped(this.prefixes.pubKey, user.appId, user.publicKey), JSON.stringify(user))`. The SQL engine (`src/storage/sql/engine.ts:93-114`) is the same shape: `const data = JSON.stringify(user); INSERT INTO ${t.users} (app_id, public_key, data) VALUES (?, ?, ?) ` + `this.dialect.upsert(["app_id","public_key"], ["data = ?"])`. There is no version/ETag column and no `WHERE version = ?`. The `AuthStore` interface (`store.ts:95-98`) promises only "Concurrent putUser for the same email under two different appIds must not lose either write" — the email index, not the record body. `engine.ts:9` echoes only "no lost write on the email index → PRIMARY KEY (email, app_id) + upsert".

4. Prior-art check confirms no coverage. `src/storage/conformance.ts:304-319` has exactly one concurrency case and it is the email index ("LOST WRITE: app2's index entry was clobbered"). `tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts` covers challenge getdel atomicity (:47-119), sequential session revocation (:121-153), same-email registration (:155-187) and duplicate connect-wallet (:189-218) — nothing where a wallet append races another write. `grep -rn "Promise.all" tests/*.ts` shows no concurrent `importWallet`/`issueSession` pairing anywhere.

Two corrections to the finding as written, which is why I lowered severity from medium to low rather than confirming it as filed:

- The attacker-assisted variant is weaker than described. A victim re-login DOES revoke the attacker's session before any blob race can matter: `issueSession` deletes the previous session from the session store (`session.ts:50-53`) and the session record is keyed independently of the UserData blob. A stale-snapshot import landing afterward only reverts the `authTokenHash` *pointer*, so the *next* login deletes an already-dead hash and leaves one live session un-revoked until TTL — a weakening of the single-active-session property, not a session-persistence bypass. The finding's framing ("the victim's own re-login... is clobbered") overstates this.

- The simpler, more reachable manifestation isn't mentioned: two concurrent `/import-wallet` calls (a double-click, or an auto-retry after a timeout) need no login at all — both snapshot at `routes.ts:527`, both append to their own copy, last write wins and one batch is gone. The same race also makes the `config.maxWalletsPerUser` check at :534 non-atomic, so the cap can be overshot.

Net: real, non-obvious, uncovered by tests, and worth reporting — but it is a durability/integrity defect with a narrow window and no security-control bypass, gated on an endpoint no shipped client calls. "Medium" implies more than the evidence supports; "low" with the concrete loss scenario spelled out is the honest label.

completed_verdicts.corrected_title: Stale-challenge login failures feed the login-failure bucket and surface as a misleading 401 (hardening; the underlying targeted throttle is the already-accepted /challenge residual)
completed_verdicts.exploit_preconditions: Unauthenticated attacker who knows a registered victim email (or the victim's base58 identity/wallet publicKey) for a valid appId, and who can land a POST /challenge inside the victim's in-flight window between their /challenge response and their /login submit. Attack is racy, bounded to rateLimit.maxAttempts writes per window, and fully self-drains one window (~60s default) after the attacker stops. No effect on key material, ciphertext, sessions, or cross-tenant isolation.
completed_verdicts.reason:
MECHANISM CONFIRMED, IMPACT REFUTED.

Mechanism (verified, not disputed): src/server/routes.ts:202-234 has no credential check and ends in `const challenge = await issueChallenge(store, appId, publicKey, config);`; src/storage/store.ts:211-215 is an unconditional single-slot write `await this.kv.set(appScoped(this.prefixes.challenge, appId, publicKey), challenge, { exSeconds: ttlSeconds });`; src/server/challenge.ts:33-35 `const stored = await store.takeChallenge(appId, publicKey); if (!stored) return false; return timingSafeEqual(stored, presented);`. So routes.ts:371-378 gives `consumed=false` for a victim holding C1 and falls to `rateLimited(req, { endpoint: "login", appId, identifier: body.email })` then `error("Invalid credentials", 401)`. That is all true.

WHY THE FINDING DOES NOT STAND AS A MEDIUM DoS:

1) Zero marginal attacker capability. The identifier the attacker must know to clobber is the SAME identifier that keys the /challenge throttle: routes.ts:222-225 `const identifier = body?.publicKey ?? body?.email; ... rateLimited(req, { endpoint: "challenge", appId, identifier })`. An attacker with that knowledge can simply spend the same ~10 requests/60s filling that bucket, at which point routes.ts:225 returns 429 to the victim's own /challenge and the victim cannot log in AT ALL — deterministically, with no race, no dependence on the victim being mid-login. The clobber path is strictly worse for the attacker (must win a race, only probabilistically denies) and produces the identical end state (victim cannot complete a login until the window drains). For the wallet flows the two buckets are literally the same key (victim and attacker both send `publicKey`), so the clobber adds nothing whatsoever there.

2) The harm class is an accepted, documented, previously-audited residual — not a new one. routes.ts:215-221: "Per-target keying still avoids the global 'unknown' lockout (H5); the residual per-target DoS is the developer's edge to own." And tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts:1-17 audits exactly this attacker model verbatim — "an unauthenticated attacker can hold a NAMED account locked out of login indefinitely... the auth handlers rate-limit `challenge` and `login` on a bucket keyed by a CALLER-SUPPLIED identifier... The attacker therefore chooses whose counter to fill" — and states the accepted bound: "That keying is a deliberate design choice and is fine on its own: a bucket that drains on schedule merely throttles, and the victim recovers within one window." That bound still holds here. src/storage/store.ts:250-266 fires the TTL self-heal ONCE at `count === maxAttempts + 1` precisely so a sustained trickle cannot hold a bucket open ("Firing on EVERY over-limit hit ... turned a throttle into an unauthenticated, targeted denial of service against a named account"). Nothing in the clobber path escapes that drain, so this is not "persistent DoS" (the rubric's bar for high) and not a new class at medium.

3) "Re-opens AUTHSESSION-3" overstates. AUTHSESSION-3's harm (tests/audit-server.test.ts:144-168) was a cheap, deterministic, race-free lockout: junk logins fed the counter until the victim's correct login was throttled. The verify-first ordering at routes.ts:369-378 still holds that invariant against junk logins — I confirmed `sigValid` is computed before any counter touch, and a junk signature still never reaches `consumeChallenge`. What remains is a raced, self-draining throttle that a plain /challenge flood already achieves better. The intent ("an attacker cannot make the victim's correct login fail") is dented; the exploitable consequence is not restored.

4) No escalation beyond throttling. Buckets are endpoint-scoped (store.ts:183-188, `ratelimit:{endpoint}:{appId}:{identifier}`), so an exhausted "login" bucket cannot bleed into "challenge"/"register"/"connect"/"search". The attacker never learns or influences the challenge the victim signs (it is server-generated and returned only to the requester), so there is no challenge-fixation or replay path — `takeChallenge` is still the atomic getdel (store.ts:217-221). Nothing touches wallet ciphertext, appKey derivation, sessions, or appId isolation. A confused victim cannot even self-destruct: re-registering the same email returns 409 (routes.ts:298-301) and the client's auto mode falls back to login, so the deterministic appKey/ciphertext are never overwritten.

WHAT IS LEGITIMATELY LEFT (low / hardening, worth one line in the report, not a medium finding): the failure is misattributed. A victim whose challenge went stale — attacker-induced, a second tab, or a retry — receives `error("Invalid credentials", 401)` rather than an honest "challenge expired", and that attempt is counted as an authentication failure even though `sigValid` was TRUE. Since a passkey/key guesser always fails `sigValid`, counting the `sigValid && !consumed` case buys no brute-force resistance. The principled fix is one branch at routes.ts:371-378: when `sigValid` is true but `consumed` is false, return a distinct 401 "Invalid or expired challenge" (as /register already does at routes.ts:312) WITHOUT calling `rateLimited`. Optionally note in SECURITY.md that /challenge is single-slot per (appId, publicKey), so a concurrent challenge request invalidates the pending one.
