strengths: PBKDF2 salt is properly domain-separated and fixed-length: `sha256(utf8ToBytes(`${appId}:${email.toLowerCase().trim()}`))` (src/core/crypto.ts:30), and APP_ID_RE at src/server/routes.ts:56 forbids ':' so no (appId, email) pair can be re-parsed into a colliding salt across tenants. Verified by tests/audit-crypto.test.ts "H2 RESOLVED".

The client-side email normalization in the salt (`email.toLowerCase().trim()`, crypto.ts:30) is byte-identical to the server-side index normalization (`normalizeEmail`, src/storage/store.ts:67-69), so an account can never resolve to a record whose app key it cannot derive.

AES-256-GCM IV handling is correct: a fresh 12-byte `crypto.getRandomValues` IV per encryption (crypto.ts:74-75), no counter, no key/IV reuse across calls, and the IV is transported alongside the ciphertext. Volume per key is a handful of wallets, far below any GCM birthday bound.

The `iv:ct` format is unambiguous by construction — b64urlEncode strips padding and emits only [A-Za-z0-9-_] (crypto.ts:53), so ':' can never appear inside a component, and `parts.length !== 2` correctly rejects both extra and missing colons.

`timingSafeEqual` (crypto.ts:155-166) is correct: it folds the length XOR into the accumulator up front, scans the full max-length window substituting 0 past the end of the shorter string (no charCodeAt→NaN dependence, audit F8), and has no early exit. Handles multi-byte and surrogate-pair strings safely since it compares UTF-16 code units.

`hashSessionToken` (crypto.ts:138-140) correctly uses a bare SHA-256 rather than a KDF — the input is `randomHex(32)`, 256 bits of CSPRNG output, so stretching would add per-request latency for no security gain. The reasoning is documented in-line and matches the API-key/PAT precedent.

`randomHex` (crypto.ts:96-106) fails closed with an explicit throw when `globalThis.crypto.getRandomValues` is missing rather than silently degrading to Math.random, and it is the single source of session tokens and challenges.

Cross-protocol reuse of the appKey is properly domain-separated: the auth keypair seed is `sha256("ttc-auth-v1:" + appKey)` (src/client/authKey.ts:14-16) and the biometric wrap key is HKDF-SHA-256 with salt = credentialId bytes and info = "ttc-biometric-unlock-v1" (src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:57-73) — the raw appKey/PRF secret is never used directly as an AES key on the unlock path.

No key material is logged, thrown in messages, or persisted: `grep -rn "console\." src` finds only an appId-default nudge and storage warnings; the app key is memory-only behind a Symbol.for-keyed non-enumerable vault with idle/hide/freeze/bfcache auto-lock (src/client/session.ts), and `withDecryptedKey` (src/client/wallet.ts:100-111) plus `useExportKey`'s 30s auto-clear keep plaintext lifetimes tight. `useSolanaSigner` even zeroes the derived secretKey with `kp.secretKey.fill(0)`.

src/core/offchainMessage.ts encodes both Ledger envelope layouts with strict bounds (`signerPublicKey.length !== 32`, `appDomain.length !== 32`, non-empty and ≤1212-byte body, printable-ASCII enforcement) and the server verifier at src/server/signature.ts:49-52 only widens the accepted PREIMAGE set — every candidate still embeds the single-use challenge and, for v0, the signer pubkey, so replay protection is unchanged.

src/server/signature.ts:10-13 explicitly rejects non-hex signature input rather than letting `parseInt` coerce garbage to zero bytes — the right pattern (which is exactly what makes its absence in `appKeyToBytes` a finding).

src/ui/passkey.ts is a well-built CSPRNG generator: `getRandomValues` only, a hard 16-byte (128-bit) floor with NaN/fractional inputs normalized before allocation, and an unbiased base-256→base-58 long-division encoder (no modulo bias).

Parameter binding is genuinely complete for values: every statement in src/storage/sql/engine.ts is a template with `?` placeholders rewritten by `this.sql()` (engine.ts:50-54) and every value arrives via the `params` array — I traced all nine AuthStore methods and found no value concatenation. tests/sql-dialects.test.ts:105-114 enforces this mechanically across all three dialects.

Expiry is enforced on the read path everywhere it matters: `getSession` carries `AND expires_at > ?` (engine.ts:205), and both `takeChallenge` branches do too (engine.ts:153 RETURNING path, engine.ts:165 MySQL locking path). `sweepExpired` is explicitly space-reclamation only and never the expiry authority.

Atomic challenge-consume is correct on both paths: `DELETE … RETURNING challenge` on Postgres/SQLite (engine.ts:153) and `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` + `DELETE` inside a real transaction on MySQL (engine.ts:162-176), with `supportsReturning: false` driving the switch. src/storage/conformance.ts:170-182 asserts exactly one of eight concurrent callers observes the value.

The email index is structurally race-free: `PRIMARY KEY (email, app_id)` in all three DDLs means concurrent registrations of one email under different `appId`s touch different rows — a lost write is impossible rather than merely avoided (postgres.ts:67-72, mysql.ts:72-77, sqlite.ts:59-64), and `putUser` writes the record and the index in one transaction (engine.ts:97-113).

MySQL's case-insensitive-collation hazard is handled correctly and at the right layer: every key column is `VARBINARY` (not `utf8mb4_bin`, which is PAD SPACE — the comment at mysql.ts:55-57 gets this exactly right), `normalizeEmail()` is applied in application code on both the write (engine.ts:110) and the read (engine.ts:122) rather than delegated to a collation, and preflight errors on any non-binary key column (mysql.ts:154-167).

The rate-limit window `CASE` is correct and atomic — one statement, and an expired row starts a fresh window instead of resuming a stale count (engine.ts:251-254), which is the permanent-lockout bug the KV port had to self-heal around. Covered by src/storage/conformance.ts:107-144.

`LIMIT` interpolation in `deleteExpiredLimited` is safe by construction on all three dialects: `Math.max(1, limit | 0)` coerces to int32 before concatenation (postgres.ts:46, mysql.ts:47, sqlite.ts:42).

Column sizing matches the server's input validation, so MySQL strict mode fails closed rather than truncating: `appId` regex caps at 64 chars vs `VARBINARY(64)`, email is rejected above 320 chars (routes.ts:59) vs `VARBINARY(320)`, wallet publicKey capped at 128 (routes.ts:191) vs `VARBINARY(128)`, `generateChallenge()` is `randomHex(32)` = 64 chars vs `VARBINARY(128)`, and SHA-256 hex token digests are exactly 64 chars vs `VARBINARY(64)`.

The session value is stored as typed `public_key` and `fingerprint` columns rather than the KV port's `"publicKey|fingerprint"` string, removing a correctness dependency on public keys never containing `|` (engine.ts:185-195), and tests/sql-dialects.test.ts:143-149 asserts it.

SQLite preflight refuses to boot when the DB file sits under a web-served directory and warns on group/other-readable file modes (sqlite.ts:114-143) — a genuinely non-obvious check for a file that is the entire credential store.

`getUser` scopes every read by `app_id` and the users/sessions/challenges/rate-limit tables are all keyed `(app_id, …)`, so cross-tenant reads are structurally impossible; conformance covers the `Acme`/`acme` and `myapp`/`myapp.example` collision cases (conformance.ts:329-384).

APP_ID SEPARATOR IS GENUINELY CLOSED ON THE SHIPPED ROUTES. `APP_ID_RE = /^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$/` (src/server/routes.ts:56) excludes ':' and bounds length, and I traced `validateAppId` being called before any store access on every entry point — /challenge:205, /register:255, /login:347, /login-wallet:393, /connect-wallet:438, /search-wallet:511, and `headerAppId()`:158-161 for /logout, /user-data, /import-wallet — including the `config.appId` fallback path. So the classic `appId="a" + key="b:c"` vs `appId="a:b" + key="c"` collision is not reachable through the SDK's own handlers.

THE OTHER KEY SEGMENTS ARE EQUALLY UNAMBIGUOUS. `validatePublicKey` (src/server/routes.ts:71-85) requires canonical base58 that round-trips to exactly 32 bytes, so the `id` segment of `appScoped` can contain neither ':' nor '|'; session keys use a 64-hex SHA-256 digest computed server-side (src/server/session.ts:89). That is what makes `decodeSession`'s split on the first '|' (src/storage/store.ts:285-288) safe, and it keeps the `pubKey:` and `session:` keyspaces provably disjoint under the shipped defaults.

UNVALIDATED HEADER INPUT CANNOT REACH A KEY. `verifySession` (src/server/session.ts:87-98) checks `session.publicKey !== publicKey` BEFORE calling `store.getUser(appId, publicKey)`, so the un-validated `ttc-public-key` header value can only reach the store if it exactly equals a stored (already-validated) session owner.

ATOMIC GET-AND-DELETE IS A SINGLE PRIMITIVE. `takeChallenge` is one `GETDEL` (src/storage/store.ts:217-221), which is natively atomic on ioredis, Upstash and Vercel KV, and single-turn on MemoryAdapter; the conformance suite pins it with an 8-way concurrent case (conformance.ts:170-182) and the negative control proves the case actually fails a get-then-delete store (tests/storage-conformance-negative.test.ts).

MEMORYADAPTER ENFORCES EXPIRY ON READ, ON EVERY PATH. `alive()` (src/storage/memory.ts:17-25) is called by `get`, `incr`, `expire` and `getdel`, so an expired key is indistinguishable from an absent one without any sweeper (adapter invariant 1). `incr` on an expired key returns 1 with the stale TTL dropped (memory.ts:47-52, invariant 2), `incr` on a live key preserves `current?.expiresAt` (invariant 3), and `expire` on an absent/expired key is a no-op because `alive()` returns undefined (invariant 4). All four are the exact invariants adapter.ts:29-46 documents.

THE PERMANENT-LOCKOUT AND SLIDING-WINDOW BUGS ARE BOTH FIXED AND REGRESSION-TESTED. `KvAuthStore.hitRateLimit` self-heals a TTL-less counter exactly once per window at `count === maxAttempts + 1` (src/storage/store.ts:250-266) rather than on every over-limit hit; tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts drives a 10-minute trickle attack against the real KvAuthStore+MemoryAdapter and asserts the victim recovers, and tests/rate-limit-self-extend.test.ts covers the window-extension variant.

RATE LIMITING FAILS CLOSED BY CONSTRUCTION. `checkRateLimit` (src/server/rateLimit.ts:25-31) is a bare delegation with a deliberate no-try/catch comment, so a store error 500s the request instead of granting permission.

THE EMAIL INDEX IS A PER-FIELD HASH WRITE. `hset(emailKey(email), appId, publicKey)` (src/storage/store.ts:203) plus the `StorageAdapter.hset` contract (adapter.ts:76-83) eliminates the read-merge-write lost-registration race, and conformance.ts:303-325 tests two concurrent same-email/different-app registrations against it.

FEATURE DETECTION STAYS TRUTHFUL THROUGH THE WRAPPER. `KvAuthStore` assigns `sweepExpired`/`close` in the constructor body only when the wrapped adapter has them (src/storage/store.ts:166-173), so `KvAuthStore` over `RedisAdapter` correctly reports no `sweepExpired` (pinned by tests/v050-storage-seam.test.ts:152-158).

THE PRODUCTION BACKEND GUARD IS PURE AND TESTED. `selectStorageBackend()` throws rather than falling back to `redis://localhost:6379` when `NODE_ENV==='production'` with no recognized backend (src/storage/resolve.ts:47-53), warns on a partial Upstash config (resolve.ts:33-38), and deliberately orders Upstash before Vercel KV; tests/storage.test.ts:31-90 covers all of it without opening a connection.

THE CONFORMANCE SUITE HAS A NEGATIVE CONTROL. tests/storage-conformance-negative.test.ts implements a plausible-but-wrong `AuthStore` with five specific bugs and asserts the suite catches each — which is what elevates the suite from decoration to an actual acceptance bar, and is rarer than it should be.

Challenge handling is correct: `consumeChallenge` requires an ATOMIC `takeChallenge` get-and-delete and does the comparison itself in constant time (src/server/challenge.ts:33-35), with `timingSafeEqual` folding the length difference into the accumulator instead of early-returning (src/core/crypto.ts:155-166). Replay of a spent challenge is covered by tests/server.test.ts:241-266 and tests/audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts:216.

Verify-before-consume ordering is right on all four signature routes (register:306-312, login:369-372, loginWallet:401-404, connectWallet:450-453): a forged signature never reaches `consumeChallenge`, so an attacker cannot burn a victim's pending challenge, and rate-limit counters are only touched on failure so a valid login is never throttled (tests/audit-server.test.ts:144).

`hexToBytes` fails loudly on odd length and on non-hex characters instead of silently coercing garbage to zero bytes (src/server/signature.ts:8-12) — the comment explicitly reasons about the `parseInt("GG",16)` → NaN → 0 trap. Covered by tests/signature-edge-cases.test.ts:20-40.

`validatePublicKey` requires a canonical base58 round-trip (`pk.toBase58() !== key`, src/server/routes.ts:80), which rejects the short/left-padded encodings `new PublicKey()` would otherwise accept, and rejects EVM `0x…` addresses because `0` is not in the base58 alphabet.

The off-chain envelope multi-candidate acceptance is genuinely NOT a trust widening, as its comment claims (src/server/signature.ts:26-35). I verified: every candidate from `offchainMessageCandidates` embeds the same server-issued single-use challenge, the verifier supplies `pubKeyBytes` itself (line 45) rather than taking a signer from the envelope, and both headers begin with the 0xFF signing domain (src/core/offchainMessage.ts:34-40) which cannot prefix a valid Solana transaction message — so a transaction signature can never be replayed through this path.

No message-format confusion between the two login messages: `walletLoginMessage` ("Sign this message to verify wallet ownership: …") and `authLoginMessage` ("Sign in to your TTC account: …") have disjoint prefixes and are verified against disjoint key material (identity base58 vs stored `authPublicKey` hex). `login` also gates on `!!user?.authPublicKey` (src/server/routes.ts:370), so a wallet-only account can never be logged into via the email path.

The email/biometric auth key is implicitly domain-separated even though `authLoginMessage` carries no appId: the ed25519 auth seed is derived from the appKey (src/client/authKey.ts:14-20), and the appKey's PBKDF2 salt is `SHA-256(appId:email)` (src/core/crypto.ts:30) / a WebAuthn-PRF secret bound to `rpId` (src/client/webauthn.ts:61-63). So the relay attack in finding 1 does NOT extend to email or biometric accounts — only to the wallet path, whose key is the same across every app.

Sessions carry only a SHA-256 digest server-side (src/core/crypto.ts:138-140, src/server/session.ts:55-62), are app-scoped, and a token minted by one app is rejected by another (tests/multi-app.test.ts:152-167).

EVM is correctly excluded from authentication rather than half-implemented: `grep -rn "viem|verifyMessage|recoverAddress|secp256k1|ethers|personal_sign" src/` shows viem only in src/client/wallet.ts and src/react/useEvmSigner.ts (key generation and local signing), never server-side, and EVM addresses are rejected as identities on every route (tests/evm-verification.test.ts). So EIP-191/EIP-712 prefixing, high-s malleability, and checksum handling are non-issues by design here.

No `Math.random` anywhere in src/ — `grep -rn 'Math.random' src/ tests/` returns only comments asserting its absence (src/ui/passkey.ts:10-11,87,95) and one test title. All randomness is WebCrypto: src/core/crypto.ts:96-106 (`randomHex` throws rather than falling back if `getRandomValues` is missing), src/core/crypto.ts:74-75 (96-bit GCM IV), src/client/webauthn.ts:39-43, src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:151-155.

Solana key generation is sound: `Keypair.generate()` (src/client/wallet.ts:38) routes to tweetnacl -> `crypto.getRandomValues`. Reconstruction is validated — `Keypair.fromSecretKey` (node_modules/@solana/web3.js/lib/index.cjs.js:8984-8998) rejects a wrong byte length and recomputes the public key from the scalar, comparing all 32 bytes, so a corrupted plaintext from `hexToBytes` throws instead of silently producing a signing key for the wrong account.

EVM key generation is sound and range-checked: `generatePrivateKey()` (src/client/wallet.ts:50) -> viem -> `secp256k1.utils.randomPrivateKey` -> `randomSecretKey` in @noble/curves/abstract/weierstrass.js:909-911, which does `mapHashToField(randomBytes(lengths.seed), Fn.ORDER)` over a 48-byte seed — uniform in [1, n-1], no modulo bias, never zero or >= n. `privateKeyToAccount` then re-validates.

The app key is genuinely memory-only. `setSession` (src/client/session.ts:196-212) writes only token, public key, email and iteration count to localStorage and never the appKey; `grep -rn 'localStorage.setItem|sessionStorage' src/` confirms no key material is written to web storage anywhere in the package. A page reload starts a new realm with an empty vault, so there is nothing to rehydrate — asserted by tests/audit-client-vault.test.ts:47-114 (H3 and CLIENTVAULT-3/4 resolved).

The non-custodial claim holds on the wire. Every outbound body is enumerable: register (src/client/authClient.ts:238-245), login (:268), login-wallet (:321-325), connect-wallet (:349-354), registerWithWallet (:374-380), registerWithBiometric (:400-407). They carry public keys, `flattenBundle(bundle)` ciphertext, challenges, signatures and `deriveAuthPublicKey(appKey)` — never the appKey, never the passkey, never a wallet secret. `flattenBundle` (src/client/wallet.ts:77-84) can only emit `EncryptedWallet` records whose secret field is the output of `encryptSecret`.

Wallet secrets are encrypted with authenticated AES-256-GCM via native WebCrypto before leaving the browser (src/core/crypto.ts:72-93), and `decryptSecret` fails closed on a wrong key or tampered ciphertext. The biometric-unlock blob uses the same AEAD with an HKDF-SHA-256-derived, non-extractable wrapping key (src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:59-91).

The app key is read at CALL time inside each `useSigner` callback and never captured at render (src/react/useSigner.ts:22-41, `const appKey = getAppKey();` in each of `decrypt`/`solanaKeypair`/`sign`) — a lock that races a render cannot leave a stale key usable. `lockSnapshot()` (session.ts:272-276) is deliberately side-effect-free so `useSyncExternalStore` cannot loop.

Cross-tab coordination leaks nothing. The only cross-tab channel is the same-origin `storage` event (src/client/session.ts:166-171); the sentinel `ttc_lock_signal` is a bare `Date.now()` timestamp (line 242) explicitly documented as 'never a secret'. `grep -rn 'postMessage|BroadcastChannel' src/` finds no key material on any message channel — the only `postMessage` is the opt-in React-Native-WebView export bridge (src/ui/ExportKeyPanel.tsx:31-35), which requires the integrator to set `postToReactNativeWebView`. There is no path by which one tab can be induced to hand key material to another origin.

Auto-lock coverage is unusually thorough for the events it does bind: `visibilitychange`, Page-Lifecycle `freeze`, `pagehide`, and — the subtle one — `pageshow` with `event.persisted` to force a re-lock after a bfcache restore that would otherwise revive the JS heap with a hot key (src/client/session.ts:144-161). The idle path also has a lazy safety net in `isLocked()` (:256-263) for when timers were paused in a backgrounded tab.

`revealSecret` correctly never touches the ambient key: it derives a one-time key from a fresh ceremony and returns without arming (src/client/authClient.ts:191-198), so Reveal -> Hide -> Reveal re-prompts each time and a reveal cannot silently extend the signing window. Asserted by tests/auth-client.test.ts:225 and tests/react-hooks.test.tsx:124-147. `useExportKey` auto-clears revealed plaintext after 30s by default (src/react/useExportKey.ts:46,84-92).

Honest documentation where it counts: src/client/wallet.ts:97-99 states plainly that JS strings cannot be truly zeroed rather than claiming zeroization, and src/ui/ExportKeyPanel.tsx:10-12 warns that any script on the reveal page can read the plaintext and tells integrators to enforce a strong CSP.

The `{ registration }` vs `{ biometricUnlock }` confusion — feeding a biometric-PRIMARY credential to an email/web3 account would derive the wrong key and lock the user out — is called out at length in the type doc (src/client/authClient.ts:36-44) and enforced by a dedicated DISTINCTION GUARD test (tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:321).

`checkRateLimit` delegates the whole decision to the store with NO try/catch, so a backend failure propagates and 500s the request instead of granting permission — fail-closed by construction (src/server/rateLimit.ts:21-31)

The SQL window semantics are correct on all three dialects: `count = CASE WHEN expires_at <= ? THEN 1 ELSE count + 1 END` with a matching CASE on expires_at makes an expired row start a FRESH window in one atomic upsert, structurally preventing the permanent-lockout bug (src/storage/sql/engine.ts:251-258); parameter order is correct for MySQL's left-to-right ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE evaluation and for Postgres/SQLite's bare-table reference in ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
Buckets are ENDPOINT-scoped, so exhausting the `login` failure bucket cannot lock a victim out of `/challenge` (src/server/routes.ts:121-123, tests/audit-server.test.ts:144-167)

Verify-first / penalize-on-failure on /login, /login-wallet and /connect-wallet: a valid credential is never charged to the counter, and a junk signature never reaches `consumeChallenge` so it cannot burn a pending challenge (src/server/routes.ts:359-379, 398-419, 447-462)

`clientIp` takes the RIGHTMOST x-forwarded-for entry after `trustedProxyHops`, not the leftmost, so a client-prepended XFF entry cannot spoof the bucket; proxy headers are ignored entirely by default (src/server/http.ts:25-37, tests/clientip-proxy.test.ts:26-61)

The KV self-heal was correctly narrowed from `count > maxAttempts` to `count === maxAttempts + 1`, killing the sustained self-extension DoS in which one request per window held a named account locked forever (src/storage/store.ts:250-266, tests/rate-limit-sustained-lockout.test.ts)

Client-supplied `pbkdf2Iterations` is bounded server-side to [100_000, 1_000_000] before being pinned, so a malicious client cannot kneecap its own account's KDF cost (src/server/routes.ts:96-100, 273-275)

`validateWallets` bounds the array at 16 entries and `encryptedSecret` at 8192 chars, and /import-wallet enforces `maxWalletsPerUser` (64) before appending — the SERVERSIDE-4 unbounded-import fix holds (src/server/routes.ts:182-197, 534-536)

`appId` is validated against a strict charset that forbids ':' and whitespace and is length-bounded BEFORE it is concatenated into any storage key, with `allowedAppIds` available as a production allowlist (src/server/routes.ts:56, 63-69)

`selectStorageBackend` throws rather than silently falling back to an ephemeral per-instance store in production, so rate-limit counters can never quietly become per-instance (src/storage/resolve.ts:47-53)

Session tokens are opaque 256-bit CSPRNG values and ONLY their SHA-256 digest is persisted, both as the session key and as `UserData.authTokenHash` — a database read (backup, replica, world-readable Supabase schema, slow-query log) yields no replayable credential. src/core/crypto.ts:109-140, src/server/session.ts:55-62. The rationale for a bare hash over a KDF (256 bits of uniform entropy, nothing to stretch against) is correct and well argued.

No session fixation is possible: the token is generated server-side by `generateSessionToken()` and there is no code path anywhere in src/server/routes.ts by which a client-supplied value becomes a session identifier. `publicUser()` strips both `authTokenHash` and the legacy `authToken` from every response (src/server/routes.ts:168-171), and `asResult` takes the raw token as an explicit argument rather than reading it back off the mutated record (src/server/routes.ts:176-178).

The raw token never appears in a URL, a query string, or an error body. It travels only in the `ttc-auth-token` request header (src/client/session.ts:341-348); `searchWallet` is the only GET taking query params and it takes a public key, not a token (src/server/routes.ts:506-521); `error()` emits fixed strings with no request echo (src/server/http.ts:10-12). No referrer/log/URL leak path exists.

Cross-app session scoping is correct and tested. Sessions are keyed `session:{appId}:{tokenHash}` via `appScoped()` (src/server/keys.ts:12-14) in a keyspace disjoint from `pubKey:`, appId is validated against `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$` (which forbids the ':' separator) BEFORE it reaches a key, and `headerAppId` fails closed to null → 401 on a malformed value (src/server/routes.ts:56, 158-161). tests/multi-app.test.ts:152-167 proves a token minted by app A is 401 under app B's header.

Expiry-is-enforced-on-read is elevated to a first-class, testable invariant of the storage port rather than left to a sweeper. src/storage/store.ts:73-91 states it normatively; SqlAuthStore carries `expires_at > ?` on every session/challenge SELECT with the app clock bound as a parameter (src/storage/sql/engine.ts:198-213); MemoryAdapter enforces it lazily in `alive()` (src/storage/memory.ts:17-25); and `sweepExpired` is explicitly demoted to space reclamation. tests/sql-dialects.test.ts:124-131 asserts every expiry-bearing read filters, and tests/storage-conformance-negative.test.ts:114 has a dedicated "an expired session is invisible" case.

UA-fingerprint enforcement is correctly per-SESSION rather than per-CONFIG: `verifySession` enforces whenever `session.fingerprint` is set, regardless of the current flag, so disabling `bindSessionToUserAgent` never silently un-binds live sessions — and tests/session-fingerprint.test.ts:88-98 pins exactly that. The fingerprint comparison itself uses `timingSafeEqual`. The config comment is also refreshingly honest that the UA is spoofable and is "a speed bump, not a control" (src/core/config.ts:110-117).

`verifySession` fails closed at every step and independently re-reads the user record, so a session whose owner has been deleted returns null → 401 (src/server/session.ts:87-98). `logout` never leaks whether the presented token was valid (constant 200 `{ok:true}`), and revocation goes through `hashSessionToken` so the store never sees the raw token (src/server/session.ts:102-104).

Client-side logout is complete and correctly ordered: auth headers are captured BEFORE the local teardown, the request uses `keepalive: true` so it survives page unload (sendBeacon cannot carry custom headers), and `clearSession()` drops the in-memory app key, all four localStorage keys, and fires registered cleanup hooks — which biometricUnlock uses to purge its wrapped-key blob and gate secret (src/client/authClient.ts:456-473, src/client/session.ts:305-323, src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:225-234). tests/client-logout.test.ts verifies the ordering and the keepalive flag.

The verify-first / penalize-on-failure ordering in login, loginWallet and connectWallet is a genuinely good design: the storage-free ed25519 check runs before `consumeChallenge`, so a forged signature can never burn a victim's pending challenge, and a valid login is never throttled by an attacker's failed attempts (src/server/routes.ts:359-379, 398-419, 447-462). `register` was brought into line with this for the wallet path (WI-5, routes.ts:303-312).

Verify-before-consume on every authenticated flow: login (routes.ts:369-372), loginWallet (401-404), connectWallet (450-453) and even the wallet branch of register (306-312) check the ed25519 signature before calling consumeChallenge, so a junk signature can neither burn a victim's pending challenge nor feed the failure counter. tests/audit-server.test.ts:144-167 proves the victim's correct login still succeeds after an attacker exhausts the limit.

Challenge consumption is a single atomic get-and-delete delegated to the store (src/server/challenge.ts:27-36 over KvAuthStore.takeChallenge / GETDEL at storage/store.ts:217-221), with the constant-time compare done in the SDK and never in the backend. Atomicity is an explicitly documented AuthStore invariant (store.ts:84-86) and a required conformance case; tests/concurrent-safety.test.ts:47-75 shows two concurrent consumes cannot both win.

Sessions are opaque 256-bit random tokens whose SHA-256 digest alone is persisted (session.ts:55-62, crypto.ts:138-140), sessions are app-scoped in the key (appScoped(session:, appId, tokenHash)), each login revokes the prior session by its stored hash, and verifySession additionally requires the presented publicKey to match the session's owner (session.ts:91). A database reader gets digests, not replayable credentials.

publicUser() strips both `authTokenHash` and the legacy `authToken` from every response (routes.ts:168-171), and issueSession actively deletes the pre-v0.5.0 raw-token field from records it rewrites (session.ts:68).

publicKey validation is genuinely strict rather than a regex: `new PublicKey(key)` plus a `toBase58()` round-trip rejects short left-padded inputs, non-canonical base58 and 0x EVM addresses (routes.ts:71-85), which is what closes the old `session:`-prefix keyspace-collision vector (tests/audit-server.test.ts:170-190).

appId is validated against a charset excluding ':' and whitespace and is length-bounded BEFORE it is ever concatenated into a storage key (routes.ts:52-56, keys.ts), so an attacker-supplied appId cannot escape its namespace even though the value is attacker-influenced.

The server-side PBKDF2 iteration band (routes.ts:96-100, 273-275) refuses a client attempt to pin a weak count, and is type-checked with `typeof n === "number" && Number.isInteger(n)` — exactly the guard the string validators are missing. Covered by tests/audit-zai-fixes.test.ts and audit-zai-glm-52.test.ts (F3).

Rate-limit buckets are endpoint-scoped and per-target, and the IP leg is skipped unless trustProxyHeaders is on, so a shared "unknown" bucket can never become a global lockout (routes.ts:115-141, H5). checkRateLimit deliberately has no try/catch so a store failure 500s rather than failing open (rateLimit.ts:20-23).

clientIp takes the RIGHTMOST x-forwarded-for entry after trustedProxyHops rather than the client-controlled leftmost one, and ignores proxy headers entirely by default (http.ts:25-37) — spoofing XFF buys nothing, as tests/server.test.ts:353-368 demonstrates.

Session UA-binding is enforced whenever a fingerprint is STORED, independent of the current config flag, so turning bindSessionToUserAgent off never silently un-binds live sessions (routes.ts:143-152, session.ts:92-97).
getUser guards JSON.parse and returns null on a malformed stored value rather than throwing (storage/store.ts:190-198), so a corrupted record cannot crash an authenticated request path.

PRF mode is a genuine cryptographic gate, not a UI check: the PRF output IS the app key (src/client/authClient.ts:392) and is imported directly as the AES-256-GCM wallet key (src/core/crypto.ts:65-67), so a patched client that skips the ceremony gets no key. The PRF secret is never persisted anywhere — it is re-derived per unlock (src/client/webauthn.ts:140-144).

The biometric-PRIMARY vs biometric-UNLOCK distinction is correctly implemented and explicitly guarded: `{ registration }` yields the raw secret while `{ biometricUnlock }` unwraps a stored key (src/client/authClient.ts:154-164), and tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:321 asserts the two resolve to DIFFERENT keys for the same credential.

The unlock wrap uses HKDF-SHA-256 with a versioned info string rather than the raw secret as an AES key (src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:59-74, `HKDF_INFO = "ttc-biometric-unlock-v1"`), and the wrapping key is derived non-extractable.

All unwrap paths use authenticated AES-256-GCM and fail closed: a tampered blob, a wrong secret, or a missing blob all throw with no fallback (src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:101-109), verified by tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:247 and :263 which additionally assert `getAppKey()` is still null after the failure (no partial/garbage key ever armed).

`userVerification: "required"` and `authenticatorAttachment: "platform"` are requested on both registration and assertion, and assertions are scoped with `allowCredentials` to the single registered credential (src/client/webauthn.ts:83-87, 127-130).

`enableBiometricUnlock` refuses to wrap a key it does not currently hold — `getAppKey()` null throws `VaultLockedError` (src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:175-176), so the feature cannot be used to mint a blob without a live authenticated ceremony first. Covered by tests/biometric-unlock.test.ts:239.
`revealSecret` derives a one-time key and never arms the vault (src/client/authClient.ts:191-198), so a biometric reveal does not silently extend the signing window.

The IndexedDB version/schema race between webauthn.ts and biometricUnlock.ts is correctly handled with a single shared opener at DB_VERSION 2 creating both stores idempotently (src/client/webauthn.ts:182-195).

The gate-mode legacy plaintext record is migrated in place on first read and the readable copy is overwritten (src/client/webauthn.ts:236-239), with a real end-to-end test against an IndexedDB shim (tests/webauthn-migration.test.ts:113-138).

Logout fires a purge hook for the unlock blob, the gate secret, and both localStorage descriptors (src/client/biometricUnlock.ts:225-234 and src/react/useBiometricUnlock.ts:46), removing the sync marker first so a half-completed purge cannot report `hasBiometricUnlock() === true`.

Storage backend selection FAILS CLOSED in production: `selectStorageBackend()` throws rather than silently falling back to redis://localhost:6379 when no backend env is wired (src/storage/resolve.ts:47-53), and the function is deliberately kept pure so the guard is unit-testable — covered by tests/storage.test.ts:55-58 including the partial-Upstash case at :82-89.

SQL storage refuses to boot on error-level preflight findings (`PreflightError`, src/storage/sql/index.ts:61-64), and the `skipPreflight` escape hatch is documented with an unambiguous "**Do not do this.**" naming the exact failures it catches (world-readable Supabase table, non-strict MySQL truncating wallet blobs, SQLite under public/).

`trustProxyHeaders` correctly defaults to **false** (src/core/config.ts:163), so x-forwarded-for cannot be spoofed to dodge per-IP limits by default, and when enabled the client IP is taken from the RIGHTMOST entry after `trustedProxyHops` rather than the client-controlled leftmost (src/server/http.ts:25-37) — tested in tests/clientip-proxy.test.ts and tests/server.test.ts:366.

`securityLevel` defaults to 2 = 600k PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, meeting OWASP 2023, and the default is pinned by test rather than left to drift (tests/audit-crypto.test.ts:41-42, tests/pbkdf2-iteration-cost.test.ts:89).

The server does not trust the client's PBKDF2 iteration count: `validIterations` clamps it to [100k, 1M] before pinning (src/server/routes.ts:96-100, 273-275), closing the client-side downgrade path (audit F3).

`APP_ID_RE = /^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$/` forbids the `:` key separator and bounds length, so an attacker-supplied appId cannot escape its storage namespace (src/server/routes.ts:56) — tested in tests/multi-app.test.ts:171-186.

No hardcoded secrets, keys, or credentials anywhere in src/ (verified by grep). `.gitignore` correctly excludes `.env` and `.env.*` with a `!.env.example` exception, and `.env.example` contains only placeholder variable names with no values.

Build/publish hygiene: `sourcemap: false` in tsup.config.ts is deliberate with a comment explaining that `files: ["dist"]` would otherwise publish .map files and the original TypeScript in the tarball; `npm pack --dry-run` confirms the tarball is dist/ + LICENSE + package.json only.

The conformance test kit is given its own tsup entry and is deliberately NOT re-exported from `storage/index.ts`, so a test harness can never be pulled into a production server bundle (src/storage/index.ts:19-21, tsup.config.ts entry map).

`createAuthHandlers` fails closed when neither `store` nor `storage` is supplied — it throws rather than defaulting to an in-memory store (src/server/routes.ts:109-113), so a misconfigured deployment cannot silently run on ephemeral per-instance state.

`bindSessionToUserAgent` is honestly documented as "Defense-in-depth only… a speed bump, not a control" with the re-login trade-off spelled out, and enforcement is per-session so disabling the flag never retroactively un-binds live sessions (src/core/config.ts:107-118, src/server/session.ts:92-97).

No XSS sinks anywhere in the UI layer: `grep -rn "dangerouslySetInnerHTML|innerHTML|eval(|new Function|document.write" src/` returns zero hits. Every secret surface (ExportKeyPanel's `secretBlock`, EmailMethod's `passkeyReveal`) renders through React's escaping text path.

Auth is a pure custom-header bearer scheme with zero cookie usage (`grep -rni "cookie" src/` -> no hits), and the SDK emits no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. That makes `logout`, `user-data` and `import-wallet` structurally CSRF-immune: a cross-origin page cannot set `ttc-auth-token` on a simple request and cannot pass a preflight. This is the right architectural choice and it is what makes the missing anti-CSRF token a non-issue rather than a gap.

`verifySession` fails closed on every path: `if (!token || !publicKey) return null;`, session-miss returns null, publicKey mismatch returns null, and a stored UA fingerprint is compared with `timingSafeEqual` and enforced even if `config.bindSessionToUserAgent` was later turned off (src/server/session.ts:87-98).

`publicUser()` strips both `authToken` and `authTokenHash` from every user record before it leaves the server (src/server/routes.ts:168-171), so `/user-data` — the response the React `AuthProvider` caches in context — never echoes session material back into the DOM tree.

`clientIp()` ignores `x-forwarded-for` / `x-real-ip` entirely by default (`if (!trustProxyHeaders) return "unknown";`) and, when trusted, takes the rightmost-after-hops entry so a client-prepended leftmost value is never honoured. tests/clientip-proxy.test.ts covers spoofed leftmost entries (line 31), negative-index hops (line 51), whitespace/empty entries (line 43) and the fallback chain — this is genuinely well covered.

`useSigner` reads the app key at CALL time inside each callback, never captures it at render, and subscribes to lock transitions via `useSyncExternalStore` with a pure `lockSnapshot()` that does not mutate or reschedule. Verified by tests/react-hooks.test.tsx:80-97 (throws when locked, flips on arm/lock).

`useExportKey.reveal` never touches the ambient session key — it calls `client.revealSecret`, which derives a one-time key from a fresh ceremony and does NOT arm the vault. tests/react-hooks.test.tsx:144 asserts `getAppKey()` is still null after a successful reveal, so Reveal -> Hide -> Reveal genuinely re-authenticates each time.

`postToReactNativeWebView` defaults to `false` with an explicit written rationale (src/ui/types.ts:258-269), so a generic web consumer never exfiltrates a revealed private key to an ambient `window.ReactNativeWebView` bridge; RN hosts must opt in.

Both passkey inputs use `type="password"` with correct `autoComplete` values, and `ExportKeyPanel` clears the typed passkey immediately after use (`setPasskey(""); // never keep the typed passkey around after use`, line 102). EmailMethod also clears its revealed generated passkey on unmount (lines 60-62).

No secret is ever logged: the only `console.*` calls in `src/` are three benign configuration warnings (src/storage/resolve.ts:35, src/storage/sql/index.ts:68, src/client/authClient.ts:125 — the default-`appId` nudge). Error strings rendered into the DOM by EmailMethod/WalletMethod/ExportKeyPanel come from fixed server messages or the fixed "Re-authentication failed — wrong credentials", never from key material.

`AuthProvider.refetchUser` uses a monotonic `fetchSeq` ref so a stale in-flight `/user-data` response cannot overwrite a newer one, and bumps the sequence when `publicKey` goes null so a response arriving after logout is discarded (src/react/AuthProvider.tsx:56-90).

Minimal runtime dependency surface, exactly pinned. `npm audit --json | .metadata.dependencies` reports `"prod": 2` — the SDK plus a single runtime dep, `@noble/hashes`, pinned EXACTLY (package.json:96 `"@noble/hashes": "2.2.0"`, no caret). That package has zero transitive deps of its own (`"dependencies": {}`) and no advisories against 2.2.0. This is about as small a shipped attack surface as an auth SDK can have.

Signature verification FAILS CLOSED on a missing dependency. `tweetnacl` and `@solana/web3.js` are STATIC top-level imports (src/server/signature.ts:2-3 `import { PublicKey } from "@solana/web3.js"; import nacl from "tweetnacl";`) and are deliberately NOT listed in `peerDependenciesMeta` — unlike the 13 peers that are marked optional. A consumer who omits them gets a hard module-resolution failure at import time; there is no try/catch, no dynamic import, and no code path where verification degrades to a no-op or is skipped. This was the highest-priority thing to check and it is correct.

Every dynamic `import()` in the codebase fails closed. All six were traced: src/storage/resolve.ts:63/73/77 (`@upstash/redis`, `@vercel/kv`, `ioredis`) let the rejection propagate out of `resolveStorageAdapter`; src/ledger/transport.ts:28/32 falls WebUSB→WebHID and then throws an explicit error rather than returning a null transport; src/ledger/useSolanaLedger.ts:145 catches only to `setIsConnected(false)` and null the refs. None of them swallow a resolution failure into a success path.

GitHub Actions workflow is hardened against the standard attack classes. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` uses `on: [push, pull_request]` — NOT `pull_request_target`; declares least privilege `permissions: contents: read` (line 14-15); `grep -c "secrets\." ci.yml` returns 0 (no secrets referenced at all); and `grep -n "github.event" ci.yml` returns nothing, so there is no `${{ github.event.* }}` interpolated into any `run:` block — no script-injection surface. Service-container credentials are throwaway test values.

Install-script surface in the dependency tree is near-zero and lockfile-protected. A full recursive walk of node_modules found exactly 2 packages with preinstall/install/postinstall hooks: `better-sqlite3@12.11.1` (`prebuild-install || node-gyp rebuild`) and `esbuild@0.27.7` (`node install.js`) — both devDependencies, both version- and integrity-pinned in package-lock.json, and CI uses `npm ci` (ci.yml:103) so the lockfile is authoritative. No postinstall hook anywhere in the shipped path.

The `files: ["dist"]` allowlist and sourcemap-off decision are correct and verified end to end. tsup.config.ts:39-42 disables sourcemaps with an explicit rationale ("files:[\"dist\"] would otherwise publish .map files (and the original TS) in the npm tarball"). `npm pack --dry-run` confirms it: 59 files, 197.5 kB, and `find dist -name "*.map" -o -name "*.ts" ! -name "*.d.ts"` returns EMPTY — no source maps, no original TypeScript, no .env, no scripts/, no tests/ in the tarball.

tsup `external` list is comprehensive and defensive. All five storage backends, all four Ledger packages, and every crypto peer are externalized (tsup.config.ts:4-33), with the DB drivers listed as "belt-and-braces so a stray import can't bundle a database driver into dist" even though they are only structurally typed. Verified in the output: `dist/*.cjs` requires `@noble/hashes/*` rather than inlining, and no `pg`/`mysql2`/`better-sqlite3` code appears in dist.

The test-only conformance kit is correctly isolated as its own entry point (tsup.config.ts:58-60, "deliberately NOT re-exported from storage/index — a test kit must never be reachable from a production server bundle"), and reading src/storage/conformance.ts confirms it is framework-agnostic and contains no destructive primitive — no FLUSHDB, DROP, TRUNCATE, or bulk-clear; the only `DROP TABLE` string is a SQL-injection test fixture at line 393.

Dependabot covers both ecosystems that matter (.github/dependabot.yml: `npm` and `github-actions`, weekly), with dev-tooling grouped so security-relevant runtime bumps are not buried in toolchain-churn PRs.

CI runs the storage conformance suite against REAL Redis, Postgres, and MySQL service containers rather than mocks (ci.yml:37-90), and the suite asserts REDIS_URL is set in CI so a missing service cannot silently reduce it to zero test cases — a genuinely well-reasoned defense against a green-but-vacuous build.

Keyless by construction: nothing under src/ledger/ ever receives, stores, or transmits private key material -- only a 32-byte public key or a 64-byte signature. transport.ts explicitly refuses to instantiate an app class so the transport factory 'can never reach a signing API' (src/ledger/transport.ts:5-7, 17-20).

Fail-closed signature length check: assert64 rejects any non-64-byte device response before it is attached to a transaction, and this is proven by a real test (src/ledger/solanaSigner.ts:25-30; tests/ledger-signer.test.ts:170-178).

The cascade does not swallow real failures: any device error that is not a 0x6a81 header rejection (user rejected, locked, blind-sign required) is re-thrown immediately rather than being retried under a second envelope, so a user rejection cannot be silently converted into a second prompt (src/ledger/solanaSigner.ts:88-92; tests/ledger-signer.test.ts:157-168).

The 0xFF 'solana offchain' signing domain is correctly emitted at offset 0 of both envelopes, which is exactly the property that prevents a login signature from being replayable as a Solana transaction signature and vice versa -- the first byte makes the envelope an invalid transaction message under both the legacy and versioned parsers (src/core/offchainMessage.ts:34-40; verified byte-for-byte in tests/ledger-signer.test.ts:184-217).

The server's multi-candidate acceptance is genuinely not a trust widening: all three accepted preimages embed the single-use, server-issued challenge, the v0 candidate additionally embeds the signer public key, and every candidate is still verified against the presented public key -- so a signature over any other payload cannot verify as a login. Explicitly tested for cross-challenge and cross-key substitution (src/server/signature.ts:32-35, 50-52; tests/ledger-login.test.ts:66-79).

Challenge replay protection is unchanged on the hardware path: consumeChallenge does an atomic take-and-compare with a constant-time comparison, and loginWallet/connectWallet verify the signature before consuming so a forged signature cannot burn a victim's pending challenge (src/server/challenge.ts:27-36; src/server/routes.ts:398-404, 447-453).

VersionedTransaction signatures are defensively copied before being attached, so a later mutation or reuse of the device buffer cannot corrupt an already-attached signature (src/ledger/solanaSigner.ts:53-56).

Transport lifecycle is handled carefully: a re-entrancy ref guards overlapping connect() calls, any prior transport is closed before a new one opens, the transport is closed on probe failure, and the 'disconnect' event tears down refs so the hook never reports connected with a dead handle (src/ledger/useSolanaLedger.ts:107-109, 126-174).

@ledgerhq packages are optional peer deps loaded via dynamic import inside the hook, and transport.ts uses a type-only import, so no browser-only Ledger code executes during SSR and non-Ledger consumers do not pull it into their bundle (src/ledger/transport.ts:9-12, 25-41; src/ledger/index.ts:3-6).

The off-chain encoders are Uint8Array-only with no reliance on a global Buffer, and both reject empty messages, oversized messages, wrong-length signer keys, and wrong-length application domains before any byte assembly (src/core/offchainMessage.ts:30-32, 72-98, 140-149; tests/ledger-signer.test.ts:225-232).
